title: Nebraska Working People Party Chair Richards running for U.S. Senate herself
description: LINCOLN — The chair of the new Nebraska Working People Party will run for U.S. Senate herself as her party qualifies two other candidates for the November election. The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office confirmed that Robin Richards of Ralston filed for U.S. Senate. Richards was a Democratic write-in candidate for Legislative District 12 this […]
text:
Former legislative candidate Robin Richards of Ralston led creation of the Nebraska Working People Party. (Photos courtesy of Robin Richards for Nebraska campaign and the Nebraska Working People Party | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The chair of the new Nebraska Working People Party will run for U.S. Senate herself as her party qualifies two other candidates for the November election.
The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office confirmed that Robin Richards of Ralston filed for U.S. Senate. Richards was a Democratic write-in candidate for Legislative District 12 this spring. She was also the runner-up for the seat in 2022. She did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Richards joins a ticket that features U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., and registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn. The America First Party also nominated Chuck Conboy of Papillion. Nebraska Democrats chose not to replace Cindy Burbank of Omaha after she dropped out.
Kishla Askins of Omaha, who came in fourth in the Democratic primary for Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District in May, was approached by the Working People Party to run for Senate. She declined, as first reported by the Omaha World-Herald.
Legal Marijuana NOW’s Mike Marvin of Omaha suspended his campaign Aug. 21 and endorsed Osborn. However, he will still appear on the ballot.
The full slate of candidates challenging U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith, R-Neb., center, as he seeks an 11th term for Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District in Congress. His challengers, from top left, clockwise, are Macey Budke of North Platte, of the Nebraska Working People Party; Mark Cohen of Lemoyne, a registered nonpartisan who petitioned to appear on the ballot; Democrat Becky Kelly Stille of South Sioux City; and David Else of Overton, nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
In other Working People Party filings, Macey Budke of North Platte qualified for the ballot for Nebraska’s sprawling 3rd Congressional District, one of the most conservative in the nation.
Budke had pledged to pursue a write-in candidacy for Nebraska’s 3rd District after she backed away from a petition drive seeking to qualify a nonpartisan bid. In that instance, she needed 2,000 valid signatures from district voters. 
In contrast, candidates for the new parties needed valid signatures from at least 25 party members either statewide or in their respective House district.
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith, R-Neb., is running for an 11th term against Democrat Becky Kelly Stille of South Sioux City, Legal Marijuana NOW’s David Else of Overton and registered nonpartisan Mark Cohen of Lemoyne, in addition to Budke.
The America First Party also nominated a House-level candidate in Dan Hartong of Lincoln. In  Nebraska’s eastern 1st Congressional District, Hartong will face U.S. Rep. Mike Flood, R-Neb., who is seeking a third term, and Democrat Chris Backemeyer of Lincoln.
In addition, Paul Rumbaugh of Omaha will appear on the ballot for Nebraska secretary of state for the Nebraska Working People Party, making that fight a four-way race. Rumbaugh and former state Sen. Bob Krist of Omaha, now with the America First Party, will join Republican Scott Petersen of Omaha and Democrat Sarah Slattery of Plattsmouth.
Also filing Tuesday were two more candidates for the America First Party: former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, for governor, and John Knight of Clay Center, for state auditor.
The order on the ballot for candidates in partisan races this fall is Republican, Democrat, Libertarian, Legal Marijuana NOW, Working People Party and America First Party. In the cases of the Senate and 3rd District, Osborn and Cohen will appear at the end. They are the only nonpartisans who successfully petitioned to appear on the ballot this year.
Tuesday was the deadline for the two new political parties to nominate candidates or for any nonpartisan candidates to join statewide races for the Legislature, State Board of Education or University of Nebraska Board of Regents. No other candidates filed petitions for those offices.
The Secretary of State’s Office confirmed enough valid signatures for all three Working People Party candidates and five America First Party candidates who filed by 5 p.m. Tuesday.
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC governor moves to oust Charleston school board member after report found possible fraud
description: The board member may have failed to file her taxes, racked up late fees from the district and lived outside the county, the report found.
text:
Gov. Henry McMaster, pictured Tuesday, March 31, 2026, asked a Charleston County school board member to defend her spot on the board in front of a panel, the first step toward removing her from office. (File/Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Gov. Henry McMaster took the first step Tuesday toward removing a Charleston County school board member after a state inspection found she may have broken multiple laws.
The inspector general’s office found evidence board member Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson may have violated board policy and state law, according to the report released last Thursday. The office referred its report to the State Law Enforcement Division and the Department of Revenue for further investigation.
McMaster pointed to three potential violations of board policy and state ethics law noted in the inspector general’s report. The investigation found evidence Dunmeyer-Roberson divulged information the board discussed behind closed doors, shared confidential emails, and got her campaign manager a contract with the district, according to the report.

2026-09-01 FILED No. 2026-19 Section 59-19-60 Notice to Dunmeyer-Roberson 
Dunmeyer-Roberson did not respond to a call from the SC Daily Gazette requesting comment Tuesday.
McMaster’s order doesn’t immediately remove Dunmeyer-Roberson, who was first elected in 2022. She will first have a chance to go before a three-person panel the governor appointed and make her case for why she should remain on the board.
Dunmeyer-Roberson has until Sept. 10 to tell the governor whether she would like to speak to the board. The panel will then tell the governor by Oct. 5 whether its members believe he should remove Dunmeyer-Roberson or not.
If she doesn’t meet the deadline, McMaster can remove her immediately, according to the order.
The investigation also found potential fraud in Dunmeyer-Roberson’s tax filings, residence and district invoices through her company. Inspector General Brian Lamkin recommended the governor consider removing Dunmeyer-Roberson from the board.
“Taken together, the actions demonstrate willful misconduct in office and persistent neglect of Trustee (Dunmeyer-Roberson’s) fundamental obligations of loyalty, confidentiality, and impartial governance,” the report reads.
Confidential information and conflict of interest
The report doesn’t name the board member accused of breaching board policy and state law. Instead, Lamkin referred only to “Trustee X.”
However, the governor’s executive order and property records indicated in the report identify the unnamed trustee as Dunmeyer-Roberson.
The investigation found Dunmeyer-Roberson forwarded confidential emails and information that fell under attorney-client privilege to news outlets 10 times, and she forwarded proprietary information to a business she ran, which had a contract with the district, 28 times, according to the report.
That information may have “afforded the vendor an unfair advantage in a contractual matter with the District,” Lamkin wrote.
McMaster asked for the investigation after another board member, Kevin Hollinshead, was indicted in March on charges of bribery after sharing confidential board information with an outside company. The grand jury in that case noted that another board member also disclosed details from closed-door meetings but didn’t name that person, according to the report.
The inspector general also found a potential conflict of interest involving Dunmeyer-Roberson’s campaign manager. In 2023, Dunmeyer-Roberson emailed a district principal to set up a meeting with her campaign manager to discuss a contract for services, according to the report.
The campaign manager’s nonprofit, Circle of Life Foundation, ultimately became a district vendor and charged the district $216 per pupil per hour to meet with a social worker, according to the report.
That could create a conflict of interest in violation of board policy and the state’s ethics laws, which prohibit elected officials from using their office for financial gain, either for themselves or anyone associated with them, the report found.
The inspector general also questioned whether that was the best use of funds, considering some district staff said they believed the schools already had people to do the same duties and the cost came in far above the standard for similar mental health-based services, according to the report.
Potential fraud
The investigation found that Dunmeyer-Roberson failed to file correct taxes for herself or her company, Next Level Educational Services, which contracted with the district. Between 2019 and 2024, the inspector general found $248,000 in income unreported on her income tax returns, according to the report.
The report also raised concerns about payments through Dunmeyer-Roberson’s company, which is listed as an educational consultant on invoices.
Before her election to the board, Dunmeyer-Roberson received more than $239,000 from the district for her work through Next Level.
The company stacked unnecessary late fees onto its invoices, exploiting a weakness in the district’s payment system and racking up costs in violation of law, according to the report. The district paid the invoices using Title I funds, which are meant to help children from low-income families, despite those not applying in this case, the report found.
In many cases, the district had paid the invoices on time, according to the report.
The procurement manager responsible for paying the invoices is on leave while the district investigates the payments, Lamkin wrote.
“Next Level’s potential fraudulent submission of the invoice(s) and the resulting payment using Title I funds caused a direct waste of educational funds,” the report reads. “Next Level caused the District to improperly disburse these funds and deprived eligible low-income students of critical services such as targeted tutoring, instructional materials, and smaller class sizes.”
Another source of potential fraud was Dunmeyer-Roberson’s address, Lamkin wrote.
Dunmeyer-Roberson may not have lived in Charleston County during at least part of her time as a board member, the inspector general found.
She filed to run in 2022 with an address in Charleston County. But documents she filed for a mortgage loan through Veterans Affairs listed her address in 2023 as being in Summerville, which is in Dorchester County.
That means Dunmeyer-Roberson “either committed VA mortgage loan fraud by attesting (she) resided in Dorchester County,” or she moved out of Charleston County while on the board, at which point she should have given up her seat, the report reads.
Altogether, the investigation found “acts of malfeasance, misfeasance, conflicts of interest, policy violations, misconduct in office, and neglect of duty in office,” the report reads.

title: Legal aid for immigrant kids remains in question after Trump administration pulls contract
text: WASHINGTON— More than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant youth remain at risk of losing their legal representation, one month after the Trump administration ended a federal contract with an organization that provided legal services to migrant children, advocates and attorneys said Tuesday.Most of those children who initially had attorneys through funding provided by Congress still have access to lawyers because the Acacia Center for Justice and its network of 100 nonprofits have continued to represent the children without pay. But unaccompanied immigrant children who have been placed into federal custody since the contract expired after July 31 are likely without attorneys as they appear in immigration court, said Michael Lukens, the executive director of the Amica Center for Justice, which is part of Acacia’s network. “Many nonprofits are not taking on new cases,” Lukens said. “We have not closed any case of a child we were already representing — that obviously is not a sustainable model. We feel both ethically and morally obligated to continue as long as we can.”Without a lawyer, fewer than 10% of immigrant children win the right to remain in the United States while their cases go through immigration court.Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, the deputy director of Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project, said the organization is currently representing 600 children, and cannot represent several children who have recently arrived in Arizona, where the group is based. “This is something that is happening across the nation,” she said. Contract expiredThe Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, which cares for unaccompanied children, let a contract with Acacia for legal services expire July 31. The center has a network of roughly 100 organizations it works with that provide legal aid and representation to immigrant children across the country in their immigration court appearances. Acacia has provided legal services for unaccompanied minors for decades. Additionally, since December, HHS has not released $65 million that Congress appropriated for legal representation of unaccompanied children in immigration cases, meaning that Acacia and its legal providers have gone for months without reimbursement.Leaders of Acacia have said the funds were withheld because attorneys refused to hand over to the Trump administration sensitive case data from the unaccompanied children, such as medical records and the types of legal relief the minors are seeking. After the contract expired in July, HHS initially awarded a single $150 million contract to a small Texas firm, headed by a former Trump official who served during the first administration. But the law firm, which only had two attorneys that specialized in immigration law and primarily focused on regulatory work, backed out of the contract. New contractIn August, the Trump administration awarded a $158 million no-bid contract to a controversial anti-human-trafficking organization called Our Rescue, a Utah-based company that was previously known as Operation Underground Railroad. The group was founded by Tim Ballard, who presented it as an “anti-sex-trafficking” organization. The group was featured in the conservative film “Sound of Freedom” that promoted several QAnon conspiracy theories. After the movie’s release, Ballard was accused of sexual misconduct by several employees and has since left the organization. Our Rescue now specializes in working with law enforcement related to child trafficking cases and is run by a former Department of Homeland Security official, Derek Benner. It’s unclear if there are any immigration attorneys on staff and the group does not have a history of providing legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant youth in immigration court.Our Rescue did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment. Bilal Askaryar, the communications director for Acacia, said Our Rescue has not been in contact with Acacia to transfer over case information.Avila-Cimpeanu said she has also not heard from Our Rescue to start the transition process for representing the children’s cases. “I think it’s very unclear what their role is,” she said. The Our Rescue contract will run from Aug. 7 until Feb. 6, 2027, according to its award.The Office of Refugee Resettlement did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

title: South Dakota utility regulator candidates clash over AI data center pause
description: A South Dakota Democratic Public Utilities Commission candidate is calling for a one-year ban on new artificial intelligence data centers in the state, while his Republican opponent calls the proposal “reckless and pandering” and says new state laws regulating the industry are sufficient. Frank Kloucek, a farmer from rural Scotland, South Dakota, and a Democ[...]
text:
The candidates for a South Dakota Public Utilities Commission seat are Democratic nominee Frank Kloucek, left, and Republican nominee Don Haggar. (Photos by South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota Democratic Public Utilities Commission candidate is calling for a one-year ban on new artificial intelligence data centers in the state, while his Republican opponent calls the proposal “reckless and pandering” and says new state laws regulating the industry are sufficient.
Frank Kloucek, a farmer from rural Scotland, South Dakota, and a Democratic former 22-year state lawmaker, proposed the moratorium. He said large data centers require large investments in electrical infrastructure — from generation to transmission — and South Dakotans should not subsidize their development through higher energy bills.
“Slow down, get the facts, protect the ratepayers and make sure South Dakota is in control of its own future,” Kloucek said.

State lawmakers passed, and Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden signed, two data center bills into law earlier this year.
One allows the Public Utilities Commission to assess data center companies the cost of regulatory reviews related to their projects. The other requires local water providers to determine whether the water use of large data centers — for cooling of spaces filled with heat-emitting servers — is compatible with the local water supply. It also requires electrical providers to establish separate terms and conditions for large data centers and to require reimbursement for all costs fairly attributed to data centers. Additionally, the law prohibits the state from overriding local ordinances limiting, prohibiting or otherwise regulating data centers.
Lawmakers rejected other proposals that would have incentivized data centers, such as a proposed sales tax exemption for data center equipment and software purchases. Lawmakers also rejected moratoriums on data center development.
Don Haggar, of Sioux Falls, who previously served five years in the Legislature, is the Republican nominee for the Public Utilities Commission. He said in a statement sent to South Dakota Searchlight that the new state laws are “the right foundation for how these decisions should be made going forward, case by case, on their unique merits.”
Haggar said the regulatory role of commissioners means “every case that comes before us deserves a fair, unbiased hearing, not a verdict decided in advance, and not a rubber stamp either.”
“It’s reckless and pandering to propose what my opponent has just done,” Haggar said in the statement.
Kloucek said the new state laws “lack any teeth.” The law regulating water and electricity use does not add any penalties for violations. Kloucek said a one-year moratorium would give the state more time to study the issue before any new projects move ahead.

South Dakota has small data centers but none of the large centers, known as hyper-scale, that have proliferated elsewhere. Proponents of data center development said during the legislative session that the state is missing out on high-paying jobs and millions in additional property tax revenue, while putting America at risk of falling behind foreign competitors. On Monday, President Donald Trump said on social media, “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backward and poor.”
Meanwhile, 23 Democratic candidates for the South Dakota Legislature have signed a pledge to implement public protections, greater transparency and local control in data center development, while opposing tax incentives. The laws approved earlier this year received bipartisan support.
Haggar and Kloucek are seeking the Public Utilities Commission seat being vacated by Republican Commissioner Gary Hanson, who is not seeking reelection. The commission has three positions, one of which is up for election this year. The election is Nov. 3, and advance voting starts Sept. 18.
The last Democrat on the commission was Steve Kolbeck, who served from 2006 to 2011. He’s now a Republican state senator but is not running for reelection to the Legislature this year.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Center for Intellectual Freedom advisers debate oversight of activities, curriculum
description: Members of the executive committee advising the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa expressed concern Tuesday about potential limitations on director decisions  and the intricacies of establishing required civics curriculum. The center advisory council’s executive committee, in their first meeting of the school year, discussed the next[...]
text:
Members of the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa advisory committee, shown here in December 2025, discussed candidates for the director position Tuesday. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Members of the executive committee advising the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa expressed concern Tuesday about potential limitations on director decisions  and the intricacies of establishing required civics curriculum.
The center advisory council’s executive committee, in their first meeting of the school year, discussed the next steps in the search for a permanent center director, as well as efforts to plan individual and collaborative programming and get started on the center’s academic staffing and offerings.
Christine Hensley, a member of the Iowa Board of Regents and chair of the advisory council, said there have been discussions addressing “the center for intellectual freedom becoming an independent entity,” but there are still questions that need answers.

“The relationship between the center and the university is absolutely important, so I’m very glad that these frameworks are in the process of being established,” said Thomas Gallanis, George Mason University law professor and executive committee member. “The academic relationship between the center and the university is particularly crucial. The center’s ability to hire both the director and faculty, and the center’s ability to offer courses for credit, minors, majors, etc. all depend on the academic framework that will be established.”
Concerns over board, university oversight
Luciano de Castro, interim director of the center for intellectual freedom, said he’s received multiple invitations from other centers to conferences “related to American culture” and the 250th anniversary of its creation but was told by members of a new board of regents committee he should not attend them in order to focus on the speaker series and director search.
The board approved a new regents committee with the mission of overseeing the center for intellectual freedom and its advisory council in July.
“There (are) other conferences … for instance, events that were organized by the other centers in UNI and Iowa State University that I was invited and planned to attend, but I have also to obtain the authorization to attend those conferences,” de Castro said.
Members of the executive committee expressed confusion and concern at the board’s restriction on de Castro’s activities, with University of Texas at Austin associate professor and committee member Richard Lowery saying “these are exactly the sort of conferences you need to go to if you’re going to be recruiting faculty and raising the profile of the center.”

Guest speakers scheduled
De Castro told committee members two guest speaker events are scheduled in September, with more events set for October but with details still being finalized. He is working to invite UI faculty to each event, he said.
George Mason University law professor Todd Zywicki will speak Sept. 3 at the UI through a partnership between the center and the Federalist Society about how American liberty was shaped.
Wilfred McClay, a historian and professor at Hillsdale College and a member of the center’s advisory council, will speak about freedom of speech on Sept. 10 at the UI. Both scheduled events are part of a speaker series focused on America’s 250th anniversary.
“We are already in the process of inviting the community, the University of Iowa community, to attend these lectures,” de Castro said.

Decisions to go to conferences or other events are usually left up to the faculty member or official going to them, Lowery said, and he doesn’t believe this is an “acceptable approach to governance at the center.”
Hensley said the timing of the conferences de Castro requested to attend “is inappropriate” as he focuses on the speaker series, and she doesn’t believe that this will be an issue in the future.
“I think the director of this center, whoever it is, is going to make a big sacrifice. But we need to make this center intellectually attractive, and this is not the signal we want to give to anybody, frankly,” committee member and Stanford associate professor Iván Marinovic said. “So I think this was a big mistake, and I think we shouldn’t make it again.”
Lowery also shared concerns about the advisory council’s scholar committee efforts to begin thinking about hiring faculty or crafting curriculum when the academic framework, as well as a permanent director who is supposed to be involved with these processes, are not yet in place.
De Castro suggested creating subcommittees within the scholar committee to focus on either hiring or curriculum curation, for which Lowery and Hensley both voiced support.
Hensley said the scholar committee should move ahead in its work with the understanding that the UI Provost’s Office and academic officers with the board of regents are also identifying currently offered courses that could meet these requirements, and “you’re going to have to come together at some point.”
“It’s going to be a three-legged stool,” Hensley said. “You’re going to have the scholar committee at the advisory council, you’re going to have the new director that’s going to want to have significant input, and you have to have an understanding of what’s currently being offered at the university.”
Lowery said he’s hesitant to “burn people’s time” on developing courses if the end result is “whatever the provost wants to happen is going to happen,” which Hensley countered by saying the council will only receive input from the Provost’s Office.
Gallanis and Lowery proposed holding a scholar committee meeting, without Hensley present but receiving minutes and other information after the fact, in order to inform members of what’s been happening with the center.
“It would be very valuable, I think, for the scholars to be able to talk among themselves about where the center is, where the center may be headed, where the center should be headed,” Gallanis said.
Candidate pool narrowed for director position
The committee received 62 applications for the center director job, Hensley said, with six that could be discussed in open session. Of the six applicants mentioned in open session, only one was moved forward in consideration — #45, whose last name is De Castro. No first names were provided during the meeting, and it is unclear whether the de Castro named as an applicant is the same as the center’s interim director.
Officially posted in mid-June, the job description for the center director position stated applications should be filed by Aug. 14 “to ensure best consideration,” with search committee chair Richard Lowery saying at a June advisory council meeting that the board of regents hopes to have someone selected in its September meeting.
Hensley told board members in a June meeting that “everything else will be on pause” with the center beyond establishing a speaker series, including offering courses during the fall semester, as the search for a director is ongoing and the council must create courses by 2028 to satisfy new requirements in civics education.

title: The Sturgeon Moon cast light on lunar mining and public land
description: One goal behind the successful Artemis II mission that sent humans (and Rise) further into space than ever before is to advance space mining. We are living through a time of remarkable scientific development across the universe that touches even the Fishlake National Forest in the Tushar Mountains. Marysvale, Utah, locals face potential mining activity […]
text:
The Artemis Accords plainly allow extraction and utilization of space minerals. But what about the testing grounds here on Earth? (Stock photo by Leonardo Fernndez Lzaro via Getty Images)One goal behind the successful Artemis II mission that sent humans (and Rise) further into space than ever before is to advance space mining. We are living through a time of remarkable scientific development across the universe that touches even the Fishlake National Forest in the Tushar Mountains.
Marysvale, Utah, locals face potential mining activity only recently made possible after seismic nodes were backpacked into the Tushar Mountains to survey underground mineral deposits. Fleet Space Technologies owns these purse-sized devices and markets them as interstellar prospecting equipment that may allow humankind to extract minerals from celestial bodies. Other companies share a dream to mine the moon, and it is legal. The Artemis Accords plainly allow extraction and utilization of space minerals. But what about the testing grounds here on Earth? An Australian company’s outer space beta test is taking place unregulated, in the backcountry, on our public lands.
This is a symptom of international companies gaining more control over our public lands. Numerous priorities of the current presidential administration are in the interest of both terrestrial and cosmic mining companies over we, the people. They include: the persistence of the grossly outdated 1872 Mining Law; the dismantling of the U.S. Forest Service; the coercion of professionals out of the civil service across national public land agencies; and the weakening of the valuable Clean Water Act — a law that supports sturgeon health and is key to restoring endangered Atlantic Sturgeon and Shortnose Sturgeon populations.
National land management agencies, the policies that they enforce, and the laws that govern them are supposed to serve each of us and the land, water and wildlife we love. They are meant to protect us and keep extraction-based businesses in check. I’ve written substantive public comments on a handful of regulatory proposals and environmental assessments pertaining to public lands on behalf of the national nonprofit organization, GreenLatinos, over the last four years. Something greater than the substance of these comments I’ve observed is the crucial importance of public input on natural resource management.
Democratic processes are responsible for allowing us to live well on our one and only home planet. As Americans, we are responsible for passing public lands on to future generations in a better condition than we received them. We shouldn’t let companies make those decisions for us. Yet, President Donald Trump’s Forest Service permitted the use of underground mineral survey technology in our national forest without public comment. The full Sturgeon Moon we just witnessed should embolden us to get a grip back on our natural and cultural inheritance, and fight for the democratic processes that make public input at the foundation of decisions about public land.
As the Sturgeon Moon transitions into a Harvest Moon on Sept. 26, we also ought to ask ourselves and each other: what would it mean to bore into and extract from the lunar subsurface? The poet Camille Hernandez called lunar craters, “evidence of care.” Each of the moon’s blemishes represent every time that the moon pulled a space rock into its orbit and saved Earth. The moon has remarkable effects on our lives and the rest of nature. The moon controls ocean life, allowing us to enjoy coasts and eat seafood. Moon light is essential for Utah’s abundant ephedra plant (Mormon tea) to pollinate. And the moon protects us from extinction by asteroid.
In conversation with colleagues aboard the International Space Station, Artemis II Astronaut Christina Koch stated that looking back at Earth, “emphasized how alike we are.” As members of creation on Earth, we should remember the “‘hum” in human, humility, and humble. It comes from the Latin humus, meaning “earth” or “ground.”
75% of voters in Utah prefer that leaders place more emphasis on protecting water, air, wildlife habitat, and recreation opportunities over maximizing the amount of land available for drilling and mining. We on Earth, given to the characteristics of the moon, have a lot more in common than we tend to recognize most days.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont ends night and weekend intake for state-funded motel rooms
description:
Motel vouchers will no longer be available after-hours through Vermont 211 as the state rolls out other changes aimed at restructuring homelessness response.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont ends night and weekend intake for state-funded motel rooms.
text:
The Travelodge Motel in South Burlington, which hosts state-funded motel rooms, seen in April 2025. Private motels and hotels in the state voucher program have been the single largest provider of shelter in Vermont in recent years. File photo by Glenn Russell / VTDigger

Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
A major overhaul of Vermont’s motel voucher program for people experiencing homelessness is now underway.
Vermonters who have no place to sleep will now be required to call the state during normal business hours, and they’ll face more questions about their health, safety and housing options. There won’t be as many motel rooms available, and people won’t be allowed to stay as long. 
The Sept. 1 changes to motel room access mark the beginning of the rollout for the Vermont Homeless Response Continuum, a refashioned structure for responding to homelessness put in place by the Legislature and signed by Gov. Phil Scott in June.
People seeking a motel voucher will no longer be able to access one in the evenings or over the weekends. Historically, the United Ways of Vermont’s 211 helpline served as the entry point to a motel voucher after the state’s offices closed. In July, Vermont 211 handled 1,024 housing assistance calls tied to the state’s motel voucher program, and conducted 541 intakes, according to United Ways director Alison Lamagna.
But late last month, state officials notified the organization that they would be ending that arrangement, Lamagna said. Going forward, people seeking shelter will need to call the state between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday.
The pivot left Lamagna disappointed and concerned. She is particularly worried about people who lack reliable access to a phone or who are facing a dangerous situation, like domestic violence.
“The impact is going to be less people able to get help when they need it,” she said. 
(211 will still be able to refer people to community-based shelters and other housing programs, Lamagna said.)
Miranda Gray, deputy commissioner of the Economic Services Division at the Department for Children and Families, said DCF decided to stop using 211 for accessing motel vouchers in part because the state is beginning to use a more involved intake process to determine a person’s eligibility for a voucher. 
A new assessment system will consider someone’s immediate health and safety risks and their possible housing options. The assessment will also be used for other types of shelter programs in Vermont in the future.
That system will help the state prioritize people for more limited space. Private motels and hotels in the state voucher program have been the single largest provider of shelter in Vermont in recent years. As of Sept. 1, lawmakers have imposed lower caps on the number of rooms the state can use throughout the year, and the maximum stay has been reduced to 70 days. (That time limit is waived during the winter months.)
Along with those changes comes a shift in philosophy, Gray said.
“It is no longer an emergency housing program,” she said. “That’s no longer in the language in the bill that was passed.” 
Motel voucher recipients will be expected to show progress toward getting into housing, with help from a case manager. That’s also a change in approach, Gray said.
Before, “it was purely: find someone a hotel room wherever you can, and I think we just know that that isn’t working,” she said. 
Gray’s emphasis on providing case management underscores one broader tradeoff at the heart of this year’s law: The state will attempt to offer better services, but provide shelter for fewer people overall.
Advocates for unhoused Vermonters, along with some lawmakers who helped shape the legislation, have argued that DCF’s interpretation of the law misses the mark. 
Brenda Siegel, executive director of End Homelessness Vermont, said the law was supposed to make access to services more flexible. The rule changes for motel use led by DCF, like more onerous processes to vet eligibility, point the other direction, she said.
“This is the highest-bar, most restrictive version of this I have ever seen,” Siegel said.

title: Kansas agency settles with Army National Guard soldier after eliminating her job
description: TOPEKA — An Army National Guard employee who accused a Kansas agency of eliminating her job because of an upcoming military deployment will receive $35,000 in a settlement agreement announced Tuesday. The U.S. Department of Justice sued the Kansas Department of Health and Environment on behalf of Staff Sgt. Stacy Gonzales, claiming the agency violated […]
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice reached a settlement with the Kansas Department of Health and Environment about their decision to eliminate a job held by an Army National Guard soldier. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)TOPEKA — An Army National Guard employee who accused a Kansas agency of eliminating her job because of an upcoming military deployment will receive $35,000 in a settlement agreement announced Tuesday.
The U.S. Department of Justice sued the Kansas Department of Health and Environment on behalf of Staff Sgt. Stacy Gonzales, claiming the agency violated terms of a federal law that protects employment rights for service members.
Gonzales was working as a local disease intervention specialist at Finney County Department of Health, a position that was under the control and supervision of KDHE, a DOJ news release said. KDHE eliminated grant funding for her position when Gonzales told them she would be deploying, the news release said.
The case was filed in 2022 and went through numerous court actions on its way to being settled. KDHE argued that it wasn’t Gonzales’ employer because it was the grant funder, an opinion upheld by a federal district judge.
In January, the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled the lawsuit filed in 2022 was improperly dismissed by the district judge.
The settlement agreement requires KDHE to update its Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994 — the federal law that protects service members — policies and procedures and to train all KDHE employees on those updated processes, the news release said.
“National Guard members are called citizen-soldiers because they must strike a balance between fulfilling obligations to civilian careers with those of military service. As a reservist myself, I know this is no easy task,” said Ryan Kriegshauser, U.S. attorney for Kansas, in the news release. “When guard members deploy, they shouldn’t have to worry that their livelihoods will be stripped away while they are off serving our country. Our government put laws in place to protect the employment rights of servicemembers.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota governor says data center transparency bill not needed
description: North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong joined private industry and economic development groups to speak against a bill that would further restrict public officials and agencies from signing nondisclosure agreements with developers of data centers and other industrial projects. The bipartisan bill, Senate Bill 2406, if passed, would mean a project developer could[...]
text:
North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong testifies in a legislative committee hearing on Sept. 1, 2026, on a bill seeking to ban nondisclosure agreements for industrial projects. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong joined private industry and economic development groups to speak against a bill that would further restrict public officials and agencies from signing nondisclosure agreements with developers of data centers and other industrial projects.
The bipartisan bill, Senate Bill 2406, if passed, would mean a project developer could see an agency permit revoked if a public official or agency agreed to a nondisclosure agreement with the company. 

More special session coverage

The bill will be considered as the North Dakota Legislature begins a special session Wednesday, but a legislative committee gathered testimony Tuesday. 
Armstrong testified in favor of an amendment by Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, one of the sponsors of the bill. The amendment clarifies that the law would not prohibit an agency from entering a nondisclosure agreement to maintain the confidentiality of information that is already considered confidential or exempt from disclosure under state law.
Armstrong said without the amendment, the bill would put entities such as the Bank of North Dakota in an awkward position as a private company provides project information during a loan consideration. 
He said the bill would allow the bank to enter a confidentiality agreement with a farm operation, but not an ethanol plant because the ethanol plant would be an industrial project. 
Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, testifies in a legislative committee hearing on Sept. 1, 2026, introducing an amendment to a bill seeking to ban nondisclosure agreements for industrial projects. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Armstrong said it could interfere with hiring consultants to evaluate potential investments. 
“When we sign agreements with people who help us analyze where and how to invest our money, almost all of them have some form of a confidentiality agreement based on them not wanting to share their analysis with their competitors,” said Armstrong, a Republican. 
Armstrong favored the amendment, but also said the state’s existing public records laws already prevent officials from signing nondisclosure agreements, also known as NDAs. 
“We have good open records law,” Armstrong said. “There’s debate about the enforcement side of it.” 
The nondisclosure agreement ban tries to add an enforcement mechanism. The bill says a company that enters a nondisclosure agreement with an agency is not eligible for actions such as obtaining a permit or a zoning change from that agency. 
If an NDA violation is found later, the company’s permit could be revoked. 
Costs, benefits of data centers take center stage at legislative meeting

Rep. Todd Porter, R-Mandan, asked witnesses testifying in favor of the bill how it improves on North Dakota’s existing open records law. 
“This new bill has teeth because you could lose your permitting,” said David Tamisiea, executive director of the North Dakota Catholic Conference. 
Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, who introduced the bill, said there is very little consequence for violating open records and open meetings laws in North Dakota law. 
But Armstrong and others said it doesn’t make sense to punish the private company if a public official signs an NDA in violation of the law. 
Terry Effertz, executive director of TechND, was among the representatives of industry and economic development organizations opposing the bill. 
“You could halt or unwind a project that a community and its workforce are ready for over a paperwork violation,” Effertz said. 
Nick Phillips, vice president, of Applied Digital, a data center company, attends a legislative hearing on Sept. 1, 2026, in Bismarck. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Mathern and other supporters said the bill provides more transparency for communities that are getting blindsided by multibillion data center projects. 
He said Harwood-area residents learned of the Applied Digital project just six weeks before the company planned to break ground. 
Mathern also outlined two proposed amendments. 
One would provide an exemption for public entities that are also an energy provider, such as a municipal utility. The exemption would allow public utility companies the ability to privately negotiate a service agreement with a large industrial user the same way an electric co-op or investor-owned utility can. 
The other amendment would eliminate a state sales tax exemption for data center developers.
Nick Phillips, executive vice president of external affairs for Applied Digital, said the company has used NDAs in North Dakota, but said it did so in compliance with state laws.
He said the NDA was in place for about six weeks while it determined whether a project was viable. As Applied Digital entered permitting, he said the NDA was lifted.
Stark Power, which is eyeing Mandan for a proposed data center, promoted during a recent community town hall that it does not plan to use nondisclosure agreements for the project.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: US House censures NC Rep. Chuck Edwards for inappropriate conduct, harassment
description: The U.S. House of Representatives voted Tuesday 413-2 to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, a Republican representing western North Carolina, for his inappropriate conduct towards two female staffers working in his office. Edwards stood in the well of the House to hear the reading of censure after the vote. A lengthy House Ethics Committee investigation released […[...]
text:
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-NC) talks to reporters as he arrives for a House Republican conference in the basement of the U.S. Capitol on September 01, 2026 in Washington, DC.  (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)The U.S. House of Representatives voted Tuesday 413-2 to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, a Republican representing western North Carolina, for his inappropriate conduct towards two female staffers working in his office.
Edwards stood in the well of the House to hear the reading of censure after the vote.
A lengthy House Ethics Committee investigation released this summer found “substantial evidence” that Edwards created a “hostile work environment.”
In its report, the House Ethics Committee found Edwards gave the two young female staffers gifts including jewelry worth over $1,000, a Las Vegas trip, and “designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.”
On another occasion, Edwards skipped a House vote to decorate a Christmas tree with a female staffer, according to the Ethics review.
Ethics Committee Chairman Rep. Michael Guest, R-Mississippi, said Tuesday while the committee found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the women, he violated rules prohibiting sexual harassment.
“The committee reviewed Rep. Edwards conduct and determined that he engaged in persistent, unprofessional, and inappropriate conduct,” said Guest. “While Rep. Edwards denies that his conduct was intended to be sexual or romantic, his pattern of behavior would lead a reasonable person to interpret it as such.”
“The committee found that Rep. Edwards was at a minimum blind to the reality, and at worst, dismissive of the impact his conduct had on the careers and well-being of the women on his staff,” Guest said.
Edwards denied the findings of the ethics committee report, insisting that his behavior, while perhaps ill-advised, didn’t rise to the level of sexual harassment. He used some of his time on the floor to apologize to the two staffers, both of whom subsequently left their jobs.
“I’m sorry that my actions, my judgment, or the way that I express the friendship ever puteither of you in an uncomfortable position,” said Edwards. “My intentions were only grounded in what I understood our friendship to be and in genuine admiration and respect I had for each of you, not only as professionals, but as people.”
Edwards then apologized to his wife.
“Teresa, you stood beside me through a lifetime of challenges, sacrifices, successes, and disappointments,” Edwards said. “I’m deeply sorry that my judgment and my actions put you in a position where you had to endure embarrassment, hurt, public scrutiny, and questions that no wife should ever have to face.”
Edwards stressed that his acknowledgement of regret and poor judgment was not an admission of sexual harassment. “Generosity is not sexual harassment,” he said. “Caring deeply about the people with whom you’ve worked for years is not sexual harassment.”
He asked his colleagues to spare him from a label that would mar his name and record in Congress.
“A censure by this House carries the weight of history,” said Edwards.
Rep. Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA), ranking member on House Ethics, dismissed Edwards’ arguments.
“Rep. Edwards may not have made physical advances or explicit propositions, but sexual harassment does not require either,” DeSaulnier responded. “His conduct was inappropriate, unwelcome, and most importantly, created a hostile work environment.”
NC Rep. Edwards drops reelection campaign following ethics probe, urging of Republican colleagues

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, D-New Mexico, called Edwards’ behavior “disgusting and horrible.”
Fernandez chastised Edwards for threatening the careers and safety of his staff with his behavior, and breaking a pledge to his constituents to act with dignity and integrity.
“These women lost their jobs because of Mr. Edward’s behavior. He should lose his,” said Fernandez. “It’s time we reform the rules in Congress, so abusers like Edwards are at least stripped of committee assignments or expelled if the offense calls for it after an investigation and after a vote of the full floor.”
After the vote, Edwards released a statement saying while he respects the U.S. House, he does not accept their conclusion.
“I will not confess to conduct I did not commit simply to make this moment easier,” wrote Edwards on social media. “The House has spoken. So have I. I will leave this chapter with my head held high and finish the job Western North Carolina sent me here to do.”
Edwards, who has represented North Carolina’s 11th congressional district since 2023, dropped his bid for reelection August 5th.
The North Carolina Republican Party selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom of Henderson County to fill Edwards’ spot on the ballot against Democrat Jamie Ager.
This story has been updated to correct the House of Representatives vote count to censure.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: CHI St. Vincent no longer part of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Arkansas network
description: CHI St. Vincent will not be part of the Blue Cross Blue Shield of Arkansas network after the Little Rock-based hospital system and the insurer failed to reach an agreement on renewing their contract, both sides announced Tuesday. The two failed to reach an agreement during negotiations over the past several months about how much […]
text:
(Getty Images)CHI St. Vincent will not be part of the Blue Cross Blue Shield of Arkansas network after the Little Rock-based hospital system and the insurer failed to reach an agreement on renewing their contract, both sides announced Tuesday.
The two failed to reach an agreement during negotiations over the past several months about how much the insurer reimburses CHI St. Vincent. 
“This was not the outcome we have been working toward, and please know that we have not and will not walk away,” CHI St. Vincent said in a statement on its website. “We remain fully committed to reaching a new agreement as quickly as possible, but the agreement must equitably address the need for fair reimbursement for the care we provide.”
Blue Cross Blue Shield of Arkansas said it was disappointed but appreciated the care the hospital system had provided to its members. 
“We are committed to exploring approaches that ensure our members receive high-quality care that is also cost-efficient, and we have communicated to CHI St. Vincent and CommonSpirit Health that if their focus or circumstances should change in the future, they have an open invitation to rejoin us in this work,” Alicia Berkemeyer, executive vice president and chief health management officer for Arkansas Blue Cross, said in a news release.
CHI St. Vincent, a part of Chicago-based CommonSpirit Health System, operates hospitals in Little Rock, Hot Springs, Morrilton and Sherwood. 
The stalemate means that claims with dates of service of Monday or earlier will continue to be reimbursed at in-network rates, Blue Cross Blue Shield said. 
Blue Cross members may be eligible to receive services with in-network coverage for the lesser of 90 days from the date they receive an out-of-network notice or until the condition for which they are being treated is resolved, if transition to another provider would be inappropriate or unsafe, the insurer said. More information about that coverage can be found online. 
The stalemate occurred as hospitals around Arkansas have had to scale back services because of the rising cost of services and the relatively low reimbursement rates they receive for providing care.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawmaker resigns from job with DA, accuses AG of ‘attempt to disrupt’ Epstein commission
description: The New Mexico state representative who leads the House’s investigation into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on Tuesday announced she had resigned from her job with a local district attorney amid mounting criticism.
text:
New Mexico Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), pictured on Aug. 5, 2026, said a recent letter from state Attorney General Raúl Torrez advising district attorneys not to hire sitting state lawmakers was an “attempt to disrupt” her work leading the state House investigatory subcommittee on Jeffrey Epstein. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)The New Mexico state representative who leads the House’s investigation into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on Tuesday announced she had resigned from her job with a local district attorney amid mounting criticism.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe) on Tuesday also said Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s recent advice that district attorneys across the state should not hire sitting state lawmakers was an “attempt to disrupt” her work leading the state House’s investigatory subcommittee on Epstein.
Romero’s employment with the First Judicial District Attorney’s Office came under scrutiny in recent weeks as Republican lawmakers called for an ethics investigation. House Minority Whip Alan Martinez (R-Rio Rancho) recently requested a legislative ethics investigation and said her work with the local DA’s office violated state laws that prohibit sitting lawmakers from simultaneously working as state employees.
Romero had previously defended her employment by citing a 2024 opinion from Torrez’s office, which cleared fellow Epstein commission member Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) to serve as a special prosecutor in the prosecution of Alec Baldwin. Baldwin’s lawyers, citing the same law as Republican lawmakers, said Reeb’s work on the case was unconstitutional. She ultimately resigned from the case.
In a Monday letter to district attorneys statewide, Torrez wrote that his 2024 opinion “has been read more broadly than intended.” He instructed any DA’s office employing a lawmaker to rectify the situation immediately and noted that he would not pursue legal action against any office that had previously hired a lawmaker “based on an honest misunderstanding of our 2024 opinion.”
In a news release responding to Torrez’s letter, First Judicial District Attorney Mary Carmack-Altwies’ office said the agency was “disappointed” by Torrez’s directive but would comply with it.
“Andrea Romero sought appropriate guidance from the Attorney General’s Office before accepting a part-time position with the FJDA, and our Office relied on that guidance,” the statement said. “Romero is a licensed attorney whose professional experience made her well suited for a part-time role in our office. At a time when New Mexico continues to face challenges recruiting and retaining attorneys in public service, we believe qualified professionals should have opportunities to serve their communities in different ways.”
In a Tuesday statement issued through a New York-based public relations firm that represents Monica Lewinsky, Romero said that she had resigned from her job at the First Judicial District Attorney’s Office and said that she had previously “sought and had received explicit authorization to be allowed to hold both positions, a fact the AG’s office was well-aware of.”
She said she was “deeply disappointed” by Torrez’s Monday letter and saw it as “an attempt to disrupt the work of our Survivor Truth Commission that seeks justice for the many young people who were harmed by Jeffrey Epstein and his co-collaborators in our state.”
Torrez early this year reopened a criminal investigation into Epstein and sued the federal government for allegedly blocking the release of files related to the late sex offender. In August, Torrez joined U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) to announce new federal legislation that he said would make it easier for law enforcement agencies across the nation to file legal challenges against the U.S. Department of Justice when it refuses to release Epstein-related documents.
Although Romero did not cite specific examples, she said that Torrez’s letter would impact other state lawmakers and force them to resign from their jobs.
New Mexico is the only state in the nation to not pay its lawmakers. Voters will have the choice in the Nov. 3 general election to change that.
“Serving as a legislator remains the greatest honor of my life, and no attempt to distract from our work will succeed,” Romero said.
The New Mexico Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Nevada Current
title: Judge halts data center construction on public land
description: A federal administrative court has temporarily revoked authorization to build a massive data center near Boulder City, concluding the federal government likely erred when it approved the project construction on public land without a proper environmental analysis.  The Interior Board of Appeals ruled Tuesday that the Bureau of Land Management’s decision to ap[...]
text:
The Bureau of Land Management “acted arbitrarily or capriciously when it determined that the data center project is 'substantially the same' as the solar plant project for purposes of its NEPA analysis,” the judge wrote. (Photo: Bureau of Land Management)A federal administrative court has temporarily revoked authorization to build a massive data center near Boulder City, concluding the federal government likely erred when it approved the project construction on public land without a proper environmental analysis. 
The Interior Board of Appeals ruled Tuesday that the Bureau of Land Management’s decision to approve the construction of the Townsite Data Center on public land using a prior unrelated environmental analysis likely violated the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).
Townsite Solar 2 LLC  — the project developer — originally received federal approval in 2023 to build a solar power generation and battery storage facility on the 88.5-acre parcel, but requested an amended right-of-way grant in 2025 to build a data center instead. 
Federal land managers did not study the effects of the data center project in a new environmental analysis, and instead approved the change in July after determining the data center project “is essentially like” the solar plant project and that it would have “similar anticipated impacts.”
The order comes after the Center for Biological Diversity and Boulder City filed an appeal in July against the Townsite data center, which became the first data center approved on BLM land in the United States.
An administrative judge determined there was persuasive evidence that BLM “acted arbitrarily or capriciously when it determined that the data center project is ‘substantially the same’ as the solar plant project for purposes of its NEPA analysis.”
The order prevents the data center project from moving forward while the Interior Board of Appeals considers legal challenges against the proposal. 
“We’re thrilled that this data center has been stopped dead in its tracks,” said Patrick Donnelly, Great Basin director at the Center for Biological Diversity in a statement. “The Trump administration is pulling out all the stops to let tech companies build massive data centers on our public lands. This tremendous victory proves communities have the power to fight back and win.”
The federal administrative court found that the appeal was likely to succeed on their claims that the BLM’s analysis of the solar plant project’s environmental effects was insufficient because the projects are not  “substantially the same”.
The temporary pause was granted after the Center for Biological Diversity “demonstrated that permanent and irreparable harm is likely to occur” if construction of the data center continued before the appeal is settled, and that those “harms outweigh the temporary financial harm to Townsite from the delay.”
Boulder City also filed an appeal and petitioned for a temporary pause on the project while their appeal makes its way through the federal process. However, the city’s petition was declared moot given the panel granted the Center for Biological Diversity petition seeking a pause. 
In the order, the Interior Board of Appeals consolidated both appeals filed by Boulder City and the Center for Biological Diversity and expedited the appeals. The panel ordered BLM to respond by Sept. 21.
Construction of the Townsite Data Center could have major implications for public lands throughout the West, and especially in Nevada where about 80% of the land is managed by the federal government.
In July, the Boulder City Council unanimously voted to appeal the BLM approval for a data center on an 80-acre BLM-owned parcel about three miles west of the city’s borders.  
Nevada Rep. Dina Titus, who represents the district where the data center would be located, sent a letter to federal land managers demanding answers about how the agency is reviewing proposals for data centers on public land following the approval of the BLM’s amended plan.
Titus Tuesday applauded the Interior Board of Land Appeals’ decision to halt the development of the Townsite Data Center. 
“The judge ruled for transparency and public accountability in granting a stay based on the BLM’s misuse of an environmental impact statement for a solar farm as justification for a data center. The two are vastly different.” Titus said in a statement. “I’ve said since day one that this was not only improper but illegal.”
Gov. Joe Lombardo, to whom Titus had also written seeking clarification about data centers on Nevada public land, and Townsite Solar 2 LLC did not immediately respond to requests of comment about the order. A spokesperson for the Interior said the department does not comment on litigation matters.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa nurses cited for patient-care issues or working without a valid license
description: State regulators have sanctioned Iowa two nurses for working more than a year without valid licenses and two nurses for patient-care issues. The Iowa Board of Nursing alleges that Baxter McNeal, 56, of Anita, while employed as a registered nurse at the Caring Acres Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Anita, failed to provide proper assessments […]
text:
Caring Acres Nursing and Rehabilitation in Anita. (Photo via Google Earth)State regulators have sanctioned Iowa two nurses for working more than a year without valid licenses and two nurses for patient-care issues.
The Iowa Board of Nursing alleges that Baxter McNeal, 56, of Anita, while employed as a registered nurse at the Caring Acres Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Anita, failed to provide proper assessments and interventions with regard to two residents of the home after they experienced a change in condition.
The board has disclosed no information as to when the alleged conduct occurred or the impact on the patients.
After charging McNeal with one count of failing to assess, accurately document, evaluate, or report the status of a patient, the board agreed to resolve the case with a settlement that calls for McNeal’s license to be placed on probationary status for one year. As part of the settlement, McNeal has agreed to complete 30 hours of educational training on ethics and standards of care.
Board records indicate that McNeal was convicted of drunken driving in 2003 and 2006, which led to him receiving a probationary nursing license from Nebraska regulators. In 2007, the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services initiated steps to revoke McNeal’s nursing license due to allegations that he had tested positive for alcohol. The board and McNeal later settled the matter by censuring McNeal and imposing a $500 civil penalty.
According to board records, McNeal was again convicted of drunken driving in 2010, which resulted in his Nebraska nursing license being placed on probation for five years.
In June 2012, McNeal received an Iowa nursing license and, according to the board, in 2014 he was convicted of felony operating a vehicle while his driver’s license was revoked. That conviction resulted in his Nebraska nursing license being suspended for six months. In September 2014, McNeal relinquished his right to practice in Iowa.
In January 2018, the Iowa Board of Nursing reinstated McNeal’s license to practice.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach McNeal for comment.
Other Iowa nurses recently sanctioned by the board include:
Sabryna Simon of Fort Dodge — The board alleges video evidence shows that on Sept. 11, 2025, Simon directed profane language at an infant client, and then “removed the client from the client’s highchair and placed the client on the floor.” The board, which has not disclosed where the incident took place, charged Simon with committing an act or omission that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare; failing to assess, accurately document, evaluate, or report the status of a patient; and engaging in behavior that is contradictory to professional decorum.
To settle the matter, Simon recently agreed to have her license placed on probation for two years. As part of the written settlement, Simon agreed to a provision that states she “shall not engage in the practice of No Home Health Care” — that terminology is left unexplained in the agreement — during her probation. Simon also agreed to complete 60 hours of educational training on ethics and documentation.
Suzanne Mentzer of West Des Moines – The board alleges Mentzer practiced as a registered nurse at The Iowa Clinic for more than a year, from April 23, 2024, through Aug. 7, 2025, without a valid nursing license. She and the board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for Mentzer to pay a $1,000 civil penalty.
Delilah Heuton of Atlantic — The board alleges that in April 2025, while Heuton worked at Heritage House Senior Living Community in Atlantic, it was discovered that she had been working without a valid nursing license for more than a year, since December 2023 when her Iowa license had expired.  She and the board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for Heuton to pay a $550 civil penalty.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Haitian college student who lost temporary protected status dies after walking into traffic
description: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. A 20-year-old Haitian college student died in an apparent suicide Monday, which his father said came after the student was forced to wear an ankle monitor by U.S. Immigration and […]
text:
Signs from a recent rally against immigration enforcement actions targeting Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal)This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.
A 20-year-old Haitian college student died in an apparent suicide Monday, which his father said came after the student was forced to wear an ankle monitor by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Pierre Damas Bel, a Wright State University student, reportedly walked in front of a semi-truck on Interstate 70 on Monday after being bullied by his classmates for wearing an ankle monitor, according to his family.  
“He called me at 8:03 on a video call, (and said) ‘I’m not feeling okay mentally because of the bullying,’ and I told him to come home so we can talk,” Damas Bel’s father Pierre Ronal Bel, said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Around 11 the police showed at my door to report that my son threw himself under a truck.”
The Ohio State Highway Patrol did not respond to a request for the incident report. 
Haitians living in Springfield are required to report to the ICE offices in Blue Ash or Westerville to accept ankle monitors. 
This started after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed President Donald Trump to end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled violence in their home country. Legal protected status for Haitians officially ended on July 27. 
“This is one of the most tragic outcomes of the Trump administration’s cruel and inhumane attacks on the Haitian community,” Guerline Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance said in a statement. 
Jozef said he believes the Trump administration is “fully responsible” in the death of Damas Bel, based on the statements the student made to his father, “that he could no longer bear the stigma that comes with having this ankle monitor device on his foot.” 
Damas Bel was a first-year student studying neuroscience and had hopes of going to medical school, according to his Instagram. He came to the United States in 2023. 
“I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn’t come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone,” he wrote in a July post. “Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience.”
“I came here to study, to build my future, and to live a better life not to be treated like a criminal. So now, how am I supposed to play college sports with a GPS monitor on my leg?”
Damas Bel graduated from Springfield High School in May. 
“We are heartbroken by this devastating loss,” Wright State President Sue Edwards said in a statement. 
“Pierre was an active honors student who was passionate about soccer and was already actively engaged in his classes and the campus community,” Edwards said in a statement. “The University mourns the death of Pierre and extends our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones during this unimaginably difficult time.” 
Damas Bel’s father said his son “felt like he was treated like an animal” because of the ankle monitor. He also said his son was not given his Reserve Officers’ Training Corps uniform at Wright State because of the ankle monitor.
Wright State had “no confirmed information regarding complaints or investigations into bullying,” university spokesperson Deena John said in an email.
“This is a horrible, horrible tragedy,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine told reporters Tuesday. 
About 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship and other legal status.
Haitian Support Center Executive Director Viles Dorsainvil has been with the family since Monday.
“I was just speechless,” he said. “Why was I speechless? It was because I have been experiencing on a daily basis what some of our Haitian brothers and sisters have been through with this program of shackling.”
Damas Bel had two younger siblings, ages 15 and 3. 
Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, said the 15-year-old is “extremely scared” of being sent back to Haiti, and though the family wishes they could send Damas Bel’s body back to Haiti, “that is not an option.”
“They just want to get through the next day,” Ruby said.
Yola Lamarre, an advocate with the Haitian Community Network, said Pierre shared a lot of his depressive thoughts with her after the ankle monitoring began. 
“Pierre was not a criminal; he was treated as one,” she said. “… we’re going to miss you.”
Hundreds of Haitians are currently wearing ankle monitors, advocates said. 
More than 40 Haitians in Springfield have been detained by ICE — including two Haitian pastors. 
ICE agents are detaining people in Springfield in shopping plazas, gas stations and apartment complexes. 
The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare,” according to the agency.
A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped in June.
