name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri AG spends $167,000 in state funds on abortion PSA ahead of November vote
description: Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s office is airing a “women’s health PSA” warning patients about abortion clinics less than three months before voters decide whether to reinstate a near-total abortion ban Hanaway supports. The video cost $167,000 in state funds and was paid for through the office’s Merchandising Practices Revolving Fund, said Ste[...]
text:
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s office is airing a “women’s health PSA” warning patients about abortion clinics (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s office is airing a “women’s health PSA” warning patients about abortion clinics less than three months before voters decide whether to reinstate a near-total abortion ban Hanaway supports.
The video cost $167,000 in state funds and was paid for through the office’s Merchandising Practices Revolving Fund, said Stephanie Whitaker, a spokesperson for the attorney general’s office. She confirmed that it was distributed through the Missouri Broadcasters Association, which serves more than 350 radio and TV stations statewide, and will air across the state through Sept. 30, as KSDK-TV first reported Tuesday.
State law allows money in the Merchandising Practices Revolving Fund to be used for consumer education and advocacy programs.
The PSA, which was also posted to the office’s YouTube account in mid-August, references a June ruling by Jackson County Circuit Judge Jerri Zhang that struck down dozens of challenged abortion regulations as unconstitutional under the reproductive rights amendment passed in 2024. Hanaway is appealing that ruling. 
“For years, our laws protected women by requiring clinics to obtain licenses, pass basic health inspections, and have emergency protocols. But Planned Parenthood sued, trying to block safety requirements that protect women,” Dr. Katy Liu, a family medicine doctor based in Missouri, says in the video. “Today, abortion clinics in Missouri are not required to meet the same basic medical standards as other healthcare facilities. Before making any medical decision, ask questions. Make sure your care meets the level of protection every patient deserves.”
In a statement, Whitaker said the video script was written by the attorney general’s office with help from the American Association of Pro-Life OB-GYNs, an anti-abortion medical organization that also connected the office with Liu.
“As the chief legal officer for the State of Missouri, the Attorney General’s Office is concerned about the current status of women’s health laws,”  Whitaker said. “She believes it is important to provide clear information to Missourians.”
The video was published less than three months before Missourians will be asked to vote on Amendment 3, a proposal placed on the ballot by lawmakers that asks Missourians if they want to repeal the 2024 reproductive rights amendment and reinstate a near-total abortion ban with limited exceptions for medical emergencies and for survivors of rape or incest in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. 
The PSA does not mention Amendment 3 or the November election. But its timing and message have drawn criticism from abortion-rights advocates, particularly because Hanaway has endorsed the amendment.
Representatives with Stop the Ban, the campaign opposing Amendment 3, accused Hanaway of being among anti-abortion politicians “using our tax dollars to bankroll their latest attempt to overturn the will of the voters and ban abortion.” 
“This misuse and abuse of our hard-earned money is the latest in a string of dirty tricks to try to take power away from us,” the organization said in a statement provided to The Independent. “But Missourians are seeing right through them.”
The PSA is among just six videos posted to the attorney general’s office’s YouTube page. The others are directed at identity theft and human trafficking.
Missouri labor unions, abortion rights groups turn unlikely alliance into ballot power

In 2022, Missouri became the first state to enact a trigger law banning abortion following the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade. In 2024, Missourians voted to overturn the ban, protecting the right to abortion up to the point of fetal viability. 
After the narrow defeat in 2024, anti-abortion leaders re-organized under the campaign name Her Health, Her Future, which now serves as the lead campaign organizing to pass the abortion ban amendment.
Hanaway is among Missouri’s top officials who endorsed Amendment 3. The messaging in the attorney general’s video also closely resembles arguments made by the campaign supporting the amendment.
“Missouri’s anti-women laws have removed health and safety standards for women’s health clinics,” the campaign’s website reads. 
Amendment 3 would also place a ban on gender-affirming healthcare for minors into the state constitution. It is already illegal in state law. 
Gov. Mike Kehoe has endorsed Amendment 3, and his wife, Claudia Kehoe, serves as the campaign’s treasurer.
In June, after 18 months of legal battles, both medication and procedural abortion access returned to Missouri with the circuit court’s ruling. 
Among the abortion laws left in place by the judge was a requirement that patients meet with a doctor in person before being prescribed medication abortion and a requirement that only physicians can perform abortions. 
But Zhang struck down most of the laws challenged by Planned Parenthood and the ACLU of Missouri as unconstitutional and unnecessary, including  special licensing requirements for abortion providers, a 72-hour waiting period between an initial consultation and an abortion, hospital admitting privileges for physicians performing abortions and a requirement for physicians prescribing medication abortions to have a state-approved complication plan.
These and dozens of other abortion regulations were litigated over a 10-day-long trial in January in Kansas City. Lawyers with the attorney general’s office argued during the trial that the laws, most of which were enacted by the legislature in recent decades, were “basic, common sense requirements” necessary to protect patients.
Attorneys for Planned Parenthood and the ACLU argued the laws weren’t designed to protect women, but rather to ensure abortion was “regulated out of existence” by creating logistical nightmares for patients and ethical dilemmas for providers without making procedures safer.
A few decades ago, prior to the passage of most of Missouri’s abortion restrictions and 2022 ban, thousands of abortions were performed in the state each year. Current data shows several thousand Missourians still accessed abortion in 2024 with the ban still in place, but had to travel to Illinois or Kansas to do so.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Lawmakers wrestle with the proliferation of e-scooters on Pa. roadways
description: E-scooters aren't legal to use on public roads in Pennsylvania, but stakeholders disagreed about whether to ban the devices or embrace them.
text:
Legislation pending in the state House would renew an e-scooter mobility program in Pittsburgh and put private users elsewhere on the right side of the law. (Capital-Star photo).Advances in battery technology and other innovations have made small, lightweight e-scooters designed to travel short distances cheaper — and faster — than ever, but Pennsylvania’s legal code and safety regulations haven’t kept up. 
The increasingly popular devices aren’t legal to operate on public streets in the commonwealth, and critics say car and truck drivers may be unprepared to share the road with their smaller counterparts.
“It’s like the wild west out there,” Scott Slingerland, the executive director of the Coalition for Appropriate Transportation, told state legislators in Lehigh Valley on Tuesday. 
Sen. Tim Kearney (D-Delaware) shares his concerns about the lack of state regulations for e-scooters on Sept. 1, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
Some lawmakers have proposed limiting who can drive e-scooters and where they can ride, similar to laws passed in over two dozen other states. Sen. Tim Kearney (D-Delaware) said thousands of people used e-scooters or similar vehicles across the commonwealth, but educating riders — especially minors — about safety considerations isn’t typical. 
“You can buy them online or in-store with ease … Retailers market e-scooters as a kid’s toy — Walmart even lets you filter for teen, tween, child and even toddler e-escooters,” Kearney said. “The reality is that e-escooters are not going away, and we cannot put the proverbial toothpaste back in the tube.”
Stakeholders agree that the vehicles should meet some minimum standards for braking, lights, reflectors and a “sound signal,” as described by Henry Beaver, who assists with multimodal transportation planning at the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation. 
Beaver added that operational requirements are critical for the safety of all road users, such as maximum legal speed limits, minimum ages to drive and where low-speed e-scooters can operate.
“Such as within bike lanes, but not between lanes of traffic or on roads with posted speed limits above a certain threshold,” continued Beaver.
But while Beaver said e-scooters should not be considered motor vehicles, thus making them exempt from state registration, titling and inspection, some law enforcement officials urged lawmakers to reconsider. 
Scott Bonn is the executive director of the Pennsylvania Chiefs of Police Association. (Screenshot from livestream)
“Our association believes the clearest and most enforceable statewide standard remains a prohibition on electric scooters on public roadways. But if the General Assembly determines that prohibition is not an option, Pennsylvania should not settle for partial regulation,” said Scott Bonn, the executive director of the Pennsylvania Chiefs of Police Association. 
Registration should be a statewide requirement if the commonwealth legalizes e-scooters, Bonn said, alongside a requirement for driver education or safety training before use.
 “The measure of any micromobility law should be straightforward: does it reduce the risk for riders, motorists, pedestrians and police while giving officers a law they can realistically enforce? If Pennsylvania cannot answer that question with confidence, the commonwealth should choose … prohibition,” he added.
 The importance of education

Others who spoke to lawmakers emphasized the utility of micromobility options like e-scooters. Whether going to school, a job or the doctor’s office, e-scooters, e-bikes or other vehicles can be more affordable and healthy for users. 
Ngani Ndimbie, the director of programs for Mobilify Southwestern Pennsylvania, shared examples of people she’d met in communities across the state who used e-scooters or e-bikes, including an older man who didn’t have the strength for long walks, a young man in a suit commuting for work and a family utilizing a city trail.
“Some of the benefits of these types of trips are increased mobility for the (older man) and the employer of the (young man) doesn’t need to provide an additional parking space,” said Ndimbie. 
Ngani Ndimbie, the director of programs for Mobilify Southwestern Pennsylvania, spoke about some of the benefits of micromobility options like e-scooters before lawmakers on Sept. 1, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
Ndimbie noted challenges for police enforcing separate laws for e-bikes or e-motorcycles, which can look very similar but have vastly different capabilities. 
These similarities “present difficulty for our officers in identifying what they’re really looking at. We don’t have a fast and accurate way,” said Allentown Police Chief Charles Roca. “It might be a feeling, but we don’t have a  weight on it. We can’t predict how fast it’s going.” 
Municipal governments are restricted from using radar to measure vehicle speed in Pennsylvania. 
Other states have mandated brightly colored tags to distinguish between types, Ndimbie added. 
Car dealerships are obligated to sell road-safe vehicles, but when it comes to the vast variety of micromobility options, Ndimbie said, “it is so easy to go online and buy something that is so far from safe and is so far from legal.” 
“One solution is education, making sure that residents understand what the product specifications are for what they’re trying to buy. This, I want to note, is I think a huge part of the problem … It’s really easy to buy something overpowered,” Ndimbie said. 
Avid cyclist Scott Slingerland is the executive director of the Coalition for Appropriate Transportation. (Screenshot from livestream)
Slingerland, with the Coalition for Appropriate Transportation, noted that PennDOT’s driver’s manual had a section on sharing the road safely with all users, including pedestrians and cyclists.
But “the challenges we see on the street are often not from new drivers,” he continued. “As a bicyclist, personally, a lot of the animosity would come from older (drivers) … and that comes from confusion about understanding a bicyclist’s place on the road or pedestrian yield laws.” 
He noted that Pennsylvania requires continuing education for many professions, including engineers like himself, lawyers, doctors and cosmetologists. The same could be done for drivers renewing their licenses, he continued.
“If there was something that were not very onerous, like watching a five-minute video from PennDOT when you renew online or at the driver’s license center, we could introduce high-priority safety topics like work zones, emergency vehicle yield laws, aggressive driving and things on vulnerable road users,” Slingerland said. 
 Kearney’s proposal

Kearney’s proposal, Senate Bill 1008, wouldn’t allow those under 16 to drive, and minors must wear helmets. Additionally, e-scooters would have a maximum speed of 20 mph, similar to the state limit on electric bikes, and could only carry one person at a time.
The legislation is named “Abby’s Law” after Abby Gillon, a 12-year-old who died when she was struck by a car while riding an e-scooter with a friend in Delaware County. Neither girl was wearing a helmet, and testifiers emphasized that helmet use is “very, very low” for e-scooter users.
When he first publicized the bill, Kearney said some of the earliest responses came “from people in their 30s and 40s who were using them for last-mile transportation.”
“They don’t want to drive the mile to go to the train station and then pay to park it,” said Kearney. “They could pop over on their e-scooters and just fold it up and carry it with them. Or lock it (up). It’s a benefit we want to keep. We want to make sure it works that way.”

E-scooters are everywhere in Pa.; this legislation would make them legal


In response to Bonn’s suggestion about mass registration, Kearney said others pushed back because it would be a “bureaucratic nightmare” when similar vehicles such as bicycles aren’t registered. Additionally, e-scooters and e-bikes don’t come with individualized identifiers — such as a car’s VIN — which would complicate proposals to register the vehicles.
“I’m not sure what the (line) is, but as the power grows stronger and the speed grows faster … then the need for registration becomes much more important,” said Kearney. “We feel like we need to make a step very soon to try to provide that kind of clarity across the commonwealth.”
He emphasized that he was open to discussions. His bill, which has bipartisan support, hasn’t yet had a committee hearing.
“Clearly the legislature has lots of work to go to put us in a better track here. I’m eager to get our legislation moving instead of languishing in committee,” Kearney continued, urging municipality leaders, families and stakeholders to pressure lawmakers on both sides of the aisle “to stop stalling and take action.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Conservative group’s anti-redistricting measure makes Colorado’s 2026 ballot
description: An effort by Democrats to pass a mid-decade redistricting plan was struck down by the Colorado Supreme Court earlier this year — but a conservative group’s countermeasure, which aims to prohibit any such partisan move in the future, is still set to go before voters in November. Backers of Proposed Initiative 256 submitted a sufficient […]
text:
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Jan. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)An effort by Democrats to pass a mid-decade redistricting plan was struck down by the Colorado Supreme Court earlier this year — but a conservative group’s countermeasure, which aims to prohibit any such partisan move in the future, is still set to go before voters in November.
Backers of Proposed Initiative 256 submitted a sufficient number of petition signatures to qualify for the 2026 ballot, the Colorado secretary of state’s office said Monday. As a constitutional measure, the initiative needed the support of at least 2% of the registered voters in each of Colorado’s 35 state Senate districts.
Colorado’s current eight-seat congressional map was drawn by its inaugural independent redistricting commission, established by a pair of anti-gerrymandering constitutional amendments passed by voters in 2018. The current congressional delegation is split 4-4 between Democrats and Republicans, with four seats rated as solidly Democratic, three leaning towards Republicans and one toss-up.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A Democratic group, in response to an unprecedented gerrymandering spree launched by Republicans at President Donald Trump’s urging, had backed a ballot measure this year that would have drawn a temporary map likely to give Colorado Democrats a 7-1 advantage in the 2028 and 2030 elections. But the state Supreme Court ruled in June that the effort violated the Colorado constitution’s single-subject requirement, which bars initiatives from appearing on the ballot if they contain multiple subjects.
The ruling also applied to several Republican counter-proposals that would have asked voters instead to tilt the congressional map in the GOP’s direction.
Separately, Initiative 256 was filed by Advance Colorado, a right-wing “dark money” group that does not disclose its donors, to block Democrats’ effort. The measure would require any mid-decade or “off-cycle” redistricting effort to be approved by both the state’s independent redistricting commission and the Colorado Supreme Court, and prohibit the approval of a map that “has been drawn purposefully to favor one political party.”
The initiative is one of up to 13 statewide measures that could appear on Colorado’s 2026 ballot. As a constitutional measure, it would need to receive 55% support from voters to pass.
Redistricting wars
Congressional maps are typically drawn once a decade after the decennial census. But Republicans launched a mid-decade gerrymandering war that began last year in Texas, where Trump had pressured the GOP into redistricting to give the party an advantage in the 2026 midterm elections. A month later, California Democrats moved forward with their own redistricting effort in response, and many other states around the country followed.
The ensuing tit-for-tat has heavily favored Republicans, who were able to push through new maps in seven other states, including Ohio and Florida, often solely through legislative action. In May, the conservative-dominated U.S. Supreme Court’s dismantling of a key provision in the Voting Rights Act kicked off another wave of redistricting in southern states, which rapidly redrew their maps to eliminate majority Black districts.
Meanwhile, Democrats’ efforts to respond have hit a variety of legal and procedural obstacles in blue states — many of which, like Colorado, already had independent redistricting commissions or other anti-gerrymandering measures in place. Voters in Virginia approved an aggressive Democratic gerrymander earlier this year, only for the state’s supreme court to block the plan weeks later.
California is the only state to have redrawn its map to advantage Democrats in 2026, though the party is also expected to gain a seat in Utah from a new map drawn as a result of a court battle that dates to 2022. Overall, the redistricting battles have given Republicans an advantage in about 10 additional districts as they look to hold on to their three-seat House majority.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah becomes 1st state to fully launch digital apostille program for international documents
description: Utah has become the first state in the nation to fully launch a digital apostille program — enabling Utahns to use an electronic platform to get international authentication for important legal documents for adoption, marriage, missionary service, education abroad or other needs in countries across the world.  “Now instead of bringing papers to the Capitol [[...]
text:
Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson speaks about the launch of Utah's digital apostille program during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 1, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Utah has become the first state in the nation to fully launch a digital apostille program — enabling Utahns to use an electronic platform to get international authentication for important legal documents for adoption, marriage, missionary service, education abroad or other needs in countries across the world. 
“Now instead of bringing papers to the Capitol or waiting for the mail, Utahns can choose to send documents and receive their apostille certificates digitally,” Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson said. “Our state is leading the nation in offering this fully-encrypted method of delivery, making the process more convenient and secure.”
Henderson, flanked by two rows of international flags, made the announcement in the Gold Room of the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Tuesday. 
“This is many years in the making,” she said, calling it a “big deal.” 
Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson speaks to reporters about the launch of Utah’s digital apostille program after a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 1, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
An apostille is an official authentication, similar to a notarization, that verifies the authenticity of a government document like a birth, marriage or death certificate so they can be legally recognized in other countries. They’re often needed for businesses looking to expand globally, families managing personal matters overseas, or students or missionaries traveling abroad. 
Apostille certificates are usually issued by designated governmental authorities like secretaries of state — or in Utah’s case, the lieutenant governor — and allow documents to be accepted across more than 125 countries under the terms of the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention. 
The Hague Conference has worked for nearly 20 years to make digital apostilles a reality. 
Utah’s official seal and Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson’s signature is shown on a poster board depicting an apostille certificate during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 1, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“We’re really proud to be the very first state to do it,” Henderson said. 
Christophe Bernasconi, secretary general of the Hague Conference on Private International Law, congratulated Utah in a prepared statement. 
“By combining electronic issuance with reliable online verification, Utah is helping to make the international use of public documents more efficient, secure and accessible, while strengthening the trust on which the Apostille Convention depends,” Bernasconi said. 
In recent years, Utah has been among a handful of states — including Washington, Montana, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Maryland, and Minnesota — to join a pilot program with the City University of Seattle and @Gov, Inc., a company based in Virginia, to make digital apostilles possible. 
As part of that pilot program, Utah issued more than 1,200 digital apostilles with a 100% acceptance rate, according to the lieutenant governor’s office. 
Now, Utah is moving to fully implement its digital apostilles for travelers, contracting with @Gov to use its ApostilleXpress platform, which the company describes as an “all-inclusive web-based platform designed to streamline the issuance of apostilles” for states and other authorities. 
Now, through an online verification portal on the lieutenant governor’s office’s website, Utahns can opt to receive their apostille certificate digitally. And starting this week, on Thursday, they can also choose to submit documents electronically. 
Utahns can still request paper authentications, at the cost of state fees that can range from $5 to $20 depending on the type of document, plus optional shipping costs. Digital authentications will cost about $75, including a $69.95 charge from the vendor and $5 in state fees. 
The state’s contracted vendor, @Gov, charges $69.95 for the digital delivery of the apostille as payment for its service, while the platform itself is “free to the state,” Chris Jackson, CEO of @Gov, said during Tuesday’s news conference. 
Chris Jackson, CEO and founder of @Gov, speaks about the launch of Utah’s digital apostille program during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 1, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
That cost is oftentimes cheaper than international paper delivery abroad, which can cost hundreds of dollars and often take three to five days, Jackson said. He also noted that a digital apostille can be used multiple times, and “technically it’s valid for life.” 
“So the savings are incredible to the constituents,” Jackson said. 
Henderson told reporters that over the past six years, demand for apostilles have increased by about 250%, from 18,000 in 2020 to more than 45,000 in 2026. In light of that growth — and in the spirit of an initiative her boss Gov. Spencer Cox launched last year to increase government efficiency and improve customer service, Henderson said she’s “proud” that Utah will be launching the program. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Until now, Utahns had to … make an appointment, travel in person to the capital, or mail their sensitive documents to my office to obtain their apostilles,” Henderson said. 
But now, the digital authentication platform is expected to reduce processing time by an estimated 80%, according to the lieutenant governor’s office.
Jonathan Freedman, president and CEO of World Trade Center Utah, applauded the new digital program, saying it will help solve a “real significant problem” for people, including Ukrainians who have come to Utah to work but run into obstacles when trying to obtain document authentication when they aren’t able to travel in-person to the Utah Capitol.
“(Worth) far more than the price of $75 … is the convenience, and it’s just such a huge barrier to getting this done,” Freedman said. “It’s really, really important to our foreign nationals here in Utah.”
A poster board depicting an apostille certificate sits on display during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 1, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)

name: VTDigger
title: Only Jews get to define antisemitism against us
description:
Good intentions don't change the nature of rhetoric that echoes old antisemitic tropes, even in the name of human rights.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Only Jews get to define antisemitism against us.
text:
Dear Editor,
VTDigger let a 14-year-old lecture Jews on what constitutes “real” antisemitism, giving her a platform that is especially inappropriate at a time of anti-Jewish hate crimes, which have surged since Oct. 7, 2023. Just as people without lived experience should not define racism for Black Vermonters or homophobia for gay Vermonters, neither should they define antisemitism for us. Only Jewish Vermonters can identify that prejudice.
Criticizing Israel is not inherently antisemitic. Our letter never said it was, nor did we call Zoya Bianchi an antisemite. No one is more critical of the Israeli government than Israelis themselves, a hallmark of a thriving democracy.
To Bianchi and Oscar Vulte, who also wrote to VTDigger recently: We believe you mean well. But good intentions do not change the nature of the acts of telling Jews which antisemitism is “real,” dismissing Jewish concerns as political cover for Israel and turning the Holocaust against Jews.
Whatever Vulte intended, his analogy asks readers to view stopping Israel’s alleged conduct through the historical lens of stopping Nazi Germany in 1941. A Nazi analogy cannot be used without invoking the memory of the Holocaust. Six million Jews were murdered in under four years, and 81 years later, our population has yet to recover. Since 1948, the Palestinian population within historic Palestine has grown fivefold. Using our attempted extermination to frame the Jewish state is Holocaust inversion. 

READ MORE

Bianchi cites a Syrian state news agency post for 73,381 deaths, omitting that the Hamas-run Health Ministry does not distinguish civilians from combatants. That framing misleads readers into seeing every death as an innocent civilian.
Nor has an international court found genocide in Gaza or Lebanon. The U.N. commission is not a court. Its Gaza statement is a nonbinding legal opinion, and it made no finding concerning Lebanon. The International Court of Justice case is pending.
Like most of the people signing this letter, I was bullied for being Jewish as a young person, and in the wake of the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust, I am still bullied as an adult. Some of us have been physically assaulted. All of us have endured verbal abuse and antisemitic taunts.
Israel is not beyond criticism. Jews are not beneath respect.
Mark TreinkmanAthens, Vt.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Public Service Commission lowers rate of return for energy company
description: The state commission regulating investor-owned utilities Tuesday reduced the rate of return that a St.Louis-based energy company can earn. The Alabama Public Service Commission voted to authorize Spire Alabama to receive a return on equity of 9.4% for the next two years, based largely on the recommendation of the Alabama Attorney General’s Office. That is […[...]
text:
A natural gas meter with pipe on wall.  The Alabama Public Service Commission Tuesday voted to reduce the return of equity for two Spire Energy subsidiaries after a rate hearing. (Bill Oxford/Getty Images)The state commission regulating investor-owned utilities Tuesday reduced the rate of return that a St.Louis-based energy company can earn.
The Alabama Public Service Commission voted to authorize Spire Alabama to receive a return on equity of 9.4% for the next two years, based largely on the recommendation of the Alabama Attorney General’s Office. That is a difference of 1.1% from the 10.5% return on equity that company officials sought, and lower than what it currently collects.
But commissioners also authorized the company, which serves roughly 500,000 customers in Alabama, to increase its monthly charge on customers by a total of $5 per month in phases. The company may increase the fixed monthly charge by $2.50 starting Oct. 1, 2026, and by another $2.50 on the same date next year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The ruling leaves customers’ utility bills steady for now by lowering the usage rate in exchange for higher monthly recurring cost.
“These recommendations lower the return on equity for both Spire companies from their current levels,” said Cynthia Almond, president of the Public Service Commission. “There is also an adjustment to the monthly customer charge.”
The PSC also reduced the ROE for Spire Gulf, the sister company that provides heating and cooling services to the Gulf Coast, to 9.6% from the 10.75% return on equity that the company requested. That is also lower than the nearly 10% it currently receives.
Representatives from the company said Tuesday they were disappointed with the PSC’s ruling.
“We know it is going to directly impact our ability to invest in growth and economic development in the state of Alabama,” said Reynolds Anderson, vice president of external affairs for Spire Energy, to reporters following the meeting. “We remain committed to providing safe, viable natural gas service for our customers.”
The hearing was part of a rate case that the PSC announced in June after the natural gas energy company could not reach an agreement with the Alabama Attorney General’s Office on an appropriate Rate Stabilization Equalization figure.
It is the first rate case that the regulatory agency convened since the 1980s, and came as the Alabama Legislature expanded the size of the commission and altered its structure amid mounting complaints over electricity prices in Alabama.
According to the Energy Information Commission, Alabama residents in June paid about 16.4 cents per kilowatt-hour, higher than the 14.89 cents per kilowatt-hour in the region.
Almond said that the monthly charge imposed on Spire is revenue neutral and does not increase the total amount of money that the utility collects.
“It shifts a portion of the recovery of fixed customer costs away from the volume metric, or usage-based, portion of the bill into the monthly customer charge,” Almond said.
Commissioners based their vote on evidence presented at a hearing presided over by Luke Bentley IV, executive director of the PSC, who served as the administrative law judge during the hearing in August.
Bently, reading from a prepared statement that was included as part of the agenda, said that “the Attorney General’s ROE recommendation is the most reasonable and more accurately reflects Spire Alabama’s cost of equity.”
Anderson said they based their request on rates that other companies received.
“As we look at economic development, first to grow and recruit business, that will probably be one area that we are going to be challenged with going forward,” Anderson said.
Sheree Martin, deputy director and general counsel of Energy Alabama, a nonprofit that advocates for renewable energy in the state, said in a statement that they were pleased with the decision from the PSC.
“Energy Alabama thanks the Commission for opening this first-of-its-kind rate investigation and for its decision to bring Spire’s return on equity down to a more reasonable level,” the statement said.
Energy Alabama sought a deeper rate reduction, suggesting that the Spire Alabama and Spire Gulf companies receive an ROE of about 8.3%.
The rate hearing is part of a process known as Rate Stabilization Equalization to decide the return rate that the company should earn. In the past, companies have typically submitted their request to earn a specific return that the PSC approves.
The PSC convened a rate case months after lawmakers passed HB 475, sponsored by Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, who eventually voted against his own legislation because of the changes the Alabama Senate made to the bill.
The bill ultimately signed by Gov. Kay Ivey expanded the PSC from three members to seven and gave Ivey four immediate appointments.  Appointees would be gradually replaced by staggered popular elections.
But the law also makes it harder for the PSC to convene a rate case. It establishes a Secretary of Energy, a cabinet-level post, with the authority to set the agenda for PSC meetings and to convene a rate case. It would take a supermajority of commissioners, five of the seven, to convene a rate case on their own or change the agenda.

title: Monique Worrell responds to rumors she’s about to be suspended again
description: Monique Worrell, the twice-elected state attorney for Florida’s 9th Judicial Circuit in Central Florida, responded forcefully Tuesday to what she described as a credible rumor she is again about to be suspended by Gov. Ron DeSantis. “Last night I received a phone call from someone telling me that my removal was imminent and that I […]
text:
Monique Worrell via her webpage. She reports she's heard rumors the governor plans to suspend her as state attorney.Monique Worrell, the twice-elected state attorney for Florida’s 9th Judicial Circuit in Central Florida, responded forcefully Tuesday to what she described as a credible rumor she is again about to be suspended by Gov. Ron DeSantis.
“Last night I received a phone call from someone telling me that my removal was imminent and that I was going to be replaced with an assistant statewide officer who used to work in this office,” Worrell said during a press conference in Orlando.
The Phoenix reached out to the governor’s office, but did not receive a response.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier — who has been critical of Worrell’s work — was asked about the rumored suspension earlier in Kissimmee and said he knew nothing about it.
“I just want people to do their job,” he said. “I want people to put bad guys away. When somebody kills another person, or tries to kill another person, I don’t want them to get a slap on the wrist. I want them to go away forever. I want to make sure that they don’t hurt another individual, and any state attorney who disagrees with me on that, in my opinion, is not doing his or her job effectively. That is negligence. That is gross incompetence. That is wrong.”
“We are doing our job, sir. And we’re doing our job very well,” Worrell fired back. 
She went on to cite crime statistics that she said made her point, saying shootings in Orlando were down 33% and overall violent crime, burglaries, and car thefts were down, as well. In Orange County, she said, crime has dropped by 28%.
“These are not my statistics. Check with law enforcement,” she added.
She went on offense against Uthmeier, referring to the leaked grand jury report concerning the Hope Florida Foundation scandal that surfaced last week.
“It was last week that I said to my staff, I have received information that some of the funds misappropriated were spent in the media market here in Central Florida, and said that we should look into it,” Worrell said. 
“Let me be very clear: In the event that I was removed, it won’t be because we aren’t doing our job, it will be because of concerns about what doing our job could look like for the people on the other end of that report.”
That grand jury report — obtained by CBS Miami and posted on its website Wednesday — did not result in any criminal charges but included multiple mentions of Uthmeier. It concluded that Uthmeier, who was Gov. Ron DeSantis’ chief of staff at the time, “was in a position of authority over those involved” in allegedly diverting $10 million from a Medicaid settlement intended to help poor children get health insurance, and that his Keep Florida Clean PAC was the prime recipient of those funds.
Uthmeier has called the investigation a “politically motivated witch hunt driven by Democrats and a far-left Democrat state attorney in Tallahassee.” However Florida U.S. Republican Sen. Rick Scott told the Tampa Bay Times in a written statement that the report was “deeply concerning,” adding that “Florida families deserve accountability, not more finger pointing in Tallahassee.”
DeSantis suspended Worrell and removed her from office on Aug. 9, 2023, for “neglecting her duty to faithfully prosecute crime in her jurisdiction,” and replaced her with former Orange County Circuit Judge Andrew Bain. She legally challenged the decision, which the Florida Supreme Court upheld in June 2024.
She ran again for the seat that fall and defeated Bain by 14 percentage points.
Uthmeier has sniped at her performance in office since she was re-elected. Last fall he accused her of refusing to prosecute pedophiles.
He later threatened her with removal because of a disagreement about whether to charge a woman who shot and killed a man who attacked her in her car during a road rage incident, writing, “Your actions likely constitute a breach of your ethical obligations. And they may also constitute misfeasance, malfeasance, neglect of duty, and incompetence.”
Worrell later dropped the murder charge.
She said Tuesday that her 2023 removal wasn’t because she wasn’t doing her job, “but because of  politically motivated decisions that were not based in fact “
“And I will not allow politics to work to distract me from the responsibility that the voters have entrusted me with,” she said. “My focus is not on political attacks, my focus is on victims, on public safety, on accountability, and on justice. And until the people in the 9th Judicial Circuit tell me otherwise, I will continue to do the job they elected me to do. That’s where my attention belongs, not on politics, but on the work.”
Since being appointed attorney general by DeSantis early last year, Uthmeier has threatened to remove multiple locally elected officials for their stances on working with the federal government on immigration enforcement, but has not actually done so.

title: USPS whistleblower predicts ‘catastrophic’ effect on elections under Trump vote-by-mail order
text: The U.S. Postal Service rushed the development of electronic tools to comply with a Trump administration policy placing new restrictions on mail-in voting, and defied a court order to stop work on the system, according to an explosive whistleblower complaint published Tuesday by Democratic U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal.The unnamed whistleblower predicted the result could be “foreseeable catastrophic disruption to our coming nationwide elections based on the reckless pursuit of readying a new, insufficiently tested, poorly planned mail-in ballot screening system.”The system contains several massive flaws and, with virtually no time to spare before the November elections, USPS officials kept on developing an online verification system in violation of a Massachusetts judge’s injunction, the whistleblower said. The system’s verification standard is “a zero percent failure rate,” meaning that any batch of ballots that contain any single ballot with an error would result in an entire batch being rejected, the whistleblower said. The verification system itself is suspect due to a hurried and untested development of an online portal that states were to use to upload voter and ballot information for verification by federal officials, the whistleblower said. Up against a tight timeline ahead of the midterm elections, the agency also continued to develop an online tool related to the regulation, despite the federal court order to pause the work, according to the whistleblower.No specific USPS officials were named as responsible for directing the work to continue in defiance of the courts. USPS did not immediately return a request for comment from States Newsroom.States were expected to begin using the system as soon as Tuesday, according to the whistleblower.Potential for millions of missing ballotsThe allegations from the whistleblower, a federal official whose exact role is not specified, were detailed in a report by Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit legal group that is representing the whistleblower. Blumenthal, of Connecticut, attached the report to a letter to U.S. Postmaster General David Steiner.“The apparently sloppy and rushed manner in which the Federal Ballot Mail Portal and supporting IT systems are being built poses significant risk,” the report said. “Potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all.”The new policy, which President Donald Trump initiated in a March executive order, has been the subject of intense legal fighting over the past few weeks that continues with an appeal now sitting at the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals. Democratic state officials and voting rights groups have said the regulation would likely disenfranchise voters.Blumenthal said the USPS should reject the policy entirely.“We urge you to abandon this ill-conceived, unconscionable plan and ensure that all Americans can exercise their constitutional right to vote, including by mail, without interference by USPS,” he wrote.‘Problems at every stage’In a final rule published Aug. 21, the Postal Service said states would use a to-be-developed online portal to upload information about the envelopes being used for mail ballots and the voters who received them. USPS would also use the portal to verify that all ballots and voters complied with the requirements set out in the new rule.But the project was beset with several challenges, in part spurred by the unrealistic timeline for development, the whistleblower said.The whistleblower’s disclosure “identifies problems at every stage of USPS’s development of the Portal, demonstrating deeply flawed plans for implementation,” Blumenthal wrote.A project of the portal’s size and importance would normally “take nine months to a year or more” to finish, according to the whistleblower’s disclosure. Smaller current Postal Service IT projects have been given eight-month timelines, according to the whistleblower. USPS began developing the mail ballot portal in June, just three months before it was to be introduced and less than five months before Election Day, according to the disclosure.Individual elements of the tool have not been sufficiently tested, “rendering meaningful testing of the project impossible,” the whistleblower said.“The Whistleblower believes that there has been insufficient internal testing of the system,” the disclosure said. “Such testing is critical to determine whether it will work on September 1, when states could be expected to start using it.”Software developers on the project have “considerable concern” that the project skipped “standard principles of testing and debugging new software before launch,” the whistleblower said.One faulty barcodeThe IT problems heighten the danger of another major issue: a policy of rejecting entire batches of ballots based on a faulty barcode on a single ballot.According to the whistleblower, “the administration has hidden the high likelihood” that standard raises for major disruptions in ballot delivery. “As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state - effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” the report said.A misread barcode could result from something as simple as a voter’s changed name after marriage or a move of address, Blumenthal said.Court orderThe whistleblower said the USPS paused work for about a month after Judge Indira Talwani in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts issued an injunction against Trump’s executive order, finding, in part, that it likely violated the U.S. Constitution’s provision granting states the power to administer elections.But USPS officials then ordered work to resume on the project, in defiance of the judicial order that remained in effect, the whistleblower said.The whistleblower added that the agency ignored another temporary restraining order Talwani, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama, issued last week and upheld Monday, and continued to work on the project.In his letter to Steiner, Blumenthal asked if that was true and posed several other questions stemming from the whistleblower's report, and asked for a response by Friday.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Rep. Diamond proposes gaming reform to save skill games and boost tax relief
description: Rep. Russ Diamond (R-Lebanon) said in a news release Tuesday that taxing slot-machine-like skill games could also provide nearly $1 billion in additional property tax relief for homeowners.
text:
A Pennsylvania Skill game in a Delaware County convenience store. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)With the future of skill games in Pennsylvania on the line, a Lebanon County state lawmaker is proposing an update to the commonwealth’s Gaming Act to legalize the gambling machines before they’re forced to go dark.
Rep. Russ Diamond (R-Lebanon) said in a news release Tuesday that taxing slot-machine-like skill games could also provide nearly $1 billion in additional property tax relief for homeowners.
“Pennsylvania’s gaming law was originally written for a much different era,” Diamond said, noting the legislation would bring skill games under regulation as the industry faces a legal deadline.
Skill games are video-based gambling devices that allow players to place a bet on the outcome of a game of chance to win a jackpot. They differ from casino games in that they offer players a chance to win back their money by completing a skill element, though few take the opportunity, opting instead to bet again for a shot at a big win.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Critics say they’re predatory, appealing to those who can least afford to lose money gambling; risk exposing children to gambling; and contribute to crime in neighborhoods where they’re common.
The state Supreme Court in June invalidated what it called “deeply flawed” lower court decisions that it said improperly excluded the machines from regulation under the Gaming Act and the Crimes Code.
State courts had ruled skill games are not covered by the Gaming Act or the state’s general ban on unregulated gambling. As a result, skill games have existed and proliferated for more than a decade in a legal gray area, becoming common fixtures in neighborhood stores, restaurants, gas stations, private clubs and even dedicated skill game parlors. 
Recognizing that thousands of small businesses and private organizations such as fire companies and American Legion posts depend on revenue from the machines, the court stayed the effect of its decision for four months. That means Skill Games will be illegal starting Oct. 13, unless the General Assembly passes legislation to legalize them.
Gov. Josh Shapiro has proposed legalizing and taxing skill games as a new revenue stream in his last two budget addresses, but the legislature has been unable to agree on the details.  
Efforts to pass skill games bills ended with an impasse last year in the Senate over the tax rate and other details. The commonwealth’s casino industry, which has lobbied heavily against them, is taxed at a hefty 55% and pushed for a comparable rate.
Skill games in a Virginia corner store. (Ned Oliver/Virginia Mercury)
Senate leaders endorsed a plan to tax skill games at 35%. Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming), whose district includes skill game maker Miele Manufacturing, sponsored competing legislation to tax the machines at 16%. Yaw and Sen. Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) also introduced a bill to impose a monthly fee of $500 per machine, a proposal favored by the industry.
Diamond’s proposal would regulate and tax skill games at 20% with a limit of five machines permitted only in clubs, restaurants and bars with liquor licenses and qualified truck stops. It would also reduce the tax rate for casino slot machines and online casino games to 49.9%.
The legislative package would establish a defined formula to maximize property tax relief, provide reliable annual funding for the Race Horse Development Trust Fund, nearly double money available for gambling addiction treatment and provide revenue for the state’s General Fund, Diamond said.
Noting that property tax relief is now “hidden away” on school property tax bills, Diamond’s proposal would make the refunds more tangible by issuing the money as a “gaming dividend” payment to each of the commonwealth’s 2.87 million qualified homeowners. 
“Every time I talk about property taxes, people complain about not seeing the relief from casinos promised by politicians more than 20 years ago,” Diamond said. “This set of bills will increase property tax relief for 96% of Pennsylvania’s homeowners and deliver it directly into their hands. The amount of relief they receive will grow in direct proportion to the annual growth of all forms of legal gaming in the Commonwealth.”
Even without growth in legal gaming in the next fiscal year or additional revenue from legal skill games, every qualified homeowner would receive a dividend payment of at least $702 annually, the news release said. In Diamond’s Lebanon County district, that would equate to an annual increase in tax abatement of $459 to $602, depending on which school district they live in.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Reynolds calls for a ‘total ban’ on kratom and synthetic variants in Iowa
description: Gov. Kim Reynolds joined state law enforcement and public health officials Tuesday in warning Iowans of the risks associated with kratom and its newer, synthetic variants. Kratom is typically marketed as a natural or herbal supplement for pain and anxiety, and is commonly sold in liquid, capsule and powdered form at gas stations and convenience […]
text:
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, center, speaks at a Sept. 1, 2026, press conference about the risks associated with kratom. (Photo by Clark Kauffman/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Gov. Kim Reynolds joined state law enforcement and public health officials Tuesday in warning Iowans of the risks associated with kratom and its newer, synthetic variants.
Kratom is typically marketed as a natural or herbal supplement for pain and anxiety, and is commonly sold in liquid, capsule and powdered form at gas stations and convenience stories.
At Tuesday’s press conference, Reynolds and others stressed that the product’s availability does not equate to safety.
“Kratom is not a supplement, it is not a medicine, and it is not safe,” Reynolds said. “These products are widely accessible, often sitting on shelves in gas stations and convenience stores, and many Iowans may not realize the serious risks they pose.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kratom contains psychoactive compounds, including 7‑hydroxymitragynine, or 7‑OH, that act on opioid receptors in the brain. Dr. Robert Kruse, the state medical director at Iowa’s Department of Health and Human Services, cited growing concerns about concentrated and synthetic 7‑OH products that are now flooding the market.
“Concentrated and synthetic 7-OH products can have powerful opioid-like effects and pose serious health risks,” Kruse said. “The fact that these products are sold over the counter does not mean they are safe. They can lead to dependence, severe illness, overdose and death.”
Reynolds and Kruse said there have been 45 kratom‑associated deaths in Iowa that have been confirmed since 2024. Sixteen of those deaths occurred in the first seven months of 2026, they said, and Iowa Poison Control has received 68 calls so far this year related to kratom exposure.
On Aug. 26, 2026, the federal Drug Enforcement Administration classified three synthetic kratom‑derived compounds — mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM‑15 and MGM‑16 — as Schedule I controlled substances. In addition, 7‑OH is currently under review for emergency classification as a Schedule I controlled substance.
DPS Commissioner Stephan Bayens urged Iowa retailers to closely review the specific products on their shelves, as any reliance on packaging claims could lead to the illegal sale of controlled substances.
Kruse and Reynolds indicated Iowa DHHS intends to expand its statewide public awareness  campaign to include new messaging about the dangers of kratom and synthetic 7‑OH. In addition, they said, the Iowa Board of Pharmacy is currently considering emergency rules to address the issue.
Reynolds: ‘I do want to see a total ban.’ 
Earlier this year, the Iowa House passed, in 69-26 vote, House File 2133, a bill that would have designated kratom products — including both substances made from the Mitragyna speciosa plant and its synthetic equivalents — as Schedule I hallucinogenic substances.
Under that legislation, people found possessing kratom would have faced a serious misdemeanor charge for their first offense, an aggravated misdemeanor for their second and a Class D felony charge for subsequent offenses.
However, the Senate version of the bill, Senate File 2192, never made it to the floor for a vote, so the products — excluding those recently classified by the DEA as Schedule I substances — remain legal for both sale and possession.
At Tuesday’s press event, Reynolds was asked why she didn’t push for passage of the Senate bill before the Iowa Legislature adjourned.
“You’re assuming we didn’t,” she said. “We did. I think this was something I supported, I was in favor of.”
She later said she had voiced her support for the measure in discussions with senators but wasn’t certain as to why they didn’t bring the legislation to the floor for a vote. “I did support it, and I don’t think that would be surprising considering my track record on illegal substances,” she said.
During the 2026 session, Rep. Ray Sorensen, R-Creston, introduced an amendment to the House bill that would have limited dosage amounts and implemented age restrictions, labeling and testing requirements for kratom products. He said such changes, by regulating rather than banning kratom, would “do more to protect Iowans than placing kratom into Schedule I (status) and pushing the entire market underground.”
“Prohibition removes safety controls,” Sorensen said at the time. “Right now kratom remains legal — products can be tested, labels can be required, age restrictions can be enforced. (If) it becomes Schedule I, the legal market disappears. Products move to black markets, there’s zero testing, there’s no consumer protection. For concerns of safety, banning the product entirely may actually make it less safe.”
Sorensen’s amendment failed in a 44-51 vote.
Reynolds said Tuesday she continues to support a total ban on not only the natural kratom products but also their synthetic spin-offs. “I do want to see a total ban,” she said, “otherwise it’s just too easy to skirt around it and we’re dealing with the same thing… I would advocate for a total ban.”
Kruse encouraged Iowans to familiarize themselves with the signs of an opioid-type of overdose and to call 911 and, when necessary, use naloxone to rapidly reverse the effects of such an overdose. For non‑emergency concerns about adverse reactions, he said, Iowans can call Iowa Poison Control at 1‑800‑222‑1222.
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration warns kratom consumption can lead to addiction, and that “several cases of psychosis resulting from use of kratom have been reported.” Additionally, medical institutions like the Mayo Clinic state kratom use has resulted in side effects such as liver damage, high blood pressure and weight loss.

name: Daily Montanan
title: In effort to move hay, governor temporarily relaxes some road rules
description: Montana has temporarily relaxed some rules for the amount of time truck drivers can be on the road in an effort to help ranchers feed their cattle.  In a Monday executive order, Gov. Greg Gianforte waived several motor carrier regulations including “hours of service” limits that dictate how much a driver can work and load […]
text:
Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte delivers the State of the State address before a joint session of the Montana Legislature on Jan. 13, 2025. (Micah Drew/ Daily Montanan)Montana has temporarily relaxed some rules for the amount of time truck drivers can be on the road in an effort to help ranchers feed their cattle. 
In a Monday executive order, Gov. Greg Gianforte waived several motor carrier regulations including “hours of service” limits that dictate how much a driver can work and load size restrictions.
Montana has been battling dry and severely dry conditions for six years, said the executive order, under a separate 2021 drought declaration. The order is set to expire on Sept. 13, 2026.
Montana Department of Agriculture Director Jillien Streit said it was an effort to cut red tape.
“When our producers are facing tight supplies and economic pressures, they do not need to also battle regulatory provisions that can slow down the essential movement of feed,” Streit said in a press release. “I appreciate Governor Gianforte lifting service requirements around hay delivery ensuring that our farmers and ranchers can do more with their precious time as it can be a bottleneck in volatile times like these.”
Hay is generally cut through the summer and into fall in Montana. Drought can adversely impact the amount of forage available to cattle throughout the summer and fall, leading ranchers to rely more heavily on bought feed, such as hay.
The press release from the Governor’s Office said the rules were relaxed for “certain carriers.” It’s not the first time Gianforte has suspended motor carrier regulations  — Governor’s Office spokesperson Charlie Roth said he did so in 2021, 2024 and 2025 for various reasons, including fire response, another hay hauling and to support fuel delivery for heating.
“With the persistent drought, it was essential that we eliminate any roadblocks that threaten the viability of our producers and their operations,” Gianforte said in a press release. “Through this executive order, we will ease motor vehicle restrictions to help producers get hay where they need it to go.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas attorney general’s race nears toss-up designation in ‘Democratic-leaning midterm’
description: OLATHE — The Kansas attorney general’s race is the latest to gain recognition from national political observers, who began cautiously adding to Democrats’ November chances following the August primaries. In a rematch from four years ago, Attorney General Kris Kobach, the Republican, is still favored to beat attorney and former law enforcement officer Chris M[...]
text:
Kris Kobach seeks a second term as Kansas Attorney General. He appears at a Kansas Chamber candidate forum on Aug. 27, 2026, in Olathe. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)OLATHE — The Kansas attorney general’s race is the latest to gain recognition from national political observers, who began cautiously adding to Democrats’ November chances following the August primaries.
In a rematch from four years ago, Attorney General Kris Kobach, the Republican, is still favored to beat attorney and former law enforcement officer Chris Mann, but Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election forecasting arm of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, readjusted its rating of the race from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican,” which is closer to a toss-up than a safe Republican seat. 
“Kobach’s hardline approach to such issues as immigration were once out of the Republican mainstream, but his style and substance is more at home in the MAGA-focused second Trump term. The question is how well that will play in a more Democratic-leaning midterm,” wrote Louis Jacobson, senior columnist for the politics center.
Republicans are still predicted to clinch key statewide and federal offices, including the Attorney General’s Office, the U.S. Senate and the governor’s seat, which has been held by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly for the past eight years. 
“Democrats getting a credible contender for U.S. Senate, as well as governor, probably helps Mann’s odds,” Jacobson said.
On Aug. 4, Sabato’s Crystal Ball adjusted the U.S. Senate rating from “safe Republican” to “likely Republican” after the Rev. Adam Hamilton won a crowded Democratic primary. He faces Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall.
Mann and Kobach faced off in 2022, when Mann lost by fewer than two percentage points.
Both the Democratic Attorney General’s Association and the Republican Attorney General’s Association have waded into Kansas, backing their respective party candidates with campaigning and advertising support.
The Republican group announced on Aug. 25 a $7 million, 13-state ad blitz that included a mix of digital and TV ads in Kansas. It described its effort as an “aggressive early offensive barrage.”
“RAGA will spend more this year politically than in any year in its 27-year history, and the stakes have never been higher,” said Adam Piper, the group’s executive director, in a news release. 
The Democratic group on Thursday criticized Kobach’s involvement with the nonprofit We Build the Wall. During his 2020 U.S. Senate campaign, Kobach violated federal election and campaign finance laws when he purchased and used the nonprofit’s 295,000-person donor list for under market value.
Kobach acknowledged to reporters Thursday that “there’s going to be a lot of outside spending” on the Kansas attorney general’s race leading up to November.
“But as a candidate, it doesn’t really change my strategy,” Kobach said. “I’m still running on the same record. I’ve still got the money that I’ve raised, and I’m going to spend it the way I’m going to spend it in terms of the advertising and things we do.”
Mann said his campaign has raised four times as much as Kobach’s in 2026. He raised about $787,000 from Jan. 1 to July 23 while Kobach raised roughly $196,000, according to state campaign finance records. Kobach had $607,000 on hand going into the Aug. 4 primary, and Mann had about $643,000.
“Those are all from the small-dollar donors,” Mann said. “I think our average donation is around $150. Eighty-three percent are from Kansas, and we’re proud of that number. If other organizations want to spend in this race on my behalf, then that’s up to them, and, frankly, we have to be able to combat the dark money that’s coming at us. So we’ll make sure that we have the resources we need to do that.”

name: Delaware
title: Del-One uses AI to nearly double lending capacity without adding staff
description: Delaware’s largest credit union says its digital assistant reviews auto-loan documents in minutes, offering other businesses a model for adopting AI within their existing systems DOVER, Del. — Del-One Federal Credit Union is using artificial intelligence to expand its auto-lending capacity without increasing its staff, offering a Delaware example of how busi[...]
text:
Pictured L-R – From Del-One, CIO Marc Kidwell, CBO John Chartrand, CXO Horacio Garcia-Korosec, President & CEO Dan McCarthy, and Joseariel Gomez-Ortigoza, Founder and CEO of Shastic.
Delaware’s largest credit union says its digital assistant reviews auto-loan documents in minutes, offering other businesses a model for adopting AI within their existing systems
DOVER, Del. — Del-One Federal Credit Union is using artificial intelligence to expand its auto-lending capacity without increasing its staff, offering a Delaware example of how businesses can incorporate AI into everyday operations.
The credit union has deployed an autonomous digital assistant named Valeria to review documents submitted by automobile dealerships through Del-One’s indirect lending program. The technology, developed by Shastic, works within Del-One’s existing MeridianLink lending platform.
Del-One said the system could help its two-person funding team increase indirect loan production from approximately $8 million to $15 million per month without hiring additional employees.
“With Valeria, we believe we can nearly double our indirect production, from $8 million a month to $15 million, without adding a single person,” said John Chartrand, chief operating officer of Del-One. “We want our people to think, not enter data.”
AI handles paperwork, employees make decisions
When an auto-loan packet arrives, Valeria reads the documents, creates a funding checklist and flags missing, incomplete or inconsistent information before a Del-One employee begins the final review.
The process takes less than 15 minutes per packet, according to the credit union. Del-One said Valeria has completed more than 500 reviews without clearing a defective packet.
The AI system does not determine whether an applicant qualifies for credit or whether a loan should be approved. Those decisions remain with Del-One employees. The technology completes repetitive document-review work and provides an auditable record of its findings.
The distinction is important as financial institutions and other businesses explore ways to use AI while maintaining human oversight of decisions affecting customers.
“The model here is that our best people manage exceptions, verification and strategy; the digital workforce handles the box-checking, staring and comparing,” said Dan McCarthy, president and CEO of Del-One.
Working within existing systems
Del-One’s approach illustrates how an organization can adopt AI without replacing its primary software systems. Instead of purchasing an entirely new lending platform, the credit union added the digital assistant to a system its employees already use.
The strategy also represents a shift from treating AI as a general-purpose tool to assigning it a specific, measurable business responsibility. In Del-One’s case, that responsibility is checking dealer loan packets for missing or conflicting information.
Del-One said it has deployed two digital assistants and identified other potential applications in lending, account opening and collections. Each would perform a defined back-office function while employees retain responsibility for decisions, unusual cases and member interactions.
A potential AI road map for other businesses
The experience provides a potential road map for other businesses considering AI. Companies can begin with a focused project inside their existing systems, while regional technology and business consultants such as Trellist Marketing and Technology can help identify appropriate processes, develop an implementation plan and manage the organizational transition.
“What Del-One is doing reflects a pattern we see across every industry right now,” said Maria Gunther, CEO of Trellist Marketing and Technology. “Businesses do not need to replace their core systems to get real value from AI. They need to give it a specific, well-defined job inside the systems they already run.
“The first step for most companies is not a big platform decision. It is identifying one repetitive, high-volume process where a person is currently doing work a machine can do faster, then keeping human judgment in charge of the exceptions and the relationships. That is how AI transformation actually takes hold in an organization — one clearly scoped responsibility at a time.”
Building a digital workforce one role at a time
Shastic describes that approach as building a “digital workforce,” with AI agents added one role at a time to perform defined back-office responsibilities.
“Every credit union is trying to figure out how to get real value from AI,” said Joseariel Gomez-Ortigoza, founder and CEO of Shastic. “Del-One has shown what it looks like in production: not one tool, but a digital workforce added one role at a time, on a platform they already own.”
The initiative could allow Del-One to process a larger volume of loans without increasing administrative costs at the same rate. It also could shorten the time between a dealer submitting a complete loan packet and receiving funding.
Del-One, founded in 1960, describes itself as Delaware’s largest credit union. Its mission is to create an easy and enjoyable banking experience in which convenience is combined with personal service.
Shastic develops autonomous digital assistants that perform lending-related administrative work within credit unions’ existing technology systems.
