Kline and Bashari helped launch Epic's Pathways program, which helps Oklahoma students age 21 to 30 complete a high school diploma. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Parwana Nazari once lived as a “very open and free girl back home” in the Jowzjan province of Afghanistan.
She was studying Uzbek literature at a university when the Taliban took control of the country in August 2021.
Nazari, who used to go to work and school by herself, suddenly was prohibited from leaving her house unaccompanied by male relatives. She became one of millions of girls and women in Afghanistan barred from attending secondary school and higher education.
Her life changed again in 2024 when she won a “golden chance” to move to America through a visa lottery.
She arrived last year in Oklahoma City alone with no documents proving her level of education. 
A program Epic Charter School created, called Pathways, has given Nazari and other Oklahoma students age 21 to 30 the chance to earn a U.S. high school diploma — an opportunity she said she never knew would be possible. Recent changes the Oklahoma Legislature enacted in state law have helped the program grow significantly.
Although she started with zero high school credit, Nazari said Epic is providing “enough support and help for me that I could finish.”
“I want to be as independent as I can because I live here on my own,” Nazari said in Dari through an interpreter. “I want to reach a level of speaking English that I would be able to run my life on my own without needing help of translation or someone else to help me.”
Since leaving Afghanistan and resettling in Oklahoma City, Nazari and other Afghan women have set their sights on earning a high school diploma, something largely impossible in their home country under ultraconservative Taliban rule. Each woman is completing free online courses — like English, U.S. history and algebra — through Epic’s Pathways program. 
The program serves Oklahomans of all nationalities and genders, but administrators at Epic said it wouldn’t exist had local Afghan refugees not pushed for an opportunity to earn an American diploma.
“These few people that were calling me daily, they changed the trajectory for thousands of Oklahomans that didn’t get the chance to finish their education in the first place,” said Misty Kline, Epic’s language and cultural services coordinator who helped found the program.
Misty Kline, language and culture services coordinator at Epic Charter School, said Afghan refugees called her daily for an opportunity to earn American high school credits. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The initiative has helped almost 500 students graduate high school since it was established in 2023 and now enrolls 1,020 students so far this school year, Epic officials said. The school spends $3.1 million annually on Pathways for the cost of curriculum, devices and staff compensation.
A high school equivalency test, like the GED, for years has been the traditional option available to adults 21 or older wanting to earn a diploma. 
Kline said Pathways is a better fit for students who have gaps in their education. Each student is assigned an individualized learning plan and a one-on-one teacher, who is “their guide, their cheerleader,” she said, and there’s no make-or-break exam at the end of the process.
Pathways started with 20 students, all from Afghanistan, and a budget of $100,000 from payment card refunds. The unusual funding source was necessary because Oklahoma law at the time forbade state dollars from supporting most high school students over the age of 20.
But, recent legislative changes created a dedicated funding stream and enabled more students to enroll.
Oklahoma lawmakers in 2024 permitted state funds to support free public high school courses for students age 21 to 25. A year later, the state Legislature raised the age limit to 30 and required these courses to be delivered online.
When Asia Stanikzai arrived in Oklahoma from Afghanistan, she was older than the maximum age of 20 to enroll in a traditional high school program. She said it left her feeling “hopeless” and “frustrated.”
Stanikzai already had finished high school in Kabul, but her family left the country without most of her education records. Pathways offered an opportunity to prove her level of learning and to study English.
“I (found) out that Epic school is offering such a program for us, and I got really excited and happy,” she said in Dari through an interpreter. “Since the day I started, I’m getting better every day. The way I’m speaking, my communication, and I’m so happy.”
She’s been taking classes for two years and expects to graduate in May. Stanikzai and her sister, Saria, also a Pathways student, said they hope to study cosmetology and own their own makeup styling businesses once they finish their high school credits.
Epic Charter School is headquartered at the 50 Penn Place complex in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Many of the original 20 Pathways students similarly lost their education documents in the rush to evacuate from Afghanistan. Tens of thousands of people, including many who cooperated with the American military, were quickly airlifted out of Kabul when U.S. troops withdrew and the Taliban took control in 2021.
Nearly 2,000 Afghan refugees have since settled in Oklahoma. Although initially welcomed, these refugees have faced recent calls for removal by some politicians in the state.
Tabasum Hussaini, one of the original Pathways students, said she and other Afghan refugees never wanted to have to leave their homes, but her life under the Taliban would be “scary” if she had stayed.
“We had no choice except coming here, and we want to build a better life for our kids, for their future,” she said in an English interview with Oklahoma Voice. “We don’t want them to go through the same thing that we went (through).”
Hussaini was in her fifth semester of law school and was working as a teacher when her family fled from Kabul five years ago. She hasn’t given up on her dream of earning a law degree. 
Earning her high school diploma through Epic has enabled Hussaini to enroll in pre-law courses at Oklahoma City Community College. Hussaini, who was working as a Walmart stocker when she first learned of Pathways, now has a job supporting other refugees at The Spero Project, which aids in resettlements.
Multiple Afghan women who spoke with Oklahoma Voice recounted similar stories of interrupted schooling and lost academic transcripts.
Others said they already had dropped out of school in Afghanistan because of marriage. 
Malaika Ander never finished her schooling after getting married at the start of 12th grade, but she said “the flame of my passion for learning and my dream of graduating never died in my heart.” 
She enrolled in Epic’s Pathways program this year to finish her education.
“This great initiative gave us a second chance to reclaim our academic identity,” she said in English.

title: Colorado River drought lawsuits may dampen Wyoming dam plans
description:
Two legal actions raise questions about Wyoming’s water supplies and plans to construct another dam in southern Wyoming.
The post Colorado River drought lawsuits may dampen Wyoming dam plans appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
As drought and over-allocation of Colorado River water shock the West, two lawsuits raise serious questions about irrigation in Wyoming and state plans to build a new dam and reservoir in Carbon County.
As soon as the federal government announced that it would cut Colorado River supplies to California, Nevada and Arizona, Nevada went to court claiming that the headwater states of Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah could more easily handle the reductions.
At the same time, Colorado conservationists argued in court that Denver’s plans to pour Colorado River water into an enlarged reservoir for the city’s use amounts to building an $819 million bathtub that might never be filled.
Together, the lawsuits raise legal arguments regarding Wyoming’s reliance on irrigation water from the Green and Little Snake rivers, whether ranchers would still have access to traditional diversions and whether a proposed dam and reservoir above the Little Snake River valley is feasible and worthwhile.
The Nevada lawsuit is a direct challenge to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s plan to cut allocations to three of the seven states that rely on Colorado River flows — Nevada, California and Arizona. Burgum’s Aug. 21 approval of the new allocations left the headwater states of Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico largely untouched.
But Burgum made “no analysis of the very real and dire economic effects to millions of municipal water users if the taps are turned off or water use must be significantly curtailed,” the Silver State’s lawsuit asserts. Instead, Nevada says, Wyoming and its headwater-state cohorts, “where water conservation has been less of a priority … have additional lower-cost options to respond [to] reduced … water deliveries.”
Three weeks before Burgum’s decree, conservation groups were in the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals in Santa Fe arguing that the city of Denver shouldn’t be allowed to complete an expansion of the Gross Dam that would bolster the city’s supplies with water from the Colorado River Basin. Among other reasons, conservation lawyers argued the city was squandering taxpayer money on a boondoggle.
“They’re building a giant bathtub, even though there’s likely no water to ever fill it,” attorney William Eubanks said on behalf of the river-protection group Save the Colorado.
Collectively the cases raise questions regarding whether Wyoming irrigators will continue to receive their traditional shares of Colorado River Basin water and whether Wyoming’s plan to build the West Fork Dam and reservoir above the Little Snake River Valley makes sense and will be challenged.
Should Wyoming share the pain?
River flows have declined from some 14.6 million acre-feet to about 12.3 million acre-feet, the Nevada lawsuit states, underscoring the shortage. Nevada’s challenge could upend what so far has been an easy ride for Upper Basin states, including Wyoming.
Wyoming was pleased with Burgum’s plan for the Colorado River because the plan would impose no administrative cuts to the state’s 7% share of river flows. Wyoming believes it has not yet used what it’s entitled to and has plans to construct the West Fork Dam on Carbon County’s Battle Creek to impound 10,000 acre-feet and irrigate every year with 6,000 acre-feet from the proposed reservoir.
An aerial view of the general site of the proposed West Fork Dam at the head of the Little Snake River Valley in Carbon County. The proposed dam would be 264 feet high, 700 feet long and made out of concrete. (Major King for WyoFile)
But while Wyoming might skate under Burgum’s plan, the suit states Burgum didn’t consider whether “to equitably reduce water distributions … between the Upper Basin States and Lower Basin States.” In other words, Nevada wants Burgum to consider mandatory cuts to Wyoming’s water use, not just voluntary ones that Burgum endorsed.
Nevada makes its case by arguing it has “a relatively meager 3.3%” of the water apportioned to the Lower Basin States and Mexico,” but that amount accounts for 90% of what’s used in the Las Vegas Valley. That region has taken significant efforts to conserve water, the suit states.
Burgum’s plan was forged without detailed consideration of impacts to Nevada residents and in violation of environmental and procedural laws, the suit states. That misstep comes with real-world consequences, Nevada claims.
As a result of flawed analyses, Burgum “obscure[s] the full extent of economic and social costs to cities like Las Vegas, North Las Vegas, Boulder City, and Henderson,” a region with an $180 billion annual economy, the suit states.
The solution may lie upstream in headwater states, the suit contends, where water conservation has been less of a priority and lower-cost options abound.
Nevada wants the Burgum plan, a 10-year program, blocked and struck down.
Water for Wyoming’s new reservoir?
The Denver water lawsuit and challenge to the city’s Gross Dam enlargement has been ongoing for years and has produced more detailed arguments and criticism that could have implications across the West. The lawyer representing conservationists said the city and federal government didn’t look deep enough into drought and climate change.
Those planners “never analyzed whether there will be any average-to-wet years in which Denver can divert the water under its existing water rights, let alone whether there will be enough of those years to ever fill this expanded reservoir of 72,000 acre-feet,” Eubanks told the court.
Denver and federal officials did not “demonstrate that there would actually be enough water during these average-to-wet years to fill this reservoir,” he said. Too, there would be “massive environmental destruction on both sides of the Continental Divide.”
Planners also failed to consider many other options to satisfy Denver’s water needs, critics say. The city’s lawyer, and one representing the federal government, argued the opposite — that relevant factors were taken into account and that there would be enough water — diverted across the Continental Divide — to fill the new storage space.
A group of natural resource law professors filed a brief supporting the conservation groups and slamming the government for not taking climate change and drought into account. In its evaluation of the Goss Dam expansion, the federal government “entirely neglected to consider the potential environmental consequences of diverting water out of a Basin experiencing its worst period of drought in over a thousand years,” the 11 experts stated.
“The proposed project on Little Snake River drainage is probably the most threatened by what’s going on in the Colorado River.”Gary Wockner
Gary Wockner, executive director of the 17-year-old Save the Colorado nonprofit, said drought could lead to mandatory cuts to Wyoming’s water use, potentially rendering the proposed West Fork Dam useless.
“Ranchers and farmers are likely going to be subject to being forced to send water downstream,” he told WyoFile. “The proposed project on Little Snake River drainage is probably the most threatened by what’s going on in the Colorado River because it’s solely for a handful of ranchers.
“If you follow just the politics of how this is playing out,” he said, “the bullseye is on agricultural water. There are more members in the U.S. House of Representatives in Southern California, in the areas that get Colorado River water, than there are in the rest of the Colorado River Basin combined.”

title: From clashes to care: Fort Washakie mom finds way out of troubled path

text:
Rock bottom happened amid yet another physical altercation. This time, Milanii Engavo Sojos said, she was in the middle of two men — one the father of her daughters, the other a new love interest. The men were fighting, punching, pulling at her, almost in a tug-of-war. There was nothing playful about it. 
There had been many fights before this; Sojos has the long, purple scars to show for them. This time, however, something shifted internally. Afterwards, when the cops had cleared out and she had sobered up, she felt immensely tired of the chaos and rudderlessness of her life. 
“It was just like, ‘My kids don’t need this. I can’t keep doing this,’” she remembers thinking. “I’m not old enough, but I feel old for how much stuff I’ve been through.”
The trouble didn’t magically end there. There was more partying, more brawling, more booze-fueled tumult on the Wind River Indian Reservation. But that inflection point tipped Sojos, who is Eastern Shoshone, to think about a different future for her two young daughters. 
And in the last year, Sojos, who is 23, has pursued those options through a hardheaded commitment. She passed her high school equivalency exam, moved to Gillette where she earned her certified nursing assistant certification and, with the help of the nonprofit organization Climb Wyoming, found a job as a home health aide. She enrolled in criminal justice classes this fall at Gillette College and has been working to stay sober with the help of her fiancé. 
After earning her certified nursing assistant certification, Milanii Engavo Sojos started working as a home health aide in Gillette. (Courtesy Milanii Engavo)
“My heart is elated that she’s changed her life,” said her mom, behavioral health specialist Erin Engavo, who lives in Fort Washakie and also studied nursing and criminal justice in college. After years of worry over her daughter, she said, “I’m just so proud of her.” 
It hasn’t been easy or seamless, Sojos said. For others who want to break out of the cycles of violence and dead ends that she found herself washing through for years, she said, it takes accountability and patience. Change doesn’t happen overnight. 
“It’s gonna be on you at the end of the day,” Sojos said from Gillette. “It’s gonna be on you to get up and make that change for yourself or others.”
In the ring
Sojos was born on a Navy base in Virginia, where her parents were stationed. They split up when Sojos was very young, and her mom moved back to Fort Washakie when she was a toddler. Her mom married her stepfather and the family moved around a lot, but Sojos and her siblings would return to the reservation every summer to visit grandparents and cousins. 
She was in seventh grade in Billings, Montana, when she got into her first fight, she said. It was a stupid beef over misplaced jealousy, but a crowd showed up outside the school and someone caught the scrum on video. It circulated through the school, and her reputation as a formidable fighter began.

Milanii Engavo Sojos with a boxing trophy. She began boxing as a teenager after getting into fights at school. (Courtesy Milanii Engavo)

More fights followed. Brawls in the alley, in the hallways, in locker rooms. Sojos never turned down an opponent, even older girls. It was around this time that she discovered her biological father had died, and in retrospect, she said, she had a lot of anger and grief over never knowing him.
Someone suggested she try boxing, and she started training in her friend’s garage gym. Though she was only 14, Sojos was aggressive and athletic, and she excelled in the ring. In a short period of time, she won a city boxing match, then a state tournament in Butte, then a national amateur tournament in Independence, Missouri. 
Her boxing career was cut short, however. Her grandma, Thelma Engavo, started having health problems. Sojos moved to Fort Washakie to be closer to her, and ringside opportunities faded. 
Transitioning to living full-time on the reservation was difficult, she said. In Billings, she had been singled out for being native, but at her new school in Fort Washakie, classmates called her “white girl.” It didn’t help that she had a big mouth and a stubborn streak, she said, and she didn’t know all the cultural norms. 
She did meet a boy, however. They began an on-again, off-again relationship that would last years. But it was toxic, Sojos said, and would help fuel the tumult that defined the rest of her teens.
Troubled times
Sojos entered a troubled patch. She dropped out of high school around age 15, and with her boyfriend, got caught up in a swirl of binge drinking and violence on the reservation. 
“We started getting drunk with each other, partying, trying to get enough money to find the next bottle,” she said. 
There were fights at parties, brawls involving bricks. Sojos’ grandfather came home one day to find her outnumbered and scrapping in the yard; he broke it up. Even her relationship became violent, she said. 
Once, after breaking it off with her boyfriend, Sojos flew to the East Coast to visit her paternal relatives. While there, she made up with her ex, who had moved to Denver. And instead of flying home to Riverton, Sojos didn’t make her connection. 
“I ended up jumping off in Denver, and he got me,” she said. They lived in motels and strung jobs together as their relationship continued its wild rollercoaster. 
At some point, Sojos’ mom came to retrieve her, bringing her back to Fort Washakie. A couple weeks before her 18th birthday, Sojos found out she was pregnant. 
That led to another reconciliation with her ex, who also returned to Wyoming, moving in with Sojos and her mom. But the birth of their daughter did not mark the end of the chaos, the seesawing of the relationship. And within a year, she had another daughter. 
Another thing that didn’t stop was the fighting. There was a fight at the Shoshone Rose Casino with a neighbor. Cops were called after a hostile mob showed up at her house late one night. Another breakup led to custody battles. She fell back into drinking with some cousins and friends. This time, it got bad, she said. 
“We weren’t eating nothing, we were just drinking, partying, finding the next house party, or whoever had bottles or could come join us,” she said. “My mom was pretty mad that I was doing that to my kids, my family.”
She moved out of her mom’s house and in with her aunt, promising to get her life on track. “But I wasn’t going anywhere,” she said. She ended up in jail a couple times. It was around that time that the tug-of-war incident happened with her ex. During the scuffle, her daughters were outside in a truck. When she realized afterwards that they had been out there alone for a couple hours, Sojos said, some clarity began to set in about how bad things had gotten. But it wasn’t until yet another fight that took place in the presence of her older daughter and left her with 20 stitches that she started to firm up her mind.  
“Reality kind of set in some more,” she said. “I was like, ‘this ain’t the life I want for me or my kids.’”
She was not quite 21 years old. 
The turnaround
There was a period of aborted attempts at settling down. Then Sojos rekindled a relationship with a guy from her past. He had also been in trouble, including serving prison time, and he also wanted to change his life. 
After he moved to Gillette to work on oil rigs, he told her that he would pay for her to get her high school equivalency through the Penn Foster program. The education provider is entirely online and flexible; there are no set class times or rigid deadlines. It relies on self-motivation. 
Sojos had made many half-hearted attempts to get her high school equivalency through the HiSET program offered by Central Wyoming College, but she never finished. With her boyfriend’s offer to pay, she said, there was more at stake.
“I was like, ‘I need to actually put some ambition into this,’” she said. She finished in about five weeks, she said, earning her diploma in December. 
After that, things started to change fast. She moved to Gillette and got a job at an Amazon warehouse. She learned about and applied for Climb Wyoming, which offers free job training and other support services for single moms through a 12-week program. Climb Wyoming helped her enroll in a CNA program at Gillette College. When she passed her nursing boards in May, she became the first in her cohort to earn her license. Climb then helped connect her to job resources; a week after getting her license, she was hired as a home health aide at Kindred Souls. 
Sojos was very clear about her goals and desires, said Climb Wyoming’s Gillette Program Manager Dane Josyln. 
“Milanii is very well-spoken, very articulate,” she said. Sojos had a bit of skepticism when it came to trusting the process at Climb, Joslyn said, but what became clear is that “she has this very strong propensity to learn.”
Milanii Engavo Sojos with her two young daughters. (Courtesy Milanii Engavo)
Currently, Sojos is juggling the home health aide work with parenting her girls, who just started Head Start early childhood education. She’s enrolled in Gillette College for more courses this fall; she wants to pursue an education in criminal justice with the ultimate goal of becoming a probation officer. 
When she went into the CNA program, she said, she felt like she needed a new adventure to keep her sober. These days, she stays plenty busy with work, school and raising her daughters. Her boyfriend, who is now her fiancé, continues to be a positive influence. And, of course, the hardheaded nature that in the past got her into trouble is now leading her in a better direction. 
“Now I’m trying to settle down,” she said.

title: Fulcher signs on to bill limiting federal agents’ access to Flock, other surveillance data
description: Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher signed on to federal legislation to limit federal law enforcement’s access to data from automated license plate readers, like Flock cameras, and other surveillance equipment.  Fulcher announced Monday in a press release that he is co-sponsoring H.R. 9716, called the Protecting Rights in Video and Equipment Acquired Dis[...]
text:
A Flock Automated License Plate Reader near the Lowe's on Overland Road in Boise,  as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun)Congressman Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho (Photo courtesy of Russ Fulcher’s official website)
Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher signed on to federal legislation to limit federal law enforcement’s access to data from automated license plate readers, like Flock cameras, and other surveillance equipment. 
Fulcher announced Monday in a press release that he is co-sponsoring H.R. 9716, called the Protecting Rights in Video and Equipment Acquired Discovery Act, or Privacy Act. The legislation would, in most cases, require federal law enforcement to obtain a warrant from a federal judge before accessing surveillance data from state and local systems, including cameras that capture images of vehicle occupants, long-range microphones, electronic fingerprint detection technology, and “substantially similar technology” as determined by the U.S. attorney general, according to the press release.  
“I’m proud to sign on to this legislation to protect the privacy rights of Idahoans from increasingly intrusive surveillance data collection and to prohibit the widespread deployment of such surveillance tools with federal dollars,” Fulcher said in the press release. “It’s simple: if the federal government wants to access state and local systems’ data on citizens, they need to get a warrant.”
The legislation would also put time limits on the retention of data federal authorities obtained, unless a court authorizes an extension or the data is needed as evidence for ongoing prosecution. The bill would also prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase or install surveillance devices, with some exceptions for systems used solely for toll collections on federally funded highways, school violence prevention programs, grants provided under the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act, and portable systems for specific law enforcement operations with a warrant.  
The bill, brought by Texas Republican U.S. Rep. Keith Self, was introduced July 15 and has not yet been voted on by a committee.

 Idahoans have expressed concerns about surveillance cameras  

A number of Idaho cities statewide have contracts for automated license plate readers, called ALPRs, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Flock is the most common and well-known brand of this type of camera. 
In July, nearly 100 residents filled the Caldwell City Council chambers, and about a dozen of them spoke about their concern about the city’s use of Flock cameras, the Idaho Press reported.
All eyes on Flock as Idaho navigates surveillance technology across the state

A 2025 Idaho state law prevents these readers from being used for anything other than “the investigation of felony, misdemeanor crimes, traffic accidents or to search for missing or endangered persons.”
However, Twin Falls cameras were searched at least 631 times in March, May and June of 2026 for immigration-related searches, the Sun reported. The searches originated from outside Idaho, and later the Twin Falls Police Department changed its network sharing policies to avoid inadvertently running afoul of Idaho law and its own restrictions on immigration searches. 
In March, then-Jerome County Sheriff George Oppedyk used Flock cameras to search for his wife’s vehicle hundreds of times between July and September 2025, KMVT reported. Oppedyk retired in April. In early August, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers across the nation had been charged with or accused of misusing the cameras to track women.
Fulcher’s office regularly polls constituents who email him, and recent polls found that data privacy was one of their top concerns, Fulcher  told the Idaho Capital Sun in an Aug. 12 interview. 
“The data privacy stuff, especially recently with the Flock cameras, that has got a lot of people on edge,” Fulcher said.

title: Trump administration’s gutting of Endangered Species Act could legalize extinction
description:
Rescinding the regulatory definition of ‘harm’ opens the door to degradation of habitat species need to survive, writes Ted Williams.
The post Trump administration’s gutting of Endangered Species Act could legalize extinction appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Had Donald Trump been president in 1973, when Richard Nixon signed the Endangered Species Act into federal law, the Gunnison sage-grouse would be extinct. Close to 90% of all Gunnison sage-grouse remaining on the planet are in the Gunnison River Basin of west-central Colorado. The rest are in Utah. They’ve been extirpated from Arizona and New Mexico.

Opinion

The species is critically endangered in fact, if not by official decree. It is protected by the act as just “threatened” because the Interior Department lost a lawsuit brought by Gunnison County, Colorado, the states of Utah and Colorado, and ranching, livestock and energy-development interests. 
Now, the plaintiffs don’t even have to fret about threatened status. The Trump administration has essentially done away with the Endangered Species Act itself. On July 14, the administration finalized a rule that legalizes the destruction of habitat that sustains all threatened and endangered life.
It’s still a crime to kill or damage any listed individual plant, invertebrate, fish, reptile, amphibian, bird or mammal. But it’s perfectly OK to destroy all habitat formerly deemed necessary for a species’ survival, which will likely render said species extinct. “Common sense” is how Trump’s Interior Secretary Douglas Burgum defines this nonsensical approach.
Wildlife advocates are outraged. “Taking habitat protections out of the ESA is like taking anti-discrimination provisions out of the Civil Rights Act,” declares Animal Wellness Action President Wayne Pacelle. “The law may still bear the same name, but its core provision and promise have been hollowed out.”
Bart Melton of the National Parks Conservation Association writes that the rule “defies common sense” and that it “paves the way for mining, oil and gas drilling, logging, and development in areas that are crucial to the survival of some of our most vulnerable species.”
Earthjustice attorney Kristen Boyles condemns the rule as violating “the core purpose of the statute and decades of legal precedent, including from the U.S. Supreme Court.”
Meanwhile, multiple lawsuits to block the Trump administration’s “harm” rule are underway. 
For half a century, “harm” had been defined by law as not just human-caused death and damage to listed species, but also as “significant modification or degradation” of their critical habitat. With that definition, the Act has saved 99% of listed organisms from extinction.
Gunnison sage-grouse remain on Earth because an intact Endangered Species Act required the federal government to write recovery plans for listed organisms. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and partners didn’t have a choice. If they had done nothing, they’d have violated federal law.
The main threats to Gunnison sage-grouse are invasive cheatgrass, wildfire, fragmentation of habitat by urban and suburban sprawl and prolonged drought caused by climate change.
Close to half the remaining grouse habitat is in private hands. So voluntary protection and restoration of habitat by landowners has been paramount. Under the intact Act, most of this protection and restoration was implemented by “Safe Harbor” agreements covering almost 100,000 acres.
Safe Harbor is a voluntary partnership between private landowners and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to protect and restore low-elevation wet meadows and sagebrush that are crucial for long-term Gunnison sage-grouse survival. In exchange, Safe Harbor signatories receive a guarantee that they won’t get hit with additional land-use restrictions or penalties under the Act if their habitat improvements attract more Gunnison sage-grouse.
When the Trump administration proposed its habitat harm rule on April 15, 2025, almost 360,000 public comments were filed. While the administration declines to list the number or percentage of negative responses, an Earthjustice analysis reveals that about 99% of the comments were opposed. The Administrative Procedure Act requires federal agencies to consider public commentary and provide a rational, evidence-based explanation for their final rule. The Trump administration routinely ignores this directive.
Without the act’s mandate for recovery plans, there will be little motivation for landowners to honor Safe Harbor agreements or sign new ones.
The Trump administration’s new, destructive Endangered Species Act is scheduled to take effect Sept. 14. Unless the environmental community succeeds with litigation to block it, Gunnison sage-grouse don’t stand a chance. And we won’t just lose the Gunnison sage-grouse. Hundreds of other listed organisms will slide into oblivion, and the most successful habitat protection and restoration law ever enacted will cease to exist.

title: Idaho’s Medicaid work requirements start in January. Here’s how they will work.
description: In about four months, low-income Idahoans on Medicaid expansion will need to prove they are meeting new work requirements to remain on the public assistance program. The new rules — made largely by the federal government — require people to prove they are working, going to school, or volunteering at least 80 hours a month […]
text:
Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest budget cuts to the state's Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)In about four months, low-income Idahoans on Medicaid expansion will need to prove they are meeting new work requirements to remain on the public assistance program.
The new rules — made largely by the federal government — require people to prove they are working, going to school, or volunteering at least 80 hours a month to maintain health insurance coverage through Medicaid expansion.
Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron presents on the agency’s budget to the Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee on Jan. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
As officials with the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare prepare to implement the new rules, they fielded questions on Monday from the public.
“There probably is some anxiety about what this will actually look like, and what this will do to individuals’ coverage,” agency director Juliet Charron said. “And I just want to say here from the get-go that the team here at the Department of Health and Welfare, we have approached this very thoughtfully.”
The virtual town hall is the first of several that the state health agency that runs Medicaid plans to host in the coming months. 
 What is Medicaid expansion?

Medicaid expansion is a program, approved by Idaho voters through a 2018 ballot initiative, that offers health insurance coverage to a group of people commonly called the working poor. Idahoans can qualify for Medicaid expansion if their household earns up to 138% of the federal poverty level, or $29,863 for a family of two each year. 
About 85,000 Idahoans receive Medicaid expansion coverage, according to figures from the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 How were the work requirements created?

The work requirements were part of a massive federal budget bill, called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed in 2025 by Congress and signed into law by President Donald Trump. 
The Idaho Legislature and Gov. Brad Little earlier this year approved the work requirements through House Bill 913. For years, Idaho lawmakers and the governor have tried to add Medicaid work requirements. 
 What are the new work requirements?

Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Division of Self-Reliance Administrator Tonya Standerfer (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare)
Under the federal law, work requirements, also called community engagement requirements, require people enrolled in Medicaid expansion to prove that they are working, doing community service or educational or training activities for at least 80 hours each month. If you can show you earn at least $580 each month, that would also work, said Tonya Standerfer, the administrator for the agency’s Division of Self-Reliance, which processes eligibility for public assistance programs.
But there are several exemptions to the work requirements, such as for:

Women who are pregnant, or receiving postpartum Medicaid coverage.
People who are caregivers of a child age 13 or younger, or for a person with a disability
People who have a physical, mental, or developmental disability that “makes it hard to do daily activities,” or people who have a disabling mental health condition, or people who are blind
People who have a substance use disorder, or are in a drug or alcohol treatment program
People who between the ages of 19 and 25 and have aged out of foster care
People who are Native American or Alaskan Native, or who are eligible for Indian Health Services
People who are already required to meet work requirements for the public assistance programs called Temporary Aid for Needy Families, which is cash assistance, or the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which is also known as food stamps
People who are incarcerated
People who are veterans with total or 100% disability ratings.
And people who have a “serious or complex health condition that requires regular medical care and limits or prevents your ability to work”

 How do the work requirement exemptions work?

Idahoans who are ‘medically frail’ are exempt from Medicaid work requirements. How do you prove it?

Officials punted questions about one exemption meant for people with disabilities, dubbed the medically frail exemption. Standerfer said that exemption would be addressed in a future town hall. She said state officials are working with a contractor to determine how to automatically pull medical claims data to verify whether someone is medically frail. Previously, state officials said patients may need to provide a doctor’s note if the state doesn’t already have “evidence of medical frailty” in its claims system.
Asked how people can prove they qualify for exemptions, Standerfer said the state’s system already has information related to many of them. But she said the state could ask for verification.
She also said the state hasn’t decided on one possible carveout — in which the state can ask for an exemption for people who live in a county with a high rate of unemployment. She said the Department of Labor would likely make that decision in October.  
 How many Idahoans could lose Medicaid expansion because of work requirements? 

Medicaid work requirements and other changes in the “Big Beautiful Bill” could kick 20,000 to 34,000 Idahoans off Medicaid expansion by 2028, according to an analysis by the Urban Institute and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. That’s lower than what some other researchers estimate.
Idaho Medicaid Deputy Director Sasha O’Connell presents to the Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel in Rexburg on Dec. 15, 2025. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
But state health officials have said they believe that most Idahoans on Medicaid expansion already meet the work requirements. In an early review of data for all 83,000 people on the program at the time, Idaho Medicaid Administrator Sasha O’Connell told the Idaho Capital Sun in July that the state agency found that 68,400 Idahoans on Medicaid expansion met the new work requirements.
 How far back do you need to prove work history under Idaho Medicaid’s work requirements?

Idaho lawmakers decided to require Medicaid expansion enrollees to prove work history for three months before their application for Medicaid. That time period, called a lookback period, is the longest allowed under the federal law. 
People on Medicaid will also be required to re-apply to the program every six months, another change under the new federal law that increases the eligibility verification frequency from once a year. 
 What can you do if you’re on Medicaid expansion?

Right now, the state cannot remove people from Medicaid expansion for not complying with Medicaid work requirements.
But starting in January, they can.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



In July, Standerfer said state officials notified all people on Medicaid expansion about how the new rules could impact them. And she said the agency’s customer service center has been taking calls and helping people navigate the new rules, including whether they may qualify for exemptions. 
Standerfer urged Idahoans on Medicaid expansion to create an account through Idalink, update their communications preferences and sign up for text alerts so they can get reminders to recertify their eligibility for the program. She also recommended that people on Medicaid expansion track their hours at work and in community service. 
Find more information about how the new work requirements work in Idaho, and about future town halls, online at the Department of Health and Welfare’s website.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: ‘It’s a powerful symbol:’ Idaho’s Liberty Bell is back on tour and coming to your county
description: In May 1950, Idaho’s very own version of the Liberty Bell arrived in the Gem State.  Nearly a year later, the bell found its home: Sitting prominently in front of grand steps leading up to the Idaho State Capitol — and being loudly rung by passersby. But before it was mounted at the state’s Capitol, the […]
text:
A replica of the Liberty Bell sits outside of the Idaho Statehouse, as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)In May 1950, Idaho’s very own version of the Liberty Bell arrived in the Gem State. 
Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office)
Nearly a year later, the bell found its home: Sitting prominently in front of grand steps leading up to the Idaho State Capitol — and being loudly rung by passersby.
But before it was mounted at the state’s Capitol, the bell toured the state on the back of a pickup truck. And as Americans commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday this year, Idaho’s Liberty Bell is headed back on tour. 
“We want to have people experience the birth of a nation,” Idaho Treasurer Julie Ellsworth said in an interview. “… We want a memorable thing that touches every place of Idaho.”
The tour starts Wednesday with a round of stops in East Idaho, starting in Pocatello and working its way further east, before visiting each of the state’s 44 counties.
But how did Idaho even get its own version of the Liberty Bell? 
The bell — modeled after the cracked original in Philadelphia that has become a national symbol — was one of many cast and given to states in an effort to sell U.S. savings bonds, according to a history of the bell prepared by the Idaho State Historical Society. 
Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell, moved from its typical home, sits on the back of a Ford F-450 flatbed truck. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office)
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Trucking a state artifact

This will be one of the few instances — outside of its recent restoration — when Idaho’s Liberty Bell has left its home at the Capitol.
State officials designed this tour to mimic the original tour of the bell from 76 years ago. 
On its journey across Idaho, the state’s Liberty Bell will sit on the rear axle of a flatbed Ford F-450 pickup. The state is leasing the custom truck for free from Kendall Ford, an auto dealer in the Boise area, Ellsworth said. 
The new truck has a few more bells and whistles than the original truck had — like enhanced suspension and Spudjamin Franklin, one of many “Revolutionary Spuds” that the state treasurer created to celebrate America’s 250th anniversary. 
But it’s also missing something that the original truck, a custom Ford R-5 flatbed, had: a loudspeaker, which was used to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds, according to Janet Gallimore, the executive director of the Idaho State Historical Society, which cares for the state’s artifacts and helped plan the bell’s recent restoration.
The 1950 tour of Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell was to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office)
“I … just love the symbology of the bell and what it means, what it meant for obviously the beginnings of our country and the founding of our country, but what that idea of liberty, justice, self-government means to people today. Because it’s a powerful symbol of those things that make us American,” she said in an interview. 
On the road, the bell will be encased in a cloth cover. At its stops in each county, it will remain on the bed of the truck for display. 
 When will Idaho’s Liberty Bell be near you?

Officials aren’t releasing a daily schedule of where the bell will be in each town at a given time until closer to the dates. But Ellsworth says every child that they see on this tour will get a copy of Spudjamin Franklin’s new graphic novel-styled autobiography, which she wrote. Ellsworth said she’ll try to join the tour as much as she can.
“It is so symbolic of everything about liberty,” she said of the bell. “But it’s tangible. It’s touchable. It’s understandable.”
On Wednesday, the bell will make its journey from Boise to Pocatello — before beginning a nearly three-week tour across East Idaho. 
Here’s a few key dates to watch:

On Saturday, Sept. 5, the bell will be at the Eastern Idaho State Fair Parade in Blackfoot. 
On Friday, Sept. 11, the bell will be at the America250 in Idaho Freedom Festival in Idaho Falls.
On Saturday, Oct. 24, the bell will be in Moscow for University of Idaho’s homecoming
On Saturday, Nov. 14, the bell will be in Boise for the Veterans Day Parade

After it first arrived in Idaho in 1950, the bell toured the state and was put on exhibit at the Idaho State Museum, before finding its permanent home in front of the Idaho State Capitol on Nov. 19, 1951.
That’s the same day this year that state officials plan to bring the bell back home.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee cattlemen brace for beef market unrest after Trump announced tariff-free imports
description: Tennessee cattle producers are preparing to sell their spring-born calves in a beef market roiled by President Donald Trump’s Aug. 21 announcement of a plan to import about 660 million pounds of beef tariff-free in an effort to ease high prices for consumers. The president’s proclamation drew pushback from national and state cattle associations and […]
text:
Cattle stand in a field at Blue Grass Farms in Bethesda, Tennessee, on Aug. 27, 2026. 
(Photograph by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee cattle producers are preparing to sell their spring-born calves in a beef market roiled by President Donald Trump’s Aug. 21 announcement of a plan to import about 660 million pounds of beef tariff-free in an effort to ease high prices for consumers.
The president’s proclamation drew pushback from national and state cattle associations and individual farmers who said the move could reduce prices for American cattle and create market uncertainty, both of which make it more difficult for farmers to recoup the costs of raising cattle and invest in growing their herds at a time when input costs are rising.
Trump and the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced multiple initiatives aimed at fortifying beef herds in the United States in the days that followed, including a promise to allow farmers to process their own beef and a program allowing producers to insure the value of breeding heifers.
But none of these initiatives are an immediate “fix” for current market challenges, and producers and economists are skeptical over whether they will be a long-term help or harm, according to University of Tennessee Extension Livestock Economist Andrew Griffith.
“When you throw out this type of information, and it causes the markets to go down quite a bit, which it has done, there’s going to be several people that aren’t happy about it because their paychecks are not going to be nearly as big as what they would have expected a few weeks ago,” Griffith said.
The cost of raising cattle has risen in recent years due to higher fuel, feed, equipment and veterinary prices. (Photograph by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
U.S. cattle producers reported 86.2 million head of cattle in January, the smallest herd since 1951, according to the USDA. There are many reasons for this smaller herd: higher costs of fuel, feed and other inputs needed to raise cattle, the fallout from drought and natural disasters, consolidation in the industry and the aging demographic of farmers, to name a few.
Beef prices were 9.4% higher in July 2026 than in July 2025, according to a USDA analysis of Consumer Price Index data.
The United States will begin importing tariff-free beef trimmings — which are used to make ground beef — from other countries on Sept. 1, and will continue for 90 days. The imports must be sold at “25 percent below the market price,” according to Trump’s proclamation. 
Trump stated in a post on his social media platform Truth Social that the plan is meant to “reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.” But economists and producers say these imports aren’t likely to translate to significant savings for consumers at grocery stores.



Quotation







They’re looking at a short-term fix when the only answer is a long-term fix. It’s going to drop our price, but our input costs are not dropping. 


– Michael Curtis, Curtis Watkins Farms


Beef cattle are one of Tennessee’s top agricultural commodities, making up nearly 17% of agricultural cash receipts, according to the Tennessee Department of Agriculture. The state is home to about 2 million cattle.
Michael Curtis co-owns Curtis Watkins Farms with his daughter, Krista Watkins in East Tennessee. “They’re looking at a short-term fix when the only answer is a long-term fix,” Curtis said. “It’s going to drop our price, but our input costs are not dropping.”
“It causes a loss of confidence in the market,” said Ben Neale, owner of Light Hill Meats in Columbia, Tennessee. Neale raises cattle and owns a small, federally inspected processing plant. The high price of beef is the result of supply and demand, he said, and the market would “work itself out” when prices rose higher than customers were willing to pay.
“The dust hasn’t had time to settle so that the market can get back to trading as it should,” Griffith said. “And we may see several more weeks of unrest, because I don’t think anybody knows what the implications of any of this are really going to be.”
USDA initiatives met with skepticism
As Curtis planned his retirement and Watkins took the reins of the family’s cattle operation, they decided to downsize from 40 head to 10. Raising cattle has become more and more expensive, the father and daughter said, with the rising cost of fuel, feed, equipment and veterinary supplies and care.
The farm mostly sells “freezer beefs,” bulk cuts from a single animal, to local families in addition to feeding themselves, Watkins said. She’d like to grow the herd again, but “with everything costing like it does, it’s just going to take some time.”
“If I had a heifer born today, and I wanted to keep her in my herd, it’s three years before she brings me any money by selling a calf,” Curtis explained. “That’s three years of input costs that I’ve still got to keep maintaining and put into that critter before she brings me a return.”
Krista Watkins and her father, Michael Curtis, own Curtis Watkins Farms in East Tennessee. (Photo Courtesy of Krista Watkins)
High demand for cattle combined with high input costs mean more pressure on farmers to slaughter heifers that might otherwise be used for breeding and herd replacement.
“I make no more money than I did 25 years ago,” Curtis said. “Cattle have gone up (in price), but not at the rate of our input costs, so we’re not making any more profit per head.”
The USDA announced on Monday a new insurance tool that would allow cattle producers to insure the economic value of a breeding heifer over a 2-year period, based on the animal’s slaughter value when they enroll. If the heifer’s slaughter value exceeds the value of keeping her as breeding stock during that period, the policy would make up the difference, according to the department. 
Griffith remains skeptical of the initiative and others announced over the last week. 
“In general terms, government intervention into markets is not efficient, so I’m afraid we’re starting to have a bunch of government intervention that will cause problems later down the road,” he said.
Other initiatives announced Monday include:

A program allowing cattle producers to use certain farm disaster recovery funding to restore acres of  conserved grassland. 
An initiative focused on support for new farmers and veteran farmers
Encouraging federal and state institutions to purchase American-raised beef
A loan program to support the establishment of small beef processors, regional processors and processor co-ops.

The processing initiative comes after Trump posted a statement on Truth Social calling out four major meat processors and describing them as a “nasty monopoly.”
Curtis said he’d like to see more competition among meat processors and a meat processor located closer to him to cut down on transportation costs — Tyson Foods announced it will close its beef processing operations in Joslin, Illinois earlier this month. 
While allowing farmers to process their own meat might be helpful, Curtis and Watkins said they don’t see this initiative making drastic changes in marketing prices, and they’d need to know more about details.
The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association responded to Trump’s pledge to allow farmers to process their own food with a statement opposing “any effort that weakens food safety” or federal meat inspection. 
Neale, whose processing plant can handle between 20 and 40 head per week, said he processes in one year what the large processing plants complete in a single day. He’s also unsure about Trump’s processing announcement, noting that it could make interstate commerce more complicated, because each state may have to agree to accept products from other states. 
Polled Hereford cattle at Blue Grass Farms, owned by Charles and Carol Bond, in Bethesda, Tennessee, Aug. 27, 2026. (Photograph by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Griffith said the processing announcement isn’t likely to make an immediate impact on the market one way or another.
What does affect the market, Griffith said, is government statements and headlines.
Neale and Curtis similarly said they don’t want government interference in the cattle market.
“Allow the supply and demand to actually work itself out,” Neale said, not controlling markets with “sound bites and Truth Social posts.”
Curtis said the beef importing plan shows a fundamental misunderstanding of how raising cattle works.
“They’re not educated. They have not a clue as to what it takes,” he said. “That’s why I say the politicians need to stay out of it.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama commission recommends simplifying, standardizing court fees
description: A state commission late last month recommended the Alabama Legislature simplify and standardize court fees that local governments rely on but which can vary significantly from place to place. The suggestions in the report from the Joint Interim Study Commission on Court Costs included creating a record of the local fees that fund courts; making […]
text:
Members of the Joint Interim Study Commission on Court Costs gather to discuss ongoing issues with court-imposed fines and fees at the Alabama Supreme Court on Monday, May 19, 2025. The commission submitted a report to the Legislature that was published by PARCA that recommended lawmakers simplify and standardize fees for the courts. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)A state commission late last month recommended the Alabama Legislature simplify and standardize court fees that local governments rely on but which can vary significantly from place to place.
The suggestions in the report from the Joint Interim Study Commission on Court Costs included creating a record of the local fees that fund courts; making fees more uniform; allowing local jurisdictions greater flexibility in spending the money raised, and continuing to fund the judicial branch with money appropriated by the Legislature.
“This is an incredible first step, but I think the takeaway is that there is still a lot more work to do if we want this system to be predictable, rational, effective, efficient, accountable to the public, transparent; all the things that you want in public finance,” said Leah Nelson, senior research associate with Public Affairs Research Council of Alabama, who has studied the issue before, in an interview Friday. PARCA published the report on its website on Thursday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state uses court fees, along with fines as punishment for crimes, to fund a large share of court costs for state and local governments.
The Legislature established the commission in 2025,  requesting that officials from the judiciary branch of state government review the status of court fees and return with a report on next action steps.
The commission, led by Alabama Supreme Court Chief Justice Sarah Stewart, found that court costs accumulated over time through separate local laws and not an overall strategy. The report found that additional fees imposed by courts are derived from “250 or more separate local statutes and about 73 local constitutional amendments.”
The laws came in waves, according to the report. Fees imposed in the 1980s, for example, tended to support the construction of correctional facilities. Those levied during the 1990s usually funded law libraries and juvenile services. In the 2000s, fees were imposed to pay for mental health courts and domestic violence programs.
Fees differ by county. According to the report, the state fee for filing a civil action is $244, but the local fee can vary enormously, with an average of $30 but Madison County charging $182.
“If you are in Madison County, it is going to cost you a lot more to file a civil suit than it will in Limestone County,” Nelson said. “And at some level, if it doesn’t matter where the jurisdiction is, people might start shopping around for places where they get more bang for their buck.”
The report also said some fees may have unclear legal standing.
“At least 13 of these local fees include “sunset” language (they were supposed to expire or end once a debt was paid), and it is not clear whether those fees are still being collected today,” the report said.
Another problem is that some of the fees imposed by the court may never generate revenue. The fees for civil cases will always be collected because the case is never brought to court unless the fee is paid. In criminal cases, however, only about 20% of the fines and fees that are imposed are received by the court.
The report states that South Carolina and North Carolina have essentially a uniform fee structure while Louisiana is more fragmented.
The study commission recommended that each new local or state court cost bill require a periodic review to determine the status of the fees. They recommended a more uniform structure, but allowing local officials wider latitude to decide how to use the revenues generated from the fees.
The report also recommended tying fees to measures like the federal Consumer Price Index to account for changes in the cost of living, and requested that lawmakers direct the Legislative Services Agency and Administrative Office of Courts to “inventory of every local court cost currently on the book,” according to the report.
The commission also wanted to shift the perspective of fines and fees.
“Consider the economic feasibility of relying on often-uncollectible criminal court costs and fees assessed at the time of a criminal offender’s sentencing as a source of revenue for the courts, law enforcement, and district attorney’s offices,” the report states.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: End of rental aid creates uncertainty for Little Rock area families facing eviction, homelessness
description: Alexis Mitchell’s teenage nephew and son took a recent day off from school to help move the family’s laundry machines, bed frames and mattresses from their southwest Little Rock house into a storage unit. They brought bags of clothes to the hotel where they’ve stayed for over a week after being evicted from the place […]
text:
Brittany Robinson (right) sits on the couch with her daughter Tessleigh (left) in the North Little Rock house their family of six rents on Aug. 18, 2026. The family will have to move by Sept. 10 after being evicted. The rental assistance program that kept her family housed has no one to administer it, leaving much of Robinson's rent unpaid. The house also has livability issues including loose floorboards Robinson covers with rugs to avoid tripping on them. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Alexis Mitchell’s teenage nephew and son took a recent day off from school to help move the family’s laundry machines, bed frames and mattresses from their southwest Little Rock house into a storage unit.
They brought bags of clothes to the hotel where they’ve stayed for over a week after being evicted from the place they called home since 2020. Mitchell saved some photos of herself and her children, and her 8-year-old son kept his stuffed animals.
“Pretty much all of the stuff that was important but not absolutely necessary, we had to leave,” Mitchell said.
The family lost their home after the People Trust Community Loan Fund stopped administering the rental assistance program that had supported them and dozens of other families in the Little Rock area.
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development paid the entirety of Mitchell’s rent until January, when the National Credit Union Administration took control of the credit union behind the loan fund. The credit union liquidated in April, according to the NCUA.
While the future of the rental aid programs has been in limbo, landlords and property management companies still needed and expected rent payments the programs’ tenants can’t afford to pay in full.
About a quarter of the state’s more than 400,000 renting households have incomes at or below the poverty line or 30% of their area’s median income, according to the National Low-Income Housing Coalition. The state would have to add more than 55,000 rental homes in order to meet the housing needs of this population.
Two out of every 100 renting households received eviction filings between Aug. 1, 2025 and July 31, 2026, according to the Eviction Lab data hub. Arkansas landlords made 10,213 eviction filings over the same time period.



Quotation







We did have a little bit of means to move the first time, but now all that money has been put into this new place, and we don’t have any money to move again.


– Brittany Robinson, a mother of five evicted from her North Little Rock home due to instability surrounding a federally funded rental aid program


 ‘Administrative circle’

The federal funding that had kept Mitchell’s family housed came from HUD’s Continuum of Care Program, which is designed to help communities end homelessness. Her rent increased from $880 per month to $967 per month in the six years the program served her, but she was never expected to pay any of it until People Trust relinquished the program this year, she said.
On Aug. 4, the Pulaski County Sheriff’s Department ordered Mitchell and her family to vacate their house in 20 days. By Aug. 12, she was facing more than $2,200 in legal fees, so she sought emergency housing assistance from the city of Little Rock, according to emails she provided to the Advocate.
The city could not provide assistance without a copy of the most up-to-date housing assistance contract from the People Trust Community Loan Fund, and the fund’s administrator did not have the document when asked for it, according to the emails.
“The consequence of that administrative circle is that my three children and I may become homeless,” Mitchell wrote to city officials Aug. 12.

Alexis Mitchell email 
City officials “tried to work with HUD on a temporary solution” after People Trust stopped administering rental assistance, but city and HUD officials disagreed on the terms of issuing temporary aid and did not come to a consensus, city spokesperson Aaron Sadler said. He did not specify which of HUD’s terms the city found unacceptable.
“We remain committed to assisting affected Little Rock residents, and the City allocated and distributed $300,000 to support those impacted while at the same time working to reach an agreement with HUD,” Sadler said.
People Trust did not respond to calls or emails requesting comment. HUD’s Departmental Enforcement Center is investigating People Trust, according to an agency spokesperson.
People Trust told KATV in June that it was “working cooperatively with HUD to address any outstanding administrative matters and to ensure that community members do not suffer unintended consequences” during HUD’s investigation.
Around the same time, Arlo Washington, founder of the now-defunct People Trust Community Federal Credit Union, told the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette that the loan fund “never got into this to hurt anybody” but would have been better off not participating in HUD programs.
 Layers of instability

HUD’s Continuum of Care initiative aims “to quickly rehouse homeless individuals, families, persons fleeing domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking, and youth while minimizing the trauma and dislocation caused by homelessness,” according to HUD’s website.
Brittany Robinson’s rental aid came from a different People Trust-sponsored initiative, the Community Housing Program, which serves people with chronic illnesses and physical disabilities. The threshold for acceptance into the program was high, and most enrollees are under a doctor’s care, said Robinson, who has a prosthetic leg.
The Community Housing Program ensured that Robinson only had to pay $244 per month for the Little Rock house where she lived with her five children and her service dog. She said she always paid her share of the rent on time, but the family moved to North Little Rock at the end of April to avoid a potential eviction after HUD’s dispute with People Trust left the rest of her rent unpaid. 


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Robinson said her former landlord didn’t return her security deposit, and she had to pay an $1,800 deposit for the new house. On top of that, the new house has livability issues, such as wires creating a fire hazard in the attic, a sewage spill in the backyard and loose floorboards that Robinson struggles daily not to trip over.
In 2021, Arkansas became the last state to pass a law requiring minimum livability standards for rental housing. Tenants’ advocates have said the law doesn’t sufficiently incentivize landlords to provide basic necessities such as electricity and potable water.
Robinson said it’s unclear whether the new landlord’s refusal to fix the house is a coincidence or a response to not receiving full rent payments since the Community Housing Program still has no host entity.
Mitchell and Robinson both said the stress of their unstable housing situation has worsened their disabilities. Mitchell told Little Rock city officials in an email that her mental health and “ability to manage prolonged stress” have been deteriorating due to the “constant calls, documentation searches, agency referrals” and other bureaucratic obstacles she’s faced.
Mitchell also said she doesn’t know where she and her children will go after they have to leave their hotel Wednesday, since they don’t have extended family in the Little Rock area.
Meanwhile, Robinson and her family will have to move by Sept. 10 after she lost her eviction court case last week. Her mother and aunt live in North Little Rock but don’t have enough space for their relatives.
Additionally, Robinson said her work cleaning houses is too infrequent to be a steady source of income.
“We did have a little bit of means to move the first time, but now all that money has been put into this new place, and we don’t have any money to move again,” she said.

description: Coloradans can use a new mobile driver’s license to get through security checkpoints at all airports in Colorado, including Denver International Airport, and other airports across the country, Gov. text:
A view of Jeppesen Terminal at Denver International Airport. (Courtesy of Denver International Airport)Coloradans can use a new mobile driver’s license to get through security checkpoints at all airports in Colorado, including Denver International Airport, and other airports across the country, Gov. Jared Polis announced Monday. 
U.S. Transportation Security Administration will now accept a Colorado mobile driver’s license, or mDL, through the myColorado mobile app or a mobile phone’s digital wallet as proof of identity. The mDL, which is REAL ID compliant, is distinct from the Colorado Digital ID, which residents can use in the state during traffic stops and to verify their name, age and address at businesses and state agencies.
“We have been working on this for years and now the federal government will accept your myColorado app identification at airport security,” Polis said in a statement. “Airport travel can be stressful but we are making it easier, and more convenient to get through TSA at more than 250 airports across the country using the myColorado app.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Coloradans should still carry their physical ID as a backup, according to Polis’ office and TSA. Colorado is one of 21 states that offers an mDL accepted by TSA. 
Credential Authentication Technology, which scans a person’s face at the airport and compares it to the photos on their ID, is equipped to read Colorado’s new mDL. People traveling through airport security can present a QR code associated with the mobile driver’s license to the TSA agent instead of their physical ID or boarding pass.
“The process of verifying identities is fundamental to ensuring transportation security,” TSA Colorado Federal Security Director Douglas Cruz said in a statement. “By enabling travelers to use mobile driver’s licenses, we are leveraging technology to strengthen security and streamline our operations. Our TSA officers are fully trained to accept and process myColorado mDLs, and we are glad to provide this convenient option for those departing DEN and our other state airports.”
More than 2 million Coloradans use the myColorado app for digital IDs, Colorado Parks and Wildlife licenses and vehicle registrations, Polis said. Users who already have the app will see a new tab to add their myColorado mDL to their mobile app and digital wallets. 
In 2023, TSA began to accept digital Colorado IDs at TSA PreCheck checkpoints at the Denver airport.
