title: Judge rules Justice Department can force-feed defendant in National Guard shooting
text: WASHINGTON — A federal judge over the weekend allowed the Trump administration to force-feed the man charged with shooting two National Guard members, killing one and injuring another, in the District of Columbia in November.For months, Rahmanullah Lakanwal has refused to eat while incarcerated. The Aug. 29 order from U.S. District Court Judge Amit P. Mehta of the District of Columbia gives the go-ahead for medical staff at the Bureau of Prisons to conduct several types of nonconsensual feeding methods “to preserve defendant Rahmanullah Lakanwal's life or to prevent a foreseeable deterioration in his condition that if not treated is likely to lead to death; replacement, maintenance, and care of defendant’s feeding tube when medically necessary; and lab work relating to the administration of nutrition.”The order will allow for a feeding tube through Lakanwal’s nasal passage and into his stomach to provide nutrients; feeding through veins; or feeding through an already established tube connected to his stomach. The order does not allow for a tube to be established through his stomach, usually done via surgery. The Department of Justice charged Lakanwal with first-degree murder in the shooting of 20-year-old U.S. Army Spc. Sarah Beckstrom and with the attempted murder of U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Andrew Wolfe. Lakanwal has pleaded not guilty to all 17 DOJ charges. He is an Afghan national who came to the United States under a humanitarian program after the Biden administration’s chaotic withdrawal from the country. Following the shooting, the Trump administration paused all immigration processing for nationals from Afghanistan. A federal judge later reversed that move.  The two West Virginia guard members last year were shot on Thanksgiving eve while stationed blocks from the White House as part of the president’s crackdown on crime, despite a continued decrease in violent crime.Mehta, who was nominated by former President Barack Obama, has in the past considered but turned down the Trump administration’s requests for a court-ordered nonconsensual nutrition supplement, noting that Lakanwal has refused meals and medical treatment. In several hearings in federal court before Mehta, Lakanwal has appeared gaunt and has used a wheelchair. Mehta’s order will remain in effect until Oct. 28 and will allow the DOJ to request an extension if needed.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: It’s time to let law enforcement speak for itself
description: For most of my career in policing, I believed the best way to serve the public was to simply do the job well. You show up. You treat people with dignity. You hold yourself and those around you accountable. You always try to make the difficult decisions with integrity and compassion. Then you go home […]
text:
A police officer speaks  with a 10 year old girl and her mother. (Photo: Getty Images)For most of my career in policing, I believed the best way to serve the public was to simply do the job well.
You show up. You treat people with dignity. You hold yourself and those around you accountable. You always try to make the difficult decisions with integrity and compassion. Then you go home and come back and do it again tomorrow.
I still believe that.
But I’ve also come to believe that doing the job well isn’t always enough. Law enforcement leaders have a responsibility to stand up for the principles that underpin the rule of law — fairness, accountability, equal treatment and respect for constitutional rights. Public trust depends not only on how we enforce the law, but on whether people believe we are upholding those principles. And without that trust, the system doesn’t work for anybody.
For our profession to earn and maintain that trust, we must actively participate in the ongoing conversations about law enforcement and public safety, even when it is difficult to do so.
When experienced voices are left out of the conversation, or choose to remain silent, the conversations don’t stop. People in our communities will still look for answers about policing and public safety, often drawing conclusions that lack context and consideration of the practical realities of police work. In those moments the public deserves to hear, firsthand, from the people who have done the work and who have navigated those complexities.
That is why a group of current and former law enforcement leaders from across North Carolina has come together to launch the North Carolina Law Enforcement Trust & Legitimacy Project. Together, we will engage in public debates over policies that affect public safety and the rule of law.
We will provide context and expertise when complicated law enforcement issues enter the public conversation. We will acknowledge opportunities to improve when the profession falls short of its responsibilities. We will push back when law enforcement is attacked unfairly.
We are professionals who have spent our careers leading agencies, developing policy, managing crises, building relationships, and serving our communities. Our goal is simple: to strengthen those communities, the law enforcement profession, and the rule of law by ensuring that conversations about public safety are informed by professional experience, by sound evidence and data and by a shared commitment to equal justice under the law for everybody.
Because when people believe the law is fair, accountable, and applied equally, communities are stronger and safer.
Today, trust in many of our institutions is being tested, and that includes law enforcement. Rising political division, corruption, unequal application of the law, and too many people speaking for law enforcement to advance their own ideological agendas threatens the trust that our profession relies upon. At moments like these, experienced law enforcement leaders have a responsibility to speak—not for any political cause, but for the values that have always guided our profession: accountability, equality under the law, professional integrity, and public safety free from intimidation, influence, or extremism.
This effort is not about defending every action taken by law enforcement. It is not about speaking for every officer or every agency. And it is certainly not about asking for blind trust.
It is about offering the perspective of people who have done the work, have made the hard decisions, and believe they still have a duty to serve.
The men and women involved in this effort come from different agencies, different backgrounds, and different experiences. We have not agreed on every issue throughout our careers, and we won’t agree on every issue in the future.
What unites us is something more important.
We believe that public safety depends on public trust. We believe the rule of law protects everyone when it is applied fairly and equally. We believe professional law enforcement should always be guided by integrity, accountability, and service. And we believe that when those principles are challenged, experienced law enforcement leaders have a responsibility to speak up.
Trust is earned every day through integrity, accountability, transparency, and service.
Legitimacy is strengthened the same way.
That is the work of policing.
And that is the work of the North Carolina Law Enforcement Trust & Legitimacy Project.
Chris Blue is a retired Chapel Hill police chief and town manager. He is a public safety consultant and founding president of the North Carolina Law Enforcement Trust & Legitimacy Project.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi prison band offers a glimpse of freedom in a lifetime of punishment
authors: Daja E. Henry, The Marshall Project
description: Members of the Parchman Band, including, from left, Steven Chambers, Lee Andrew Smith (back), Charles Glassco, Michael Snell and Leonard “LJ” Stevenson Jr. performed at a concert at the GRAMMY Museum in Cleveland, Miss., in May 2026.
text:
CLEVELAND — Just 30 minutes down the road from the Mississippi prison where they are serving time, Lee Andrew Smith and six other incarcerated people felt free — for a few hours.
On stage before a crowd of more than 100 people at the GRAMMY Museum Mississippi, Smith riffed on his guitar alongside fellow members of the Parchman prison band. About halfway through a rendition of Luke Combs’ “15 Minutes,” tears begin to stream down his face.
All kinds of things cross your mind
With all this doin’ time
And a chain gang waitin’ in a long line to use this phone
Same old view, a cinder block room, same old jumpsuit on
I’m just tryna make the best of the rest of this life sentence
But enough about me, I only get 15 minutes
The 44-year-old Smith — who has a close haircut and a salt-and-pepper beard — turned his back to the crowd. He continued playing his guitar, standing there in his well-worn brown cowboy boots and prison-issued, green-and-white striped pants, before walking off stage. After a moment, he returned.
In the audience, tears flowed down his wife’s face. “I feel what he feels,” Joann Smith said. “He was thinking about home … he misses his children, misses his mom, wants to be home with his mom, so all of those things probably ran across his mind.”
Lee Andrew Smith is a member of the Parchman Band, which is composed of people incarcerated at the Mississippi State Penitentiary, in Parchman, Miss. Credit: Rory Doyle for The Marshall Project – Jackson
The concert this summer was the third stop on the Parchman Band’s tour through the state with country singer-songwriter Charlie Worsham. It’s part of a musical tradition that dates back to the early 1930s at the prison. The Mississippi State Penitentiary, a prison farm, has a long history of brutality and sits on about 18,000 acres of flat, fertile land in the Mississippi Delta, where the blues were born.
“The torch has been passed down to us,” said Leonard “LJ” Stevenson Jr., 33, a founding member of the latest iteration of the band. They’ve since played at other prisons and festivals and shared the stage with blues legend Bobby Rush. “I’ve heard some of the old ’60s Parchman Band originals, and I can relate to it because I’m living it firsthand,” Stevenson said. “That was basically prison blues.”
Playing in the band offers the incarcerated men a chance to experience life outside the walls, said Marc McClure, the former superintendent at Parchman who restarted the group in 2023. Proceeds from the band go into the state’s inmate welfare fund.
“(The band) gives them that opportunity for one moment to be human and be accepted, which leads them down the road to forgiveness and redemption, and they can be different than what got them there,” he said. “The crime doesn’t dictate their life forever. That band gives them that hope.”
The Mississippi State Penitentiary, a prison farm, sits on about 18,000 acres of land in the Mississippi Delta. Credit: Rory Doyle for The Marshall Project – Jackson
With Smith on lead guitar and Stevenson playing bass, the band also includes Houston Jones on keyboard, drummer Jakellsey Hollis, and vocalists Steven Chambers, Charles Glassco and Michael Snell. The white and green stripes on their pants are indelible reminders of their biggest mistakes, but their music — and the album that will be coming out next year — are a testament to them being so much more.
On that spring night at the museum, the band played its way through a full spectrum of emotions, from slow ballads serenading women they love to electrifying originals that talk of wild times before prison. They also backed Worsham on some of his own songs, and recreated some country covers that evoked the reality of doing hard time in Mississippi.
Stevenson played in the background, laying the bassline that undergirded the songs. As he and his band members got into a groove, a slight smile peeked out from behind his cinnamon-brown beard. Smith’s fingers, almost a blur to the naked eye, glided effortlessly across the strings as he traded solos with Worsham and Jones.
Houston Jones, left, and Lee Andrew Smith, both members of the Parchman Band, in a rehearsal room at the Mississippi State Penitentiary. Credit: Rory Doyle for The Marshall Project – Jackson
Though he stood at the back of the stage, Smith performed in a way that demanded attention. He smiled and pointed out the prettiest woman in the room — his wife — before the band performed a soulful rendition of Chris Stapleton’s “Tennessee Whiskey.”
You’re as smooth as Tennessee whiskey,
You’re as sweet as strawberry wine
You’re as warm as a glass of brandy
And honey, I stay stoned on your love all the time
Smith stepped to the front of the stage, not missing a beat as he stared into his wife’s eyes. He walked his fingers up and down the electric guitar’s neck, delivering a complex solo that drew applause and cheers from the audience.
“Music is his freedom,” his wife said. “He’s free when he’s dealing with any type of instrument.”
The men took turns in the spotlight, telling stories of love and redemption through songs that will be featured on their upcoming album.
Vocalist Charles Glassco, also known as Beast, introduced a high-energy song he wrote for his wife called “Love You Out Loud,” about proclaiming his love publicly, no matter where they are. And Jones, who played both guitar and keyboard in the show, introduced a low-key ballad he wrote to his daughter, who he described as “a great friend.”
I tried my best, just couldn’t give it all to you
I couldn’t be who you needed me to be
But I just wanted you to see
…
I would climb the tallest mountain
Part the Red Sea
Just to have you right here next to me
The themes of love, hard times and redemption in their music have roots in the Delta. It’s a place where Black people — ensnared in the traps of racial terror and White supremacy — made meaning of life on a prison farm as they provided free labor for the state. Incarcerated people worked in the fields, picking cotton, hoeing corn, and working for the state in what historian David Oshinsky called “the closest thing to slavery that survived the Civil War.” They worked to the sounds of field hollers to keep the work tempo and pass the time.
Over the past century, legal action brought an end to corporal punishment, including with a leather whip named “Black Annie”; the end of prisoners given the power to shoot fellow incarcerated people; and upgrades to Parchman. Yet, violence, rampant drug use, poor security, and a brutal underground economy run by gangs have endured.
The music has endured, too, except for a gap in the 1990s.
Like more than 2,000 Mississippians today, Smith, Stevenson, Jones and Chambers have been sentenced to spend the rest of their lives in prison. Stevenson said his life sentence is torture, mentally. “I have a family. I’m engaged now. I have a kid,” he said. “It’s hard being on the phone with them, and not being able to hear first words, see first steps, first heartbreak, first game.”
But he and the other band members are among the few who get to leave the prison grounds and play music in the free world.
“This is as good as it gets for guys like Houston, guys like LJ, because they’re never going home. This is home,” said Trish Doty, a former prison warden who once did vocal coaching with the band and coached LJ in softball. “What sort of justice does it serve to lock them up and throw away a key and give them nothing?”
After the show ended, Smith took the stage again.
“I can’t help but to cry with certain things going on, because this is a thing that I dreamed of all my life. And even though I have this on,” he said, his voice cracking as he pointed down at his green-and-white stripes before pointing up toward the sky, “God’s still fulfilling his promise for me. I’m so grateful.”
“God is good,” an audience member shouted out.
“Yes,” Smith said, “He is.”
This article was published in partnership with The Marshall Project – Jackson, a nonprofit news team covering Mississippi’s criminal justice systems.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Mining projects opposed by Alaska tribes get support from Canada, British Columbia and First Nation
description: This story was first published by ICT. The salmon and the ooligan that spawn in the Unuk and Stikine rivers have no say in the expansion of mining operations in British Columbia. Neither do the Alaskan tribes that live on the same rivers. The power lies across the border in Canada, where the mining companies […]
text:
Louis Wagner Jr. pulls up ooligan nets on the Unuk River in southeastern Alaska in March 2024. He and his wife, Cindy Wagner, have fished in the area for years. (Photo by Sonia Luokkala/courtesy of the Southeast Alaska Indigenous Transboundary Commission)This story was first published by ICT.
The salmon and the ooligan that spawn in the Unuk and Stikine rivers have no say in the expansion of mining operations in British Columbia. Neither do the Alaskan tribes that live on the same rivers.
The power lies across the border in Canada, where the mining companies and the provincial, federal and Tahltan Nation authorities have joined forces in a modern-day gold rush to expand the Red Chris Mine at the headwaters of the Stikine River. Plans are also underway to restart the idled Eskay Creek Mine on the Unuk River.
The investment of a half-billion Canadian dollars supporting the expansion of the Red Chris mine by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has heightened an international conflict between the Native peoples and others in southeastern Alaska and the First Nations people in Canada who support the project.     
A pictograph of the rising sun along the Unuk River is thousands of years old and reflects the influence of the Tèiḵwèidi Tlingit Clan of the Sàanyàa Ḵwáan, the people of the Unuk River, according to river advocates. (Photo by Sonia Luokkala/courtesy of the Southeast Alaska Indigenous Transboundary Commission)
 
Seven tribal nations could be affected by the Eskay Creek Mine, and the Red Chris expansions poses similar threats, according to officials with the Southeast Alaska Indigenous Transboundary Commission, or SEITC, a collective of 14 Haida, Tlingit and Tsimshian nations that have united to uphold stewardship over the lands, waters and sacred sites in their territories.
“The expansion of Red Chris means more risk in the headwaters of a river that has sustained our people since time immemorial, “ said SEITC President Esther Aaltseen Reese, Eagle Tsaagweidí (Killerwhale) from Ḵéex̱ʼ Kwáan (Kake), who lives down river of the Red Chris Mine.
“We are salmon people,” Reese told ICT. “The Stikine is part of who we are. We are already seeing contamination from Red Chris entering waters that feed the Stikine, yet British Columbia approved a major expansion without consulting the tribal nations downstream whose ways of life are on the line.”
The Tahltan Nation, which has agreements in place for both mining projects, did not respond to questions about the project posed by ICT via email.
In November 2025, the SEITC filed a judicial review in the British Columbia supreme court to force “meaningful consultation” with Alaskan tribes on mining projects in the headwaters of the Unuk, Stikine and Taku rivers.
“There is no legal or moral basis for B.C. to exclude our tribes who have deep ancestral ties and relationships to land and territory on both sides of the border,” Reese said in a statement issued at the time. “We deserve a seat at the table when decisions are made upstream that could obliterate our way of life.”
Canada’s Ministry of Environment and Parks responded to ICT questions in a written statement.
“We are not expediting projects at the expense of meeting our consultation obligations or compromising our high standards of environmental protection — we are finding opportunities that can do both in our processes,” according to the statement.
In regards to concerns from Alaskan tribes, officials said, “The matter of consultation with Alaska tribes for the environmental assessment of the Eskay Creek project near the B.C./Alaska border is currently before the courts, we are not able to comment.”
 Eskay Creek Mine
The Unuk and Stikine rivers are part of the transboundary watershed, a collection of rivers, streams and tributaries that also include the Taku and Salmon rivers that flow south from British Columbia into Alaska and then on to the Pacific Ocean.
The watershed is crucial spawning grounds for salmon and other fish, and provides sustenance to Indigenous people and others along the rivers.
Cindy Wagner, Haida/Tsimshian, is concerned that the rapid expansion of mining in Canada will have significant environmental impacts on the transboundary watersheds in Alaska.     
Louis Wagner Jr., rear left, delivers ooligan with his daughter Lee, center, and wife Cindy in this undated photo. (Photo courtesy of Cindy Wagner)
 
Wagner, assistant executive director of the SEITC, and her husband, Louis Wagner Jr., live downstream of the Eskay Creek Mine on the Annette Islands Reserve in Alaska on the Unuk River, where she has lived and fished all her life.
She has seen first hand the impact of mining on the Unuk.
The Eskay Creek Mine operated from 1994 to 2008, and the ooligan fishery on the river was closed in 2001. In recent years, ooligan, a small fish also known as eulachon, have begun to return, along with salmon and mackerel.
But she fears that could change with the reopening now underway of the Eskay Creek Mine on a much-larger scale. The mine received its Environmental Assessment Certificate in January.
“This is all for the Unuk River,” Wagner told ICT.  “It’s a major salmon river, an ooligan spawning river, a mackerel spawning river, and vital to southeast Alaska.”     
Ooligan, shown here, are small fish used in a variety of ways by Indigenous people and others in southeastern Alaska. (Photo by Sonia Luokkala/courtesy of the Southeast Alaska Indigenous Transboundary Commission)
 
Reese says her people are concerned about a possible overflow or dam breach at the tailings  ponds that collect the mining byproducts. In 2014, a breach at the Mount Polley copper and gold mine tailings dam resulted in billions of liters of wastewater spilling into the waterways. The mine is owned by Imperial Metals, which also owns a share of the Red Chris mine.
“Contamination or a failure at Red Chris could travel downstream, across the border, and through one of the most intact salmon systems left in the world,” Reese said. “The cumulative impacts of multiple large mines only magnify that risk.”
 A waterway in transition
Tribes on the American side of the border have been living with the impact of mining for decades and fighting, to no avail, to stop expansion, local officials said.
On June 19, however, the province of British Columbia approved the transition of the Red Chris mine from an open-pit mine to a block cave mine that would largely be underground. On July 2, the Canadian government approved the funding support.
The Tahltan Nation in British Columbia has signed on with Red Chris mine’s owners and operators, Newmont Corporation and Imperial Metals, according to a statement from the companies.
The outlook is not as rosy downstream. The Annette Islands Reserve of the Metlakatla Alaska Native Community is Alaska’s only reservation, with other Native lands transferred to Alaska Native Corporations under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, or ANCSA.
The reserve sits on the pristine Alexander Archipelago about 250 miles south of Juneau.     
The Tongass rainforest towers over the Unuk River in southeastern Alaska. (Photo by Sonia Luokkala/courtesy of the Southeast Alaska Indigenous Transboundary Commission)
 
Wagner has lived off the Unuk River for most of her life, and in recent years has been defending Alaska’s waterways against mining development in Canada.
“I have always been fishing, even as a child,” she said. “My parents brought us out, all four of us, on a little 35-foot boat … I met my husband. The first time I helped him was down on his brother’s boat. He was selling ooligan and he didn’t have anyone to help him, and so I helped him.”
Wagner and her husband have always watched the waters of the Unuk River, and taken note of how clean and deep they were, and how the fish changed in appearance and in number. Then, in 1999, after the Eskay Creek Mine began operating, they noticed that industrial waste was piling up in the low part of the river.
“We are way up this river,” Wagner said. “How does a rusted-up oil drum get this far? How does all this plastic and old tarps and old pallets get up here? This looks to be an important part where the moose stepped into the river to get across, and it’s blocked with junk.”
The fish noticed, too, she said.
“In about 2001, we started noticing the ooligan bypassing the Unuk River,” she said.
Ooligan are different from mackerel and salmon, which return to the waters where they were spawned. Ooligan go to where the water is best, she said.
 Dramatic escalation 

The Unuk River was beginning to recover after the Eskay Creek Mine shut down in 2008, Wagner said, when a mining boom began on the Canadian side, in an area in northwest British Columbia called the “Golden Triangle.”
By 2022, just two mines were in operation, BruceJack and Red Chris. But four mines were proposed, seven were under development and seven more exploration projects were underway, mostly to dig for gold, according to a provincial report on mines. The ore extracted from the ground is processed to pull out the valuable gold and copper that it can contain.
Guy Archibald, executive director of the transboundary commission and a self-described “reformed miner,” said the transition from an open-pit mine to a block cave mine at Red Chris will mean a dramatic escalation involving hydraulic fracturing, known as fracking, a controversial method also used for extracting natural gas.
Archibald said the SEITC member nations “upholding their sovereign rights and defending the transboundary Stikine, Taku and Unuk Rivers from rapidly expanding mining development occurring in the Canadian headwaters.”
An environmental chemist, Archibald has been with the commission since its inception in 2014. Before that, he worked in the uranium industry in southeastern Utah and the oil shale industry in western Colorado in the 1970s and 1980s, he said.
Archibald explained the process behind a block cave mine.
“They’ve mined out the ore body that’s closest to the surface, and in order to go deeper, they’re going to have to access it underground,” he said. “They’re going to drive a ramp underneath the ore body, and then … they’re going to fracture the ore body pretty much the same as they do hydraulic fracturing, fracking for natural gas.”
The crumbled ore falls into the ramp and is carted above ground, he said.
“They’re going to just start scooping it out from the bottom as this cavity, this cave, just naturally collapses in,” he said. “It’s just going to turn into a big crater in the earth, and that’s block cave mining.”
The practice is not new, but in the past, miners would use drilling. With this project, they’ll use fracking.
“Block cave mining has been around for a long time,” Archibald said. “The only difference I see with the way Red Chris is doing it is by doing the hydraulic fracturing from the surface, drilling down and then pumping high pressure water into the ore body to break it up.”
The introduction of fracking to the block cave operation is a major concern to the SEITC. Officials say the mine can’t contain its current tailings, which already end up in the groundwater.
“The studies have been showing the tailings dam leaks into the groundwater 26 percent of its volume every year,” Archibald said. “Those tailings have to be constantly covered with water so that they don’t oxidize and turn acidic. We already have downstream pollution problems in groundwater and surface water…Using more water to frack this ore body is not going to help that situation.”
 ‘A critical step’
The Red Chris mine operation is a joint venture partnership between the Newmont Corporation, which owns 70 percent, and Imperial Metals, which owns 30 percent.
The Red Chris was one of 18 major projects named by Canada’s Major Projects Office, the new federal department created by the Carney government to push forward his “Build Canada Strong” strategy. The half-billion-dollar investment may be just the beginning.
“With the authorizations granted by the province and the support of the Tahltan Nation, the stage has been set for the development of Red Chris into a Block Cave mine,” Imperial President Brian Kynoch said, following the approval of the British Columbia government. “These approvals are a critical step in advancing a final investment decision by the joint venture partnership.”
Newmont officials welcomed the news in a statement promising that the project would not only increase Canada’s copper production by an estimated 15 percent but that the infrastructure could be a hub for mining for decades.
“The project is expected to extend the life of the current Red Chris mine by approximately 14 years and sets the foundation for decades of potential additional mining,” Newmont stated. “It represents a significant opportunity to create long-term value for Newmont’s shareholders, strengthen critical mineral supply chains, and deliver long-term benefits for local communities, Indigenous partners, British Columbia, and Canada.”
Canada’s Major Projects office is promoting both production and Indigenous participation, stating that the project was “developed in close collaboration with the Tahltan Nation, whose Traditional Territory overlaps directly with the mine site” and that “the project supports reconciliation while strengthening Canada’s role as a reliable supplier of critical minerals.”
Provincial leaders have changed the laws, however, to eliminate participation of U.S. tribes when it comes to environmental impacts. The province passed Bill 15 in April to amend the dispute resolution processes in British Columbia’s Environmental Assessment Act to limit participation of tribes in the U.S. and exclude them as “participating Indigenous nations.”
Archibald says the moves have raised concerns for taxpayers as well.
“Subsidizing the Red Chris just furthers the privatization of profit while transferring the risk on to the taxpayer,” he said. “If Newmont and Imperial Metals can’t afford their own infrastructure, what assurance do we have that adequate funds will be available for long-term tailings management, closure, and cleanup to protect the Stikine River for hundreds of years into the future?”
The Eskay Creek Mine, owned by Skeena Gold + Silver, is an open-pit gold and silver mine that is being redeveloped with a projected 12-year mine life.
In approving the mine’s expansion, British Columbia Premier David Eby hailed the relationship with First Nations.
“Today marks success for yet another multibillion-dollar investment in our province that will deliver prosperity, jobs and stability for all British Columbians, achieved in true partnership with the Tahltan,” Eby said in a Jan. 27, 2026, press release. “Congratulations to all who were involved in this important work. Those who want to end our work with First Nations would not have delivered these thousands of jobs, period. Following their advice would leave us poorer, tied up in court and in a place of uncertainty.
Kerry Carlick, president of the Tahltan Central Government, issued a statement in the same press release.
“This is a hugely important day,” Carlick said. “TCG’s decision to consent to the Eskay Creek Project reflects a historic, precedent-setting process that affirms Tahltan Nation’s authority over development in our Territory, recognized by the Province and Skeena Gold + Silver.”
When asked to comment regarding concerns of Indigenous Alaskans about environmental concerns, a spokesperson for Skeena Gold + Silver responded that they had answered those concerns.
“We have already addressed many questions regarding concerns from the Alaskan groups, as we were going through our permitting process,” Galena Maleger, the vice president of investor relations told ICT in an email. “There is a significant amount of information available online as to how Eskay Creek is adhering to the highest standards in environmental management.”
 Looking ahead
Downstream on the Unuk River, Wagner and her husband are already seeing more and more boats hauling material north to the dam site. They can only imagine the size of the massive project based on the garbage that piles up in the river.
Wagner has a message for the Tahltan Nation whose members will profit from the two mines.
“I think they should be more aware of what’s coming down the river, because it’s not staying up there on their territory,” Wagner said. “It’s coming down on my territory, my tribe’s territory, all southeast territory, and we have to deal with it.”
This story was originally published by ICT, formerly Indian Country Today.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: USC leaders tout buildout, enrollment growth amid broader higher ed headwinds
description: USC has been on a massive construction spree while also setting new records around enrollment, fundraising and state dollars to fund it.
text:
Renovations continue on the University of South Carolina campus in Columbia, S.C., as seen on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The University of South Carolina has been on a massive construction spree while also setting new records annually around student enrollment, private fundraising and securing a large share of state taxpayer dollars to make it all happen.
At least $1.8 billion worth of construction underway or in the planning stages includes:

a new, state-of the art healthcare campus and neuro hospital, both funded by state dollars and debt.
upgrades to the football stadium to match the offerings of others across the Southeast, funded with athletic fees and private donations.
major renovations to the main campus library, student center and buildings around the historic Horseshoe.
plans for a new district centered around engineering and energy, which will seek state and private funding.
a total revamp of the area south of the Statehouse to add student housing and retail, funded by the school’s development foundation.

It’s a 180-degree turnaround from the USC of five years ago, when the school was stumbling through leadership changes gone awry, fallouts with major donors, and reckoning with multiple allegations of sexual harassment by employees, who have since resigned.
Lately, the news has been about ribbon cuttings and ground breakings.
Students walk past Thomas Cooper Library on the University of South Carolina campus in Columbia, S.C. pictured on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. The library is on a long list of buildings slated for upgrades. (Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)
The university seeks to keep that momentum going even as higher education undergoes major changes across the country.
“The university is in a position better than it’s ever been in,” outgoing Board of Trustees Chairman Thad Westbrook told the SC Daily Gazette in an exclusive interview last Thursday, nearly a week after he handed over the title to the school’s first female chair.
“We’re hitting on all cylinders at a time when higher ed is facing some headwinds,” added the Columbia lawyer who’s been chairman since 2022.
Colleges nationwide are competing for a shrinking pool of potential students due to a declining national birth rate. And federal funding cuts have led to reduction in national grant funding that has hit some colleges harder than others. This has left some schools facing budget deficits, hiring freezes, and in the case of smaller private schools, closure, as they struggle to make up for the loss in tuition dollars and research funding.
Leaving the ‘noise’ behind
Westbrook credits much of that to USC President Michael Amiridis, the school’s former provost who returned to South Carolina in 2022 after spending seven years as chancellor of the University of Illinois-Chicago.
University of South Carolina President Michael Amiridis pictured Tuesday, Feb. 11, 2025, during Carolina Day at the Statehouse. (Photo provided by the University of South Carolina)
He came in after a politically-charged presidential search landed the school in hot water with accreditors following the appointment of former West Point Superintendent Bob Caslen.
The retired three-star Army general successfully led the school through the COVID-19 pandemic but resigned in May 2021, after less than two years at the helm, following a blundered commencement address. Not only did he mistakenly refer to graduates as the “newest alumni of the University of California,” but he plagiarized part of his speech, quoting from a Navy SEAL’s 2014 address in Texas without crediting him.
Former President Harris Pastides was asked to return in an interim role until the school could make a new hire.
“I knew that we had the basics and we had them very well,” Amiridis said of his decision to take the job. “At the same time, there was noise. And the problem was, let’s get the noise behind us and let’s move forward in what we want to do.”
Amiridis and Westbrook knew they had to regain the confidence of state legislative leaders if the school was to receive financial support to accomplish its lofty goals.
So, the school prioritized its budget requests on things leadership knew could benefit the state as a whole.
It started with a network of clinics to diagnose and treat tough cases of Alzheimer’s and dementia around the state.
They followed that up with data on the clinics’ success when they returned to ask for money for an even higher-dollar project — a $350 million neurological hospital to conduct research and train the next generation of brain doctors on treating the most severe cases and the latest in rehabilitation. Taxpayers covered $150 million of the construction cost.
The school’s next ask will be $100 million for a nuclear workforce training center, an amount that will be matched by private investment. The announcement comes amid efforts to restart construction of a pair of partially built nuclear reactors in the state.
University of South Carolina students walk past a construction sign at the Woodrow residence hall on campus in Columbia, S.C. on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)
“I think we’re better aligned with the state than we’ve ever been,” Westbrook said.
What legislators are saying
State budget writers agreed.
“They are, at the present time, bringing a lot of research in to help build the reputation and name of South Carolina to convince the best, most prolific minds to come here,” said Sen. Ronnie Cromer, who chairs the Senate’s higher education budget panel.
The Newberry Republican acknowledged that USC has been doing a lot of building.
“But it’s necessary to continue to attract the best and the brightest,” he said.
House Ways and Means Chairman Bruce Bannister also praised USC’s efforts around brain health and called the nuclear center “a good idea to explore.”
“I’m not concerned that they’re just willy-nilly spending money,” the Greenville Republican said.
He said the laundry list of new construction certainly can’t continue indefinitely.
“At some point they’ll have to slow down and take stock of where they are,” he said. “But I think they’re doing the right thing by the university.”
Both Cromer and Bannister also pointed out that colleges across the state are catching up on about two decades worth of renovations and maintenance after years of cost-cutting following the Great Recession.
Spending questioned
Not everyone is enthusiastic about the latest spending levels.
“If the state is going to keep providing seemingly endless resources, it would be foolish for the university to say ‘no,’” said South Carolina Policy Council Research Director Sam Aaron. “Ultimately, I think the responsibility falls on lawmakers for allowing university spending and state support to grow at such a high rate.”
Students walk past Russell House student union on the University of South Carolina campus in Columbia, S.C. pictured on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. The student center is on a long list of buildings slated for upgrades. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)
The government spending watchdog has been critical of taxpayer dollars directed to the state’s largest public college, particularly money sent to keep tuition rates steady for in-state students over the past eight years. The allotments are part of the Legislature’s “tuition mitigation” initiative, a priority of Gov. Henry McMaster, that’s kept in-state tuition frozen at public colleges statewide.
“South Carolinians are subsidizing this activity, even though a sizable percentage of people in this state did not attend college and will never attend college,” Aaron said. “I think the university needs to practice living within its means rather than returning to the Legislature every year requesting increased funding.”


Freshmen enrollment by the numbers
Applications to attend USC’s Columbia campus this fall: 69,000 
Out-of-state applicants: 54,000 
In-state applicants: 15,300
SC’s college-ready high school graduates (Class of 2025): 12,700 
In-state admissions: 70% (For those roughly 2,000 in-state students who didn’t have the necessary test scores, the school offered support programs to help students get their grades up enough to qualify.)
Total: 7,800 freshmen (compared to 6,150 freshmen in 2021)
In-state enrollment: 4,100 (That means 41% of in-state students qualified for and ultimately accepted USC’s offer and 13.4% of out-of-state students accepted.)
Source: USC and SC Department of Education


“While I understand the tuition mitigation dollars are intended to benefit South Carolina students, a growing share of the overall university enrollment is coming from out of state,” Aaron added. “That raises a fair question about why South Carolina taxpayers should continue to finance the rapid expansion of facilities that increasingly serve students from outside the state.”
Westbrook and Amiridis said it’s true USC has built a national reputation but not at the expense of in-state students.
“We have more students on campus in Columbia than we’ve ever had before, and most importantly, we’re educating more South Carolinians than ever before,” Westbrook said.
They also said, thanks to state funding, steady enrollment growth and internal budget controls, USC is in a better place financially than several other state schools, such as West Virginia University, Washington State University and Arizona State University.
“We’re not freezing hiring and we’re not cutting our budget out of necessity because a CFO (chief financial officer) has sounded an alarm,” Westbrook said. “But we’re also getting tremendous state support.”
Internally, USC cut back on administrative expenses, starting nearly a decade ago, and put those savings — $60 million to date — into an account it could use for hiring faculty and building the medical school.
“I think there are institutions that put themselves in a tough spot because they’ve overbuilt too quickly,” Westbrook said.
We’re the flagship institution. It’s our responsibility to make sure we do these things in a responsible way,” Amiridis added. “Build it and they will come is great for Hollywood, but it’s not a reality.”

Roger Marshall said he is “frustrated” President Donald Trump is importing beef from foreign countries, sparking fear among domestic cattle producers that the action could undercut their markets. text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall prepares to speak to a group of Kansas business leaders on Aug. 27, 2026, in Olathe. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall said he is “frustrated” President Donald Trump is importing beef from foreign countries, sparking fear among domestic cattle producers that the action could undercut their markets.
He rationalized the president’s move, arguing imported beef is necessary to replace the Mexican cattle exports lost to screwworm infections that plagued herds earlier this year. 
A Perry resident expressed nervousness during a telephone town hall Friday about selling her 25 head of cattle. She said she and her husband are self-employed, their fertilizer bill had tripled this year and their diesel prices doubled. He assured her that the cattle market is solid nonetheless.
“My point to the White House is when he does this, this sends the wrong signal to the rancher to keep his heifers rather than selling them into the market,” Marshall said.
He said he was as “frustrated as anybody” by the beef imports.
At a separate event Thursday, in one of the first public meetings between Kansas’ U.S. Senate candidates, the Republican incumbent highlighted his involvement in international trade accomplishments in the past six years and their effects on agriculture.
He said at a candidate forum in Olathe hosted by the Kansas Chamber of Commerce that in his second year in the U.S. Senate, he traveled to Mexico to help negotiate the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement on behalf of agriculture. Mexico is Kansas’ largest exporter, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. He visited Mexico City again in June.
“I think it’s those extra efforts where we can go forward and develop these long-term relationships,” he said Thursday. “But at the same time, you have to be tough.”
Marshall left the event that hosted all candidates for statewide office early, lingering after he finished speaking for only a few moments to hear his opponent.
In November, Marshall will face the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor in the Kansas City area whose fundraising and campaigning abilities match Marshall’s deep well of national Republican support. 
The candidates received a set of questions in advance and were given the same amount of time to respond. They discussed regulation, trade, agriculture and their vision for Kansas.
Hamilton attributed some of the pains in Kansas’ agricultural sector to Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran. Marshall, too, expressed eagerness to end the war in Iran, in alignment with Trump, but not at the expense of Iran possessing nuclear weapons. There is a place for tariffs, Hamilton said, but consistent ones.
Hamilton also pointed to immigration as a way to help increase Kansas’ population and help businesses, particularly in agriculture and the restaurant industry.
“So right now, when you travel to southeast, southwest Kansas, you’re talking to people in the meatpacking industry, the cattle industry, and they’re saying, ’40% of our workforce are immigrants, and we need them, and we care about them. These are our people,’ ” Hamilton said.
He said Kansas needs legal and safe immigration.
“Stop demonizing them,” Hamilton said. “Figure out a plan to bring immigrants in where it’s legal for them to be here, and where we can welcome them instead of having to live in fear in our businesses or our communities.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A summer of recalls exposes holes in the nation’s food safety net
description: This year’s tally of food recalls is roughly in line with numbers in recent years. But experts worry about the scope, severity and scale.
text:
Jalapenos. Frozen berries. Beef. Alfalfa sprouts.
A summer of food recalls, including the record-shattering cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce that has sickened thousands, has raised many Americans’ fears of contracting a foodborne illness.
The recalls have focused attention on the Trump administration’s decision to cut funding and staff at several public health agencies, and prompted questions about whether those changes have made consumers more vulnerable.
In fact, this year’s tally of food recalls is roughly in line with the numbers in recent years. About 48 million people each year get sick from a foodborne illness. But experts worry that the scope, severity and scale of outbreaks and their associated food recalls are growing.
While the United States sees some cyclosporiasis cases every year, this year’s outbreak has crushed records: Since May, the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed more than 17,000 cases, with another nearly 12,000 reported cases still under investigation. The outbreak has resulted in at least 922 hospitalizations and two deaths.
Federal officials have blamed this year’s multistate outbreak on processed iceberg lettuce from central Mexico. The lettuce was brought to the U.S. by Taylor Farms, a distributor that supplies foods to thousands of restaurants and grocery stores, including Target, Taco Bell, Whole Foods, Kroger, Walmart, Costco and Jack in the Box.
The CDC and the Food and Drug Administration are investigating at least six other clusters for which a source hasn’t yet been confirmed.
Cuts at the CDC and FDA haven’t necessarily increased consumers’ chances of food contamination or outbreaks, said Jennifer McEntire, a food microbiologist and the founder of a food safety consulting firm. However, McIntire said, “I do think the cuts may have influenced the way outbreaks unfold.”
“I think there are valid questions around the timing of the response, the time it took for agencies to recognize the outbreak and to start to investigate it, get boots on the ground in Mexico,” she said.
Darin Detwiler, a food safety expert and professor emeritus at Northeastern University, noted that the U.S. is seeing more recalls affecting multiple states, rather than a small area. He added that more recalls are being tied to a problem earlier in the food chain — such as contaminated irrigation water at a large lettuce farm rather than, say, improperly stored deli meat at a sandwich shop  — which can spread the pathogen to a far higher number of people and make it harder to track and contain.
“We’re seeing so many people impacted, so many states impacted, and the recalls are dragging on for a long time,” Detwiler. “There’s ambiguity or lack of transparency over who’s even behind a recall.”
The White House dismissed concerns about the federal government’s ability to handle outbreaks.
“The Trump Administration has never cut FDA food inspectors or other frontline personnel for domestic disease response,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told Stateline in an email. “President Trump’s top priority is the health and safety of the American people, and the federal government remains capable of robustly addressing any future outbreaks.”
Fewer staff, less funding
Last year, the Trump administration laid off thousands of employees at federal public health agencies including the CDC, which tracks and responds to disease outbreaks, and the FDA, which oversees and regulates food safety.
While some of the layoffs were reversed through lawsuits or by Congress, the nation’s health public agencies remain at diminished capacity. The CDC workforce has been reduced by 28% since December 2024, the month before Trump took office, according to a Stateline analysis of data from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management. Employee numbers at the FDA are down 23% during the same period.
Last year, U.S. inspections of foreign food facilities, such as the Mexican farming operation linked to the cyclospora outbreak, plummeted to historic lows following those staffing cuts. The FDA suspended a quality control program for food testing. And the parasite surveillance staff at the CDC, which responds to outbreaks, was downsized last year by the Department of Government Efficiency from 11 people to three.
Sandra Eskin, a food safety expert who worked in the office of food safety at the U.S. Department of Agriculture during the Biden administration, likened federal public health cuts to the game Jenga, where players construct a tower of wooden blocks and then remove the blocks one at a time while trying not to make the tower fall.
“I think that’s what we’re seeing,” said Eskin, who now leads a public health nonprofit called Stop Foodborne Illness, which advocates for stronger food safety policies. “Whether it’s cuts in staff, cuts in funding that trickle down to the states, or late responses to outbreaks — these are all pieces of wood in that game where you start pulling them out and then the whole thing collapses.”
The federal government also has delayed requiring companies to comply with new food safety rules, included in a law enacted more than a decade ago, that would help regulators track where food comes from and where it’s going during outbreaks.
Detwiler and other experts say the new rules could have helped speed the government’s sluggish response to the cyclospora outbreak investigation after Taylor Farms initially tried delaying the recall.
Last year, the Trump administration also drastically scaled back FoodNet, an early warning surveillance system that required tracking of infections caused by eight different foodborne pathogens. The federal-state collaboration is now only required to track two pathogens: salmonella and Shiga toxin-producing E.coli. The other six pathogens, including cyclospora, were made optional.
The CDC says the change was made because other surveillance systems monitor those pathogens. But McEntire and other food safety experts want them reinstated on FoodNet.
State impacts
Infectious outbreaks like cyclosporiasis are typically investigated by state and local health departments, which largely rely on federal dollars distributed through the FDA and CDC. Public health has been chronically underfunded for decades under several administrations, experts say.
But the Trump administration since last year has terminated $5.78 billion in CDC grants — funds that were appropriated by Congress but had not yet been spent.
Michigan, at the center of the cyclosporiasis outbreak with the highest number of cases and clusters, is one of 23 states (plus the District of Columbia) that successfully sued the Trump administration in June 2025 over federal funding cuts.
Changes to federal funding last year affected public health infrastructure across Michigan, a representative from the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services told Stateline. During the cyclosporiasis  outbreak, the state used its own resources to bolster local responses.
“While we are able to support this investigation on a local level, sustained investment in public health capacity is essential to ensuring Michigan can respond effectively to future regional and statewide public health threats,” said department spokesperson Lynn Sutfin.
This story was first published Aug. 31, 2026 by Stateline.

title: Immigration losses and a Medicaid cliff test senior care system
description: We all need care as we age. Adam Scott leads New England’s largest nonprofit provider of senior care and living communities. He says demand is rising as the Commonwealth’s average age continues to increase. This week on Health or Consequences, John McDonough of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Paul Hattis of the Lown Institute talk with Scot[...]
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Paul Hattis & John McDonough
GUESTS: Adam Scott, president and CEO of Hebrew SeniorLife






HEBREW SENIORLIFE lost 35 employees in a single day this summer. It was the largest one-day staffing hit in the history of the senior care and housing organization, which has shed about 100 employees over the past year amid shifting federal immigration policy.  
The president and CEO says the losses compound a MassHealth financing squeeze he calls unsustainable for the long-term care sector. 
Adam Scott, one year into the top job at New England’s largest nonprofit senior care and housing provider, joined hosts John McDonough of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Paul Hattis of the Lown Institute on a Health or Consequences edition of The Codcast. 
The 35 employees, all Haitian nationals, lost their jobs after the US Supreme Court’s June ruling cleared the way for the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians. Massachusetts is home to 45,000 Haitian TPS holders, and the state estimates at least 2,000 work in nursing facilities and home care roles. 
The terminated workers had averaged 13 years at Hebrew SeniorLife, with most working there since the devastating 2010 earthquake in Haiti.  
“These are important jobs and they’re meaningful jobs,” Scott said. “And people make a difference in people’s lives. And what’s hard is replacing that loyalty.”  
The federal travails facing the sector include changes to MassHealth, the state Medicaid system, which covers 75 percent of Hebrew SeniorLife’s long-term care patients. Scott said the 2025 federal reconciliation law, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, could cost Massachusetts $2 billion a year in MassHealth funding once fully phased in. Long-term care already consumes 10 percent of the state’s $22.7 billion MassHealth budget, he said. 
“We can’t raise prices,” Scott said, describing rising health benefit and labor costs colliding with flat MassHealth reimbursement rates. 
“And so that means we have to look at ways to cut our costs and cut our costs more,” he said. “And that’s in the face of affordability challenges for every resident of the Commonwealth. We can’t cut our nursing salaries. We have to increase them because our nurses are facing rising heat costs and rent costs. And so, the rubber has to meet the road somewhere.” 
Scott placed his organization’s struggles in the context of a shrinking statewide sector: Massachusetts has lost 34 skilled nursing facilities and 3,500 nursing beds since 2020, even as demand climbs among residents over 85. About 1,200 hospital patients a day are stuck waiting for discharge because of limited space at skilled nursing facilities, he said. 
On top of the looming Medicaid cuts and sudden staffing challenges brought by the stripping of TPS status for a group that makes up a vital share of the long-term care workforce, there is a growing cost crisis facing those who rely on the sector.  
Scott pointed to Washington state’s new payroll-tax-funded long-term care benefit as one model worth watching, while cautioning that its $36,000 lifetime payout covers only a couple of months of care. 
“The middle class really has no way to pay for care except by impoverishing themselves,” Scott said of the country’s long-term care financing gap. 
On the episode, Hattis, McDonough, and Scott discuss the Hebrew SeniorLife workforce losses (6:10), the MassHealth financing outlook (14:15), and the future of dementia care at the Wolk Center for Memory Health (27:00).

Social Security. NPR’s Ashley Lopez is reporting, “The Social Security trust fund is running out, and yet it’s not a top campaign issue.”Congress has about six years to shore up the Social Security trust fund, which is expected to run out of reserves by the end of 2032.Enacting a solution is liable to be a significant political battle, likely involving cutting benefits for some Americans or raising taxes on higher earners, or both.
And so far, congressional leaders haven’t made it a top-tier issue.
Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno proposed raising the payroll tax for some Americans. Revenues from the tax go into the trust fund. But that bipartisan effort was immediately panned by conservative groups, and little else has emerged as a serious solution.
Civil Rights. Ideastream’s Conor Morris is reporting, “Why one Ohio civil rights activist’s sacrifice still matters today.”
Fifty years ago this month, a federal judge ordered Cleveland schools to desegregate.But it took decades of activism by parents and others — and the loss of one activist’s life — to get to that point.
The Rev. Bruce Klunder, a young white Cleveland Presbyterian minister, died in 1964 when protesting schools that remained de factor segregated in Cleveland, years after the Brown v. the Board of Education U.S. Supreme Court decision deemed segregation unconstitutional.
Lake Ontario. KOSU’s Sarah Liese is reporting, “Lake Ontario name change erases Indigenous history, Wyandotte Nation leader says.”
Chief of the Wyandotte Nation, Billy Friend, took offense to Trump’s decision to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America. The tribal nation is now headquartered in northeast Oklahoma, but has history in the Great Lakes region.Trump’s executive order claims to restore names that honor American greatness, but Friend said it is another act of forced removal and erasure. He said his ancestors, who spoke Wendat, gave Ontario its name, Ontari’io, which means “the lake is big” or ‘the lake is beautiful.”
“It’s not about politics; it’s about history,” Friend said in a phone interview. “It’s about respecting a tribal name and the people whose language gave that name to the lake.”

name: Nevada Current
title: US House Dems at Las Vegas shadow hearing link Trump ‘corruption’ to affordability crisis
description: Nevada’s Democratic House members heard testimony from expert witnesses on Friday who tied President Donald Trump’s policies and “self-enrichment” to the rising costs of gas prices, groceries, housing costs, and energy bills.  Nevada Reps. Susie Lee, Dina Titus, and Steven Horsford were featured in a congressional shadow hearing in Las Vegas focused on affor[...]
text:
Democratic Reps. Susie Lee (NV), Robert Garcia (CA), and Maxwell Frost (FL). (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Nevada’s Democratic House members heard testimony from expert witnesses on Friday who tied President Donald Trump’s policies and “self-enrichment” to the rising costs of gas prices, groceries, housing costs, and energy bills. 
Nevada Reps. Susie Lee, Dina Titus, and Steven Horsford were featured in a congressional shadow hearing in Las Vegas focused on affordability and the cost of living. 
The hearing was held byDemocratic members of the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and the House Oversight Committee, including California Rep. Robert Garcia – the ranking Democrat on the committee.
Donald Sherman, president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), laid out a laundry list of actions by Trump and his administration he said demonstrated “corruption” and “self-enrichment,” adding that those actions have exacerbated the affordability and cost of living crisis hitting American households. 
Since winning the 2024 election, Trump has created 59 companies, and he reported at least $233 million in revenue from them in 2025, according to a CREW analysis. 
“While folks in Nevada and across the country struggle with the cost of basics like gas, groceries, and health care, 2025 was the most lucrative year of Trump’s life,” Sherman said. 
Those decisions have come at the cost of Nevada’s economy, said Sherman. He pointed to Trump’s decision to host the 2026 G20 Summit at the Trump National Doral Miami golf resort, which directly benefited the president’s private business.
“He’s holding the G20 summit in Miami so that his business can benefit when cities like Las Vegas could also use the economic boost,” Sherman said.
In March, Huffpost reported that Trump’s golf trips have cost taxpayers over $100 million in security and travel costs—much of which has gone to his own resorts. Propublica also reported that a company linked to Donald Trump Jr. received a $620 million loan from the Department of Defense. 
“There’s the direct profiteering by Trump, his family, and his cronies off of your hard-earned money,” Sherman said. 
During the hearing, Titus also criticized Trump for using his public office to directly profit from selling early access to his social media posts on Truth Social, which has raised concerns about insider trading. 
“Now you’ve got the president not only buying up companies, creating companies, investing in companies, getting grants for friends’ companies, but he’s going to sell his tweets or whatever they are now,” Titus said. 
“This is really direct corruption in the American presidency. You have the president’s family potentially making — could be billions, could be hundreds of millions, by some estimates — in contracts, in loans, in crypto schemes, while the American public and their cost in gas and groceries and food continues to go up,” Garcia said.
Liz Pancotti with the left-leaning policy group Groundwork Collaborative said the affordability crisis is a result of several cost of living expenses increasing simultaneously. 
Since the start of Trump’s second term, household electric bills are up 16% nationally, said Pancotti. Fuel costs are also on the rise as a direct result of Trump’s war in Iran. Nationally, gas prices reached an average peak of more than $4.50 a gallon in May, about 50% higher than they were in February, and the national price remains close to $4 a gallon.
The average price of a gallon of regular is $4.82 in Nevada, a dollar more than it was a year ago, according to the AAA fuel price tracker.
In Nevada, the number of SNAP participants has declined by more than 20% since last summer, following the implementation of new work requirements set by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Juanny Remoero, CEO of Las Vegas-based Mothership Coffee, described razor-thin margins at her business as a result of tariffs and rising fuel costs. The Supreme Court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful and must be refunded to firms that paid the taxes on imports, but was appealed by the Trump administration.
“Unfortunately, there’s only been one importer that actually provided refunds on the tariffs,” Remoero said. “I can’t control tariffs. I can’t control gas prices. I can’t control wars, and it impacts my business.”
Ted Pappageorge,secretary-treasurer of the Culinary Workers Union Local 226, cited statistics to the committee indicating how Trump administration policies have damaged Nevada’s largest industry, tourism. 
Last year, Las Vegas saw the largest ever single year non-COVID drop in visitor volume, going back to 1970. Visitation to the city dropped by over 7% in 2025, with over 3 million fewer visitors compared to 2024, according to data from the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority.
Total passenger count at Harry Reid International Airport has been declining for 18 straight months, and the year-to-year date count through July is down nearly 7% percent compared to last year.
Pappageorge added that he believes the slowdown has been aggravated by Trump’s hostility towards allies, especially Canada, long the Las Vegas tourism market’s  largest source of international visitors. 
“It’s no surprise when you make it clear that folks are not welcome in this country that they choose to go somewhere else,” Pappagageorge said. “In Las Vegas, fewer visitors to Las Vegas means fewer customers in the casinos and hotels, fewer covers, fewer tips in the restaurants, and all that means fewer hours and shifts and layoffs for our members.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Controversial Flock cameras are found across CT. What to know.
description: The cameras capture information from every passing vehicle, raising questions and concerns about privacy and surveillance in CT towns.
text:
Towns across Connecticut are facing questions and concerns from residents about their use of automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, sold by companies like Flock Safety.
The cameras are continuously monitoring, capturing images of passing vehicles that are then used by police departments to investigate crimes like stolen cars and missing people. They serve a different purpose than traffic cameras, which are used to monitor activity like speeding or red light violations.
Here’s what to know about these cameras and how they are used.
What are ALPRs used for?
These cameras capture images of passing vehicles and record information such as license plate number, vehicle make, model, color, location and the date and time the vehicle was photographed. Some systems can also identify characteristics of a vehicle even when its license plate is not visible.
Police can search ALPR systems for vehicles connected to an investigation or receive alerts when a vehicle on a law enforcement watch list passes a camera. Investigators can also search for vehicles that were in a particular area when a crime occurred.
But because the cameras, which don’t use facial recognition technology, capture information from every passing vehicle, they have raised questions about privacy and surveillance.
The companies that sell the cameras, like Flock Safety, have examples on their websites of times the cameras have proven useful to police. But there is little information available about how effective the technology is in Connecticut specifically.
Who determines where these are installed?
Individual cities and towns decide whether to install the cameras, which technology to use and how long to keep the systems.
That means the number of cameras, the vendor and the policies governing their use can vary from one community to another. A Flock Safety spokesperson recently told Connecticut Public that at least half of the state’s police departments use some of the company’s services, including the license plate readers and drones.
Some Connecticut communities have in recent months paused or reconsidered additional installations amid resident concerns about privacy and data sharing.
Gov. Ned Lamont has also asked municipalities to pause new camera installations while state officials develop additional guidance.
Are ALPRs the same as traffic cameras?
No, and automated license plate readers are not used to enforce traffic laws.
ALPRs are different than traffic cameras because they are not triggered by an action like speeding. The cameras continuously capture vehicle information.
How long is the information kept?
Privacy advocates have raised concerns about what happens when individual vehicle sightings are collected over time. A network of cameras can potentially provide a broader picture of where each vehicle has traveled.
A new law in Connecticut was signed in May and includes some provisions that go into  effect in October and beyond. It attempts to address those concerns by limiting how long ALPR information can be kept and how it can be used. Under the law, agencies generally must delete data after 21 days unless it is tied to an active criminal investigation. 
Can police share the information?
Yes, but there are restrictions.
The new Connecticut law prohibits ALPR data from being used for immigration enforcement. It also restricts its use in certain investigations involving reproductive healthcare, gender-affirming healthcare and activities protected by the First Amendment.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ House candidates increasingly skip League of Women Voters debates
description: Congressional candidates in both parties are more likely than ever to dodge debates planned by the League of Women Voters.
text:
Republican Michael McGuire, left, is seeking to unseat Rep. Herb Conaway (D) this fall in the 3rd Congressional District, and McGuire claims Conaway is ducking a planned debate. (McGuire photo courtesy of his campaign/Conaway photo by Dana DiFilippo/U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray)The League of Women Voters, a century-old nonpartisan voting-rights organization, has long hosted public debates around the country as a way for citizens to engage with the political candidates running to represent them.
But in recent years, the number of candidates on both sides of the aisle who duck their debates has climbed, with GOP officials in Cape May County urging Republicans up and down the ballot this year to avoid league events altogether.
To Jesse Burns, who heads the league in New Jersey, the trend is equal parts troubling and baffling, especially as participation in voter guides produced by the group wanes too.
“We have refusals across the state right now,” Burns said. “We’re just looking to provide information to voters so that we can increase voter turnout and have voters feel confident that they have the information they need to cast a ballot and actually understand what candidates’ policies are and not just the party that follows their name.”
Feud escalates between NJ governor, GOP over voter registration gaffe

Election observers say debate-dodging is a longtime campaign strategy that has become more common in the social-media era as candidates — especially incumbents and front-runners — try to avoid gaffes that could go viral and cost them votes.
That happened earlier this month, when Republican Sen. Darline Graham — facing a runoff election to retain her late brother Lindsey Graham’s U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina — flubbed a question about national security in Taiwan and the South China Sea.
“National security is not my thing,” she said in a moment that earned her widespread drubbing on social media. “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham prevailed despite the debate stumble.
A gotcha moment during a New Jersey gubernatorial debate last fall echoed long after Democrat Mikie Sherrill, who went on to win, and Republican Jack Ciattarelli left the stage. Sherrill accused Ciattarelli, a former medical publisher, of killing “thousands” of people by printing propaganda for the opioid industry.
“A lot of people thought that moment was over the top, and there were questions about whether it was a fair charge or whether it was a distorted charge,” said Micah Rasmussen heads the Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics at Rider University. “But it put him on the defensive for the rest of that debate, and really after the debate. He had to answer those questions at a time when he needed to be on the offense.”
Those debate moments show why some candidates prefer to play it safe, steer clear of the debate stage, and carefully control their messaging, Rasmussen said.
“Most of the time, modern campaigns are designed around that scripted moment, and debates are essentially that one time when it’s not scripted, when you could be asked a tough question,” he said. “It’s a high-risk, low-reward situation for a lot of candidates who are ahead, and they would just rather run out the clock.”
But skipping debates can backfire because it gives a candidate’s campaign rivals ammunition to attack, as Republican Michael McGuire did last week in his bid to unseat Rep. Herb Conaway, the Democrat incumbent in Burlington County’s 3rd Congressional District. McGuire blasted Conaway for skipping a League of Women Voters debate.
“For more information — or if you’re Congressman Conaway changing your mind about debating — please contact the campaign,” McGuire’s team cheekily wrote in a news release.
Conaway didn’t respond to the New Jersey Monitor’s request for comment. He told the league’s Monmouth County chapter he had a scheduling conflict, said chapter spokeswoman Mary Donnelly. McGuire also did not confirm his participation, Donnelly added. McGuire’s team told the New Jersey Monitor he sent the chapter a letter indicating he would participate if the forum is held in person before Sept. 19, when ballots begin going out.

“The most effective attack you can make against an incumbent is that they’re not doing their job, and voters broadly perceive engaging with the public as being part of doing your job,” said Dan Cassino, a political science professor and pollster at Fairleigh Dickinson University. “So if you dodge debates, this opens you up to attacks: ‘Oh, this person’s afraid of us. This person won’t speak to the public. This person won’t reveal their views.’”
In Cape May County, GOP chair Michael Donohue said his guidance to Republican candidates to avoid league events there has more to do with local leadership, which he does not regard as nonpartisan, rather than opposition to the group broadly.
“They are very vocal. And — God bless them — I’m not saying they’re doing anything wrong by being far to the left. That’s their prerogative in a free country. I’m just saying that from the standpoint of a Republican candidate, why would you go to a forum hosted by those folks?” Donohue said.
Burns denied any bias and pointed to debate format as proof why partisan fears are unfounded.
“League debates are pretty standard,” she said. “In general, it is a league moderator asking questions that we get from the audience, which is community members. And these are not gotcha questions. These are usually questions like, ‘What are your policy priorities and why?’ So it’s not like we’re setting candidates up to fail in these debates.”
Bias questions aside, Donohue said he struggles to see the point of debates at a time when journalism is shrinking and people are getting their information from a wider array of sources.
“I don’t hate debates, but there’s an analysis from a campaign political standpoint: What’s the value?” Donohue said.
Donohue has run for state Assembly twice and served as his county’s GOP chair since 2010, except during a four-year stint as a state Superior Court judge. He said candidates used to embrace debates in hopes of landing media coverage that would deliver their message far beyond the voters in the debate audience. But now, many news outlets don’t air or cover debates, and even social media can’t reach all the voters a candidate — especially at the local level — can reach by knocking on doors and other such activities, he said.
“Debates end up being just a discussion to your supporters,” he said. “There’s rarely any serious substance in these things, and even if they ask questions that should get substantive answers, typically the candidates just pivot back to some hot-button issue that they want to push to the base. We’re in this Twitter/X moment, and everybody just wants these little sound bites.”
Cassino also sees broader trends at play.
“Debates really are an invention of the TV era, and so it’s possible that they’re going away as the TV era comes to an end,” he said.
Voters increasingly rely on partisan cues as politics becomes hyper-polarized, rather than investing time in listening to debates or seeking out other unfiltered sources of information about candidates, he added.
“In some sense, voters don’t need as much information because the partisan heuristic is more powerful than it’s been in the past,” Cassino said. “So, if I’m a Democrat: ‘I don’t need to know anything about Democratic candidates. They could be the worst candidate on earth, and I’m going to vote for them anyway.’ Most voters are really just: ‘I’m a Democrat. I’m a Republican. Therefore, I know who to vote for.’”
Independent voters still have to do their homework to learn about candidates, he said.
But, he added, “I’ve been teaching college for 20 years. I can tell you nobody likes doing homework. So those voters, by and large, just don’t turn out to vote at all.”
Voters should pay attention when candidates dodge debates, though, Rasmussen said.
“They should want candidates who are accountable, and this is one more form of accountability,” he said. “It’s one more form of: ‘I’m not afraid to answer questions. I’m not afraid to have you measure me up against my opponent. Ask me anything you want.’ That kind of accountability is what we should all want from our elected officials.”
