title: Alabama state library board creates sample policies to implement controversial rule changes
description: The Alabama Public Library Service unveiled a set of sample policies earlier this summer that they say will allow local libraries to remain in compliance with controversial administrative code changes adopted in the past two years. The set includes three examples, known as A, B and C, with different formats, but all contain the elements […]
text:
Books on display in the teen section of the Fairhope Public Library on March 2, 2026. The APLS created sample policies for local libraries to use that align with the recent changes to the administrative code. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Public Library Service unveiled a set of sample policies earlier this summer that they say will allow local libraries to remain in compliance with controversial administrative code changes adopted in the past two years.
The set includes three examples, known as A, B and C, with different formats, but all contain the elements of changes approved by APLS in 2024 and 2025 that directed local libraries to restrict content or risk losing state aid.
“We wanted to make sure they had examples that they could use,” said John Wahl, chair of the APLS Board and Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, in an interview Thursday. “Nothing that was required, just ideas where they could take them to their local boards, make any edits they wanted to make and streamline their process, especially for libraries that didn’t have someone to draft policies for themselves.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In 2024, board members ratified updates that required libraries to create policies restricting minors’ access to  materials that are considered obscene, sexually explicit “or otherwise inappropriate.”
In 2025, members of the APLS Board updated the administrative code for a second time to prohibit library materials that dealt with gender ideology, but without defining the term.
“In the past we would have policy requirements that were much more broad and open, and allowed for individual library boards to tailor those policies to the specific needs of their communities,” said Mary Campbell, president of the Alabama Library Association. “These do not allow you to do that.”
The changes came after right-wing activists targeted libraries in Alabama and around the nation, claiming youth sections of libraries contained explicit or sexually suggestive materials. Some of the books targeted used inclusive pronouns, and critics said the books were being targeted for having LGBTQ+ themes or characters.
Read Freely Alabama, a group that organized to oppose the changes, criticized Wahl and board member Amy Minton in a statement, saying the policies “make clear that this was never about protecting children from explicit content.”
“Libraries are being compelled to treat books about transgender people and gender identity as inherently ‘sexually explicit,’ a vague term that seems to change to reflect whatever John Wahl and Amy Minton want it to regardless of actual sexual content,” the statement said.
Thus far, the Fairhope Public Library has been the lone library to forfeit state aid for refusing to move specific materials that the APLS board objected to.
Example policies have the same statement that bans discrimination, but with an added caveat to accommodate the administrative code changes.
“Exercising discretion in the location of sexually explicit material or other material deemed by the public library board to be inappropriate for children or youth does not constitute a denial of service on the basis of age,” the policies state. “Taking age into account when recommending, displaying or otherwise actively promoting library materials does not constitute a denial of service on the basis of age.”
The sample policies differ in their specificity. But all include sections that refer to specific elements within the administrative code and provide justification.
“Different libraries have different structures with their bylaws for the codes, and we wanted them to have options that fit well with the structure of their local protocols,” Wahl said.
The main changes that board members imposed on the administrative code dealt with library collections and reshelving materials, library cards, displays for content and membership with the American Library Association.
Example A appeared to be the least specific. The selection criteria section had bullet points for relevance, quality and demand, along with a statement that “These criteria safeguard minors from sexually explicit or other material deemed by the public library board to be inappropriate for children or youth.”
The section to reshelve library materials outlined the same criteria that restricted minors from having access to specific library materials and had a statement regarding the gender ideology ban.
“Under this rule, any materials regarding transgender procedures, gender ideology, or the concept of more than two biological genders shall be considered inappropriate for children and youth,” the example policy states.
Example C included more details. It had a section titled “Application and Purpose” that referred to “protecting minors from obscene, sexually explicit, or other material deemed by the public library board to be inappropriate for children or youth.”
The section for selection materials had a numbered list of rules that largely aligned with the paragraphs in Example A but had other particulars.
“All materials intended for minors must be reviewed and approved by designated library staff,” the policy states.
The physical location section in Example C laid out criteria for filing complaints related to library materials.
“Citizens may, upon furnishing proof of residency, initiate a Request of Reconsideration of any library material by filling out the applicable form,” the example policy states. “Requests for Reconsideration are reviewed according to established criteria and procedures, guaranteeing transparency in the decision-making and ensuring that every citizen has a voice in the process.”
Campbell said that the sample policies could help smaller and more rural libraries without adequate staffing to develop policies aligning with the administrative code. But she said it will not solve other issues.
“One of the main issues is the subjectiveness of some of some of the requirements, like what is ‘inappropriate for children,’” Campbell said.
The set of sample policies is one approach that APLS staff have tried to address issues that local libraries face to comply with the administrative code changes.
APLS Director Kelyn Ralya is still considering whether to fill a post that was created to coordinate with local libraries to comply with the administrative code changes. That decision remains pending.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee slightly sheds jobs for 8th month in row, inflation at 3.4%
description: The state’s top economic advisor at the University of Tennessee isn’t concerned yet, even as job numbers show that, for the eighth month in a row, the number of people employed in the state has slightly dropped.  Tennessee’s economy has experienced year-over-year job growth since an initial spike in unemployment at the start of the […]
text:
Tennessee shed jobs for the eighth month in a row, according to federal data. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The state’s top economic advisor at the University of Tennessee isn’t concerned yet, even as job numbers show that, for the eighth month in a row, the number of people employed in the state has slightly dropped. 
Tennessee’s economy has experienced year-over-year job growth since an initial spike in unemployment at the start of the coronavirus pandemic. Then in 2022, the state experienced a few months of job losses, but still managed to add more jobs over the course of the year. 
But the latest economic data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics show that from December 2025 to July 2026, roughly 55,000 fewer Tennesseans have jobs. More than 3.42 million Tennesseans were employed in November 2025, and as of July, that number was 3.37 million. 


Don Bruce, a professor with the University of Tennessee’s Boyd Center for Business and Economic Research, said that the short-term drop in employment numbers is not something he’s concerned about until it becomes a multi-year trend.
“We are still above where we were pre-pandemic,” Bruce said. “I’m comfortable that our state economy is strong enough to weather short-term fluctuations in employment.”
TN unemployment low, but sheds jobs for the 5th month in a row

Despite shedding jobs, Tennessee’s unemployment rate fell in July to 3.4%. Outside the early pandemic months, Tennessee’s unemployment rate has remained below 4% since April 2017. 
Tennessee’s unemployment rate still remains low because fewer people are working. Economists at the University of Tennessee have attributed this to a steady increase in retirements, the rise of artificial intelligence and recent crackdowns on immigrant workers. 
The other economic concern for state officials is inflation, which sits at about 3.4%. Typically, the U.S. Federal Reserve targets a yearly inflation rate of 2%.
Bruce said oil prices are driving inflation, which makes it less likely that the U.S. Federal Reserve will cut interest rates this year. The increase in oil prices reverberates throughout the economy, making almost every shipped product more expensive. 
The price of oil spiked dramatically in February after President Donald Trump launched a war with Iran. Prices have fluctuated more widely over the past six months because of the war, and remain higher today than at any point in 2025.

title: Summit forfeits two CO2 storage permits in North Dakota, continues legal fight over third
description: Summit Carbon Solutions is abandoning two-thirds of its planned project to store carbon dioxide underground in North Dakota.  The company, which had been granted permits to store CO2 in three designated areas in central North Dakota, has requested permits for two of the areas to be canceled.  “Summit #1 and Summit #2 have determined as […]
text:
Summit Carbon Solutions representatives pictured at an event in Sioux Falls in January, 2025. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Summit Carbon Solutions is abandoning two-thirds of its planned project to store carbon dioxide underground in North Dakota. 
The company, which had been granted permits to store CO2 in three designated areas in central North Dakota, has requested permits for two of the areas to be canceled. 
“Summit #1 and Summit #2 have determined as a matter of business judgment that they will not proceed with development, construction, operation, or implementation of either proposed storage facility,” Summit said in a filing with the North Dakota Supreme Court. 
A North Dakota district court voided permits for all three areas earlier this year. Summit and the state are appealing that decision. But the company is now asking the Supreme Court to limit the appeal to one of the storage areas, known as Summit #3. 
The company’s decision to abandon two of its storage facility permits is a victory for many of the landowners opposing the project. Most of those landowners have objected to what they characterize as the company’s unwillingness to negotiate on matters of liability and compensation. Only one of the landowners involved in the litigation owns property in the third storage area. 
Courts order North Dakota to pay landowners’ legal fees in two lawsuits

In an email last week, Summit said it is prioritizing Summit #3, where the company has about 98% of the storage rights secured.
Summit’s filing stated the Industrial Commission, a three-member board chaired by Gov. Kelly Armstrong that regulates CO2 storage among other things, had approved the two permit cancellations. 
The company’s original proposal involved transporting carbon dioxide from ethanol plants in five states to central North Dakota where it could be injected into rock layers deep underground. The injection sites were located at the intersection of Mercer, McLean and Oliver counties. 
Summit announced a change of plans earlier this year. The company now plans to transport carbon dioxide to a storage site in Wyoming for injection underground, but did not close the door on continuing to pursue its North Dakota operations to some degree. 
Summit said in an email that its North Dakota pipeline route easements and storage rights are still valuable assets.
“Over time, we expect to further develop and utilize these assets as opportunities materialize,” the statement said. 
The company’s storage permits from the Industrial Commission, the state law authorizing the Industrial Commission to issue those permits, and the pipeline route permit from the Public Service Commission are all the subject of litigation in North Dakota. District court judges have voided the storage permits and struck down the underlying law; both cases are on appeal to the Supreme Court. The third case is waiting on a decision from the district court.

text:
Thursday’s ruling, which was backed by two of former President Donald Trump’s nominees to the bench, marked the third major legal challenge of the 2010 law to fail at the nation’s highest court.
At stake was the health care coverage of more than 21 million people nationally who have gained insurance through the marketplace. (Getty Images)
Last week, a pair of Democratic lawmakers from the Michigan House and Senate shared that they were working on legislation to ensure more Michigan residents can access healthcare. 
State Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) and state Sen. John Cherry (D-Flint) on Wednesday announced that they had each introduced legislation to create a Medicaid buy-in program, with Xiong introducing House Bill 6274 and Cherry introducing Senate Bill 1152. 
If the bills are signed into law, Michiganders earning between 133% and 200% of the federal poverty level who do not qualify for Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program would have access to health benefits at a lower premium that what they would pay through a qualified health plan purchased through the Affordable Care Act’s Health Insurance Marketplace. 
State Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) on the House floor on May 1, 2025. | Kyle DavidsonState Sen. John Cherry (D-Flint) speaks in support of bills to repeal Right to Work laws, March 14, 2023 | Laina G. Stebbins
“Health premiums are skyrocketing and too often workers on the frontlines of the construction, food service and home care industries are forced to budget out the largest percentage of their paycheck just to keep their families covered,” Xiong said in a statement. “Our legislation gives hardworking Michiganders who don’t qualify for public healthcare assistance programs an affordable option. No matter what job or industry someone works in or income level, they deserve access to healthcare.”
New York, Oregon, Minnesota and Washington D.C. have already adopted similar legislation making use of an option in the Affordable Care Act allowing states to create a basic health program. The program covers both citizens and lawfully present noncitizens.
“Michiganders are already stretched thin with ever-increasing costs,” Cherry said. “Our constituents should never have to choose between keeping food on the table or seeking care. With the introduction of this legislation, we take an important step toward reducing healthcare costs for those individuals stuck at wit’s end in the marketplace.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Flock tracks your license plate. We tracked the $2M it spent on lobbying.
description: Flock Safety has poured more than $2 million into federal and state lobbying since 2025 as the fast‑growing surveillance company faces mounting scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties and privacy advocates over its ever-expanding network of license‑plate‑tracking cameras. The company spent nearly $1.3 million between January 2025 and July 2026 on federal lob[...]
text:
A Flock camera on the corner of La Harpe Boulevard and North Chester Street in Little Rock on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate) 

Flock Safety has poured more than $2 million into federal and state lobbying since 2025 as the fast‑growing surveillance company faces mounting scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties and privacy advocates over its ever-expanding network of license‑plate‑tracking cameras.


The company spent nearly $1.3 million between January 2025 and July 2026 on federal lobbying and at least another $1 million in statehouses across the U.S., according to OpenSecrets’ federal lobbying data and an analysis of lobbying disclosures across all 50 states. Flock has hired lobbyists in dozens of states – often former government employees passing through the political “revolving door” – including in places where weak disclosure laws mean spending totals are not publicly reported.
Flock has drawn increasing criticism over the vast, largely unregulated network of automated cameras it operates nationwide. The cameras record license plate numbers and other characteristics of all vehicles passing by, allowing thousands of law enforcement agencies in 49 states (all except Alaska) to search and share Flock’s data across jurisdictions. This enables police to track vehicles in real time and build investigative dossiers from billions of scans collected each month.
Several Arkansas cities pull plug on Flock cameras

While police agencies praise the system as a tool for locating missing people and tracking suspects, privacy advocates warn the technology enables mass surveillance without a warrant. And amid a nationwide wave of protests and vandalism targeting the company’s cameras, more than 120 agencies or jurisdictions have canceled, suspended or rejected a contract – or deactivated their cameras – since January 2025, according to a tracker maintained by DeFlock, a group that opposes their use.
Many of those terminations followed concerns raised about improper data access, including instances in which officers conducted personal searches – raising a central question: What, exactly, does Flock want from this lobbying push? OpenSecrets reached out to the company for comment but did not receive a response.
Torin Monahan, a professor at the University of North Carolina and co-editor of the peer-reviewed journal Surveillance & Society, identified several likely items on Flock’s lobbying agenda. He said the company is likely focused on securing long-term contracts with municipalities and counties as well as avoiding potential restrictions that could require police to obtain a warrant before using the system or limit the cross-jurisdiction data sharing that underpins Flock’s network.
“Some of the things they’re lobbying for are things that they’re worried about,” Monahan told OpenSecrets. “I would imagine those are areas where they would like to head those restrictions off at the pass, if they could.”
He also suggested that Flock “wants to become the monopoly for this particular service” of license plate readers because the network gains power as the user count grows.
Flock says it has deals with more than 5,000 law enforcement agencies across 6,000 communities. The company leases its cameras to governments, private neighborhoods and other groups, typically charging an annual fee of $2,500 to $3,000 per camera.
“So if you have more adoption throughout the country, then it probably will … barring any political blowback, persuade other clients that this is the right company that they should contract with for these services,” Monahan said.
Flock’s federal lobbying spending nears $1.4M
Flock is coming off its highest-spending quarter since it began lobbying the federal government in 2024. Between April 1 and June 30, 2026, the company reported $220,000 in federal lobbying spending after spending $210,000 in each of the five preceding quarters.
In total, it has spent nearly $1.4 million on federal lobbying, including $840,000 in 2025 and $430,000 so far in 2026.
While the company has not reported lobbying on specific bills, its 2026 filings show activity focused on both chambers of Congress and the White House, including the Office of Administration. Its lobbyists have been working on broad issue areas including homeland security, law enforcement, crime and criminal justice – an agenda that aligns with the company’s efforts to expand its camera network.
Several of Flock’s competitors also are active on K Street, though those legacy firms operate far larger product portfolios.
Axon Enterprise, a weapons and tech company formerly known as Taser, has spent nearly $5.3 million on federal lobbying since 2024 on a range of issues topped by homeland security, law enforcement, crime and criminal justice. Motorola Solutions – the parent of surveillance vendor Vigilant Solutions – has spent about $5 million in the same time frame, with its most frequently cited issues including the federal budget and appropriations, telecommunications, defense and intelligence. But the lobbying activity by those companies is not broken out by subsidiary or product line, making it unclear how much of their spending is tied specifically to automated license plate reader systems.
Much of Flock’s lobbying work has been handled by veterans of the revolving door – former public servants now advocating on its behalf. Five of the seven lobbyists hired by Flock this year fall into that category.
Among them: Bryan Lanza of Mercury Public Affairs, who served as communications director for President Donald Trump’s first transition team; Jennifer Lawkin Lukawski of BGR Group, the first executive director of the Republican Study Committee in the House of Representatives; and BGR Group President Erskine Wells, a former deputy chief of staff for Sen. Roger Wicker (R‑Miss.).
Flock lobbying in statehouses with mixed disclosure requirements
An OpenSecrets review of all 50 state lobbying disclosure databases showed Flock with active lobbyists in 34 states in 2025 and/or 2026. Those filings documented at least $1 million in state-level lobbying during that span – but that figure almost certainly understates the company’s true spending because many states do not require lobbyists or their clients to report compensation.
In 18 of those states, Flock’s lobbyists were active but no spending totals were available. State disclosure laws vary widely, from detailed quarterly reports to systems that exclude retainer fees entirely, and those gaps in reporting requirements create blind spots in understanding the company’s full financial footprint.
In Arizona, for example, Flock retained Molera Alvarez – a prominent Phoenix lobbying firm co-founded by a former state superintendent of schools and staffed with several former state and municipal government employees – to represent its interests in 2025. Yet the state’s lobbying database shows no reportable expenditures. Arizona law excludes lobbyist compensation and retainer fees from disclosure. The secretary of state’s summary of principal expenditures from the previous year also lists $0.
Similarly, in Alabama, the company hired former Secretary of State Beth Chapman in 2025 to lobby state officials. But Flock’s quarterly disclosure forms list $0 in reportable spending, consistent with state ethics rules that do not require companies to disclose private retainer fees.
Flock’s largest known expenditure came in California, where since January 2025 it spent $30,000 in each quarter for a total of $180,000. The company focused its efforts on bills adding guardrails around vendor contracts for license plate reader systems – including measures requiring data that fails to produce a hit to be purged within 30 days, mandating audits, requiring case numbers for queries and blocking cross-agency sharing without authorization.
Of those six bills, only one passed both chambers. That bill would have established data protection requirements for license-plate-reader systems, but Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) vetoed it in September 2025. The others died in committee or stalled in the appropriations process.
“I view the lobbying money … in the same category of trying to influence in advance what the particular outcomes might be,” Monahan said.
Flock also spent $169,000 since January 2025 on lobbying in Massachusetts on issues related to police, fire and law enforcement organizations, and $102,000 in Wisconsin lobbying on state Senate and Assembly bills to establish grants for law enforcement agencies to purchase license-plate-reader systems. In Tennessee, where lobbying disclosures include ranges instead of specific spending amounts, Flock paid its lobbying team between $25,000 and $50,000 in both 2025 and 2026 while recording less than $10,000 in expenses in both years.
By comparison, Flock’s contracts with municipalities and universities routinely climb into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. Monahan noted that some universities pay $750,000 to lease Flock’s systems and city and county deployments can top $1 million.
“It seems like a drop in the bucket compared to the size of their contracts,” Monahan said.
In a sign of its expanding lobbying footprint, Flock registered a lobbyist in Wyoming on June 29.
Minimal spending on campaigns by Flock leaders
Compared to Flock’s lobbying spending, the political activity by its leadership is scant.
Corporations are prohibited from donating directly to candidates or political action committees. Flock Safety does not operate a political action committee for its employees to contribute to, and there is no record of any independent expenditure committee – or, a super PAC – funded by the company or its executives. Nor is there any record of the company or its leaders donating to Trump’s inaugural fund, a legal loophole that allows corporations to give unlimited sums.
OpenSecrets data shows CEO Garrett Langley donated $1,000 in 2024 to Health Jobs Justice, the leadership PAC for Sen. Jon Ossoff (D‑Ga.). Beyond that single contribution, there is no visible federal political giving from Flock’s top executives.
Beyond lobbying: The data question
But Flock’s ambitions extend beyond shaping policy. Monahan said the company is diversifying its portfolio beyond license-plate readers and adding drones, gunfire location systems and citywide “safety dashboards” that aggregate public data.
Taken together, it’s a sign that “the law enforcement space is getting pretty crowded” and that mounting scrutiny may be pushing the company to expand, Monahan said.
But that expansion raises questions that go beyond lobbying dollars, because Monahan said the data Flock collects isn’t used just for law enforcement purposes. It also trains the company’s proprietary AI models.
“What we don’t know, as the public, is where all those data are going. How might compromising data be included in these models? What controls might we have about the applications that these AI systems are being put toward?” he said.
Those are questions, Monahan said, that Flock’s lobbying disclosures don’t answer – and that neither regulators nor the municipalities signing contracts with the company have yet to seriously ask.


This article was originally published by OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that tracks money in politics.

title: ICE released man formerly detained in Aurora without his ID in unfamiliar state
description: Rudy Villeda Mejía, who spent just over four months in immigration detention in Aurora, is home with his family in northern Washington state.  His journey home was drawn out, as his family and attorney struggled to locate him when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released him in a state more than 2,000 miles from home […]
text:
Rudy Villeda Mejía runs a roofing business in northern Washington that has struggled since U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested him in March. (Photo courtesy of Mabel Shaffer)Rudy Villeda Mejía, who spent just over four months in immigration detention in Aurora, is home with his family in northern Washington state. 
His journey home was drawn out, as his family and attorney struggled to locate him when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released him in a state more than 2,000 miles from home after the agency nearly deported him.
A judge ordered on Aug. 3 that ICE release Villeda Mejía, 47, from detention because he has a pending application for a T visa, which is designated for victims of human trafficking. That makes him part of a protected class under a May court order from California that blocked ICE from detaining immigrants with pending T visa applications, along with other visas for crime victims. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Villeda Mejía is adjusting after his return home and is back to work at his roofing business, which suffered financial losses while Villeda Mejía was detained, struggling to repay debts for new equipment the company purchased. 
“Now he’s just trying to catch up with work,” Genaro Shaffer, Villeda Mejía’s stepson, said. “We have all these roofs that we’re doing, and he’s just constantly working, working, working every day. It’s got to be exhausting after going straight from detention to work.”
Villeda Mejía, originally from Honduras, has lived in the U.S. since he entered without authorization in 2010, when he was kidnapped by a violent cartel in Mexico that brought him over the border, according to a notarized personal statement Villeda Mejía submitted with his visa application. 
​He fled gang violence. Now this ICE detainee in Aurora tries to avoid deportation.

ICE arrested Villeda Mejía at Denver International Airport on March 30. He was detained at the ICE detention center in Aurora until early August, when ICE moved him across the country to a “staging facility” in Louisiana — the final stop before ICE deports someone, according to Henry Hollithron, Villeda Mejía’s Denver-based attorney. 
Shortly after he arrived in Louisiana, Judge Regina Rodriguez of U.S. District Court in Colorado ordered his release. Her order prohibits ICE from re-detaining Villeda Mejía unless it demonstrates at a hearing that he is a flight risk or danger to the community. 
Stripped of passport
Villeda Mejía’s wife flew to Louisiana, where the couple rented a car to drive back to Washington, according to Shaffer. That was only after the family and Hollithron scrambled to narrow down exactly where ICE released Villeda Mejía.
ICE told one family member he was still in Aurora. Another person detained in Aurora told a different family member he was no longer in Aurora. Hollithron’s office heard he was in Oakdale, Louisiana. Then that changed to Alexandria, Louisiana, and again to Winnfield, Louisiana. 
“We’re sure he’s in Louisiana somewhere. We just don’t know where in Louisiana he actually is, because the left hand doesn’t know what the right hand is doing,” Hollithron said. “This is the reality of families dealing with immigration detention. You can’t even find your relatives half the time.”
Shaffer said he ultimately learned that ICE flew Villeda Mejía to Arizona and then to Texas, and he was driven from Texas to Louisiana. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



ICE has arrested and deported thousands of immigrants across the U.S. since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 as part of his mass deportation scheme, which ensnares immigrants who lack permanent legal status. While the Trump administration has said those efforts target criminals, many of those arrested do not have criminal records, only civil immigration violations.
The latest hurdle was getting back Villeda Mejía’s passport and work permit, which remained in Colorado after ICE transported him to Louisiana. Without an ID, Villeda Mejía couldn’t fly home from Louisiana, Hollithron said, and even if he had his ID, his family feared that ICE would attempt to detain him at the airport again. 
ICE’s Denver Field Office declined to answer Newsline’s questions about Villeda Mejía’s transport out of Colorado, plans for his deportation or its retention of his personal documents. 



Quotation







This is the reality of families dealing with immigration detention. You can't even find your relatives half the time.


– Henry Hollithron, immigration attorney


Shaffer said Villeda Mejía has now received back his passport and work permit with support from U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen’s office. Larsen is a Democrat who represents the district in Washington where Villeda Mejía’s family lives. 
“My office stands ready to help people detained by ICE access legal services and help loved ones locate their family members in ICE custody,” Larsen said in a statement, which included a link to his visas and immigration page. “After an individual or their family member fills out a privacy release form, my staff can advocate on their behalf to federal agencies like ICE and (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services).”
‘Imagine the worst day of your life’
While the immediate legal hurdles have ceased, Shaffer said his stepfather is now regaining strength after months in detention led to new difficulties with back pain. Hollithron said some of Villeda Mejía’s Bell’s palsy symptoms also flared up after he didn’t receive medication while detained. Shaffer said Villeda Mejía’s hair has started to turn gray, too.
“The conditions that he lived in were like, imagine the worst day of your life, and then imagine living that … for 120 days straight,” Shaffer said. “Worst sleep, worst food, people threatening to beat you up, it’s horrible.”
He said what his family has gone through with ICE can happen to anyone. 
“Rudy had perfect records, like, you couldn’t be more clean,” Shaffer said. Villeda Mejía attended every check-in scheduled at the Seattle Field Office until he was detained this spring.
Shaffer said hiring a good lawyer and asking members of Congress for help are the best ways to get movement from ICE. 
“ICE will do everything against you possible unless they are personally liable for their actions,” Shaffer said. “The only thing that matters to them is a (judge’s) order.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas expects millions from Meta settlement. Here’s where other social media cases stand.
description: Arkansas is on track to receive at least $172 million in a landmark multistate settlement over online child safety. But the state’s other cases against social media platforms are still winding through the courts. Attorney General Tim Griffin and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders have been pushing for more scrutiny on social media firms through lawsuits […]
text:
(Photo Illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Arkansas is on track to receive at least $172 million in a landmark multistate settlement over online child safety. But the state’s other cases against social media platforms are still winding through the courts.
Attorney General Tim Griffin and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders have been pushing for more scrutiny on social media firms through lawsuits and legislation. The Republicans hailed the settlement with the parent company of Facebook and Instagram as a win for that effort.
Meta’s $17.1 billion settlement with 51 attorneys general requires the company to enact new safety measures. The agreement requires court approval.
Here’s a look at where the state’s other cases involving social media stand:
TikTok
Griffin in 2023 filed lawsuits against TikTok in Cleburne and Union counties, accusing the social media platform of misleading parents about the availability of mature content.
The lawsuits accused TikTok of violating the state’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act. 
TikTok argued that the lawsuit was barred by Section 230 of the 1996 Communications Decency Act, which protects Internet companies from being sued because of users’ posts.
But a Cleburne County judge rejected TikTok’s motion to dismiss the case, and a trial is scheduled in March 2027. The Union County case is also pending but a trial date has not been set.
Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement

Google/YouTube
A 2024 lawsuit Griffin filed in Phillips County against YouTube, Google and their parent companies accuse them of intentionally targeting children with addictive and harmful content.
A judge rejected the companies’ argument that the case should be dismissed because of the Communications Decency Act’s protections. That decision has been appealed and is pending before the Arkansas Court of Appeals.
Snapchat
Griffin in June filed a lawsuit against Snap Inc., the parent company of Snapchat, claiming that the California-based company’s social media platform was deceptively designed to addict minors who used it.
Snap has sought to move the case, which was originally filed in Phillips County, to federal court. The attorney general has filed a motion to move the case back to Phillips County.
Discord/Roblox
A June lawsuit Griffin filed in a Los Angeles court accuses the social gaming platforms Discord and Roblox of putting children at risk of sexual predation.
The lawsuit accuses the platforms of violating the state’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act and Public Nuisance Law.
A hearing in the case has been scheduled for November.
Social media restrictions
The lawsuits are progressing as Arkansas is defending its reworked law that would have required age verification to create new social media accounts.
A 2023 version of the law was struck down as unconstitutional. A federal judge in April temporarily blocked enforcement of a new version approved in 2025.
The state has appealed that decision to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which is expected to hear arguments in the case next month.
The blocked law also includes other restrictions, including a requirement for social media platforms to maintain certain default settings for minors. 
Another appeal pending before the 8th Circuit concerns a 2025 law that makes it easier for parents to sue social media platforms. 
A federal judge in December blocked the law, which allows parents to sue social media platforms if exposure to content on their sites results in their child developing eating disorders, committing or attempting suicide, or becoming addicted to the platform’s feeds. The state appealed that ruling.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: The danger for the Alabama GOP in the data center issue
description: There’s an apocryphal quote attributed to Fisher Ames, one of the first congressmen from Massachusetts. You can find different versions of it out there, but the idea is this. Monarchy is like a trim wooden sailing ship, with a captain delivering orders to officers who execute them without question. The vessel is a marvel, swiftly […]
text:
Residents of Lowndes County holding up signs that read "No Data Center" at a County Commission meeting on Aug. 24, 2026, in the Lowndes County Courthouse in Hayneville, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)There’s an apocryphal quote attributed to Fisher Ames, one of the first congressmen from Massachusetts. You can find different versions of it out there, but the idea is this.
Monarchy is like a trim wooden sailing ship, with a captain delivering orders to officers who execute them without question. The vessel is a marvel, swiftly slicing the waves and turning with precision. But if it hits a rock, it sinks quickly.
Democracy is like a raft. It’s slow; it’s hard to maneuver, and your feet are always wet. But if it hits a rock, it stays afloat.
The Alabama Republican Party is neither clipper ship nor inflatable. It’s more of a wooden tub. Yet it’s gotten so used to favorable winds and calm water that it appears to be overlooking a major reef up ahead.
Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s insistence that data centers are good and their opponents are communist stooges hasn’t stopped the public outrage over the facilities. One data center proposed in Lowndes County — taking up 800 acres and reportedly using enough electricity to power 42% of all the homes in Alabama — drew at least 150 people to a county commission meeting last week.
Lowndes County isn’t alone. Across the state, local governments have tried to stop data center development or heard from large numbers of residents demanding they do so. Democrats have gotten behind gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones’ call for a yearlong moratorium on the facilities.
Tuberville, meanwhile, treats them as inevitabilities and makes dubious claims that they’ll be important revenue sources for their communities. Downballot Republicans may be trying to soften the blow, but in that deferential, whatever-you-say-boss manner that tells you where they’ll land.
After all, the Alabama politician is a creature who believes that “economic development” is magic that can take the place of governing (even though it probably doesn’t work). The Alabama politician ignores your concerns and tells you the real problem in Alabama is the fact corporations pay taxes in the first place.
That’s Alabama’s top-down approach to governing. Politicians believe they can tell voters what’s important. Zealots and lobbyists, in turn, can convince those officials that their weird or destructive obsessions are what matter.
Let’s be honest. If you ran into someone at a party loudly complaining about transgender people, they would come across as an obsessive and likely a creep. Yet a handful of bigots ensured that the GOP embraced obsessive creepiness in 2022 and 2024.
I want my children to learn American history with all its inspiration and tragedy. But a small group of brittle men in the Legislature not only made the teaching of a vague list of “divisive concepts” difficult but  gave schools like the University of Alabama an excuse to shut down spaces for Black and LGBTQ students.
Tuberville and other politicians bullied a Islamic school in Hoover and tried to make a controversy out of interfaith gatherings. With zero justification. And a spittle-drenched hatred straight out of Alabama’s Jim Crow era.
Did the public demand these attacks? Of course not. Ask Alabamians what they want from state government, and most will say a lottery or the end of the grocery tax.
Our grandees can’t deliver those. So they started telling voters in Alabama’s ever-lower turnout elections what they should care about. And it seemed to work.
No surprise, then, that the GOP’s gubernatorial nominee, cocooned in Alabama’s lickspittle conservative media, thinks he can order you to love data centers. If you don’t, he seems to assume that he can ignore the objections once elected.
And he’s probably right.
No other issue in recent years has better illustrated Alabama’s fundamental lack of democracy than data centers. County governments are often powerless to stop them because the state constitution denies them zoning authority (a point raised by both the Association of County Commissions of Alabama and the Lowndes County Commission). Even cities that have that authority are creatures of the Legislature. They may not want data centers, but anything they do – like setting a minimum wage – can be vetoed by lawmakers.
And the Alabama House and Senate? Dominated by Republicans, most of whom represent heavily gerrymandered, uncompetitive districts.
But despite all their institutional advantages, this is a genuine risk for Republicans.
Here is a broadly unpopular trend. Here are cities and counties rejecting the facilities. And here is a majority party that doesn’t see a problem.
Data centers will not turn Alabama purple. They will not magically transform Republicans into Democrats. What they could do is keep Republican voters home, a development the Alabama GOP can’t afford in a year where they face a clear enthusiasm gap. It’s possible screaming about socialism or Tuberville’s threats to subject Montgomery, a majority-Black city, to military occupation will draw some of those people to the polls. I wouldn’t count on it.
I’m not betting that Republicans will lose this fall. I’ve seen the great GOP ship steer confidently through trouble and over public opinion in the last 16 years. The data center issue may not be enough to sink it.
But the Republican captain is confident that it won’t. And he’s steering the vessel toward the rock.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Tuberville, AG, GOP ask Alabama Supreme Court to affirm residency challenge dismissal
description: Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville Thursday asked the Alabama Supreme Court to affirm a lower court’s dismissal of a case challenging his residency, with the backing of the state Attorney General’s Office and the Alabama Republican Party.  In a 62-page brief filed Thursday evening, attorneys for Tuberville called the plaintiffs’ appeal “prepos[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaking at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Tuberville on Thursday evening asked the Alabama Supreme Court to affirm the dismissal of a case challenging his residency. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville Thursday asked the Alabama Supreme Court to affirm a lower court’s dismissal of a case challenging his residency, with the backing of the state Attorney General’s Office and the Alabama Republican Party. 
In a 62-page brief filed Thursday evening, attorneys for Tuberville called the plaintiffs’ appeal “preposterous,” writing that the Alabama Legislature has severely limited the courts’ abilities to hear election-related challenges under a law first passed in the 19th century.
“In truth though, there are multiple countervailing provisions of the Constitution that counsel against court action. To the extent that courts has a ‘special duty’ here because the Constitution is implicated, the duty extends to several other provisions,” the brief said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Messages seeking comment were left Friday with attorneys for the plaintiffs challenging Tuberville; Tuberville’s campaign and his legal team. 
The lawsuit argues that Tuberville does not meet Alabama’s seven-year residency requirement for the governorship. Tuberville has faced questions about his residency for years, and the plaintiffs’ complaint cites reporting including a homestead exemption in Auburn that Tuberville said he has been on since 2018 but was not added to until mid-2024, and a 2023 Florida driver’s license.
The case before the Supreme Court is not challenging Tuberville’s May primary win. It is seeking to allow the lower court to hear arguments about Tuberville’s residency.  
Tuberville has maintained that he meets the requirement, but does not deny that he owns a home on the Florida coast. In the Thursday brief, his lawyers argue that temporary absences do not strip a person’s resident status. 
“People that spend most of their time as agents of the state in Washington DC – like a U.S. Senator – would not lose their status as a ‘resident,’” it said. “Nor would they lose Alabama ‘resident’ status because they made regular visits to a Florida beach house they own or leave to go out of state on business every Sunday night to return on Friday night.”
His lawyers did not make it clear that Tuberville’s Auburn home – the listed address for his Senate candidacy, and often referred to as the “Game Day House” – is his primary residence. 
“Above all, (Section) 117 of the Constitution calls for the governor to be a ‘resident.’ In common parlance that probably means a shelter with a roof and walls that could be used as a place for sleep,” the brief said. “It does not obviously mean that being a ‘resident’ of some other place is forbidden. There is no adjective that disqualifies if the place is not a ‘primary residence.’”
The lawsuit made its way to the Alabama Supreme Court after Montgomery County Circuit Judge Brooke Reid dismissed the case in July due to a lack of jurisdiction after an hourslong hearing. Reid did not rule on the merits of the case. 
Does the Alabama Supreme Court have jurisdiction?
The Heflin-Torbert Judicial Building in downtown Montgomery, Alabama, seen on January 24, 2023. The building houses the Alabama Supreme Court and the state appellate courts. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall and the Alabama Republican Party also submitted amicus briefs on Tuberville’s behalf on Thursday. 
Plaintiffs are seeking relief known as quo warranto, Latin for “by what authority,” challenging Tuberville’s right to hold office. Marshall argued that while courts do have jurisdiction over quo warranto cases and election challenges, the plaintiffs in this case erred in asking for it in this instance. He said that the case is a political issue, and it is up to the Legislature to resolve any election challenges.
“Courts have a vitally important role to play in many election disputes, but not this one,” he wrote in a 46-page brief.
Plaintiffs challenging Tuberville’s residency have argued that quo warranto it can be applied to party nominees like Tuberville as “quasi-officers” like Tuberville. Tuberville’s lawyers disagreed in Thursday’s brief.
“Alabama precedent rejects the conclusion that ‘quasi-officer’ status is sufficient to be challenged in a quo warranto action,” the brief said. 
Marshall wrote that Tuberville is only a public officer if he can perform the “sovereign functions” of the office, which he says the U.S. Senator cannot do as a gubernatorial nominee.
“A role defined by party governance and subordinate to party control is not a public office,” he wrote. “So the quo warranto statute, limited by its terms to public officers, does not extend to such party positions.”
During the lower court hearing, Tuberville’s lawyers asserted that the Alabama Republican Party and the Alabama Legislature have the authority to decide if the U.S. Senator meets the constitutional requirements for governor. The Alabama Republican Party dismissed a primary election challenge against Tuberville in June. 
In a Thursday afternoon brief, attorneys for the ALGOP argued that any further challenges should be dealt with by the Legislature.
“Moreover, the Legislature intentionally limited courts’ jurisdiction from hearing election disputes, instead granting the State’s political parties’ exclusive authority to settle their respective primary election contests,” the 31-page brief said.
Tuberville’s lawyers said the lawsuit is not “justiciable,” and nothing about that changes because the Legislature is a Republican supermajority.
“Changing the rules in the middle of an election is not good politics and sometimes becomes judicially actionable,” the brief said. 
Plaintiffs also requested oral arguments, but only if the justices have questions that are not answered in the briefs filed this month. Tuberville’s lawyers and Marshall objected to the request.
“There is no need to explore in oral argument the wisdom of an ‘extension’ of existing law. In the event this case cannot be resolved by summary disposition, it is likely moot, given the pace of the election process,” Tuberville’s brief said.
The Secretary of State certified all opposed state and federal candidates on Wednesday. The last day to withdraw from the ballot was Aug. 24. 
Tuberville’s lawyers also argued that the case is irrelevant because there can be no feasible relief at this point, since ballots are certified.
“As the debate is limited by the relators not to involve the elections, and no relief sought against any official that confers anything on Tuberville. Moreover, there is no person injured by Tuberville’s merely being a nominee,” the brief said. “Thus, in claiming they do not care that Tuberville won that election, they are the kind of litigants who merely want to debate, not resolve an injury in just fashion.”
The plaintiffs have one week to file a reply brief.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: After two years of limbo, Kentucky’s kinship care is back on track
description: After two years of limbo, the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services has started implementing a 2024 law to help families who step in to raise a minor relative, known as kinship care families.  The Kentucky legislature approved and Gov. Andy Beshear signed SB 151 in 2024 to provide financial relief to grandparents and […]
text:
Michelle Tynes, of Hickory in Graves County, and her grandson, Ashton, are a kinship care family. An estimated 59,000 Kentucky children are being raised by relatives other than their parents. (Photo provided)After two years of limbo, the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services has started implementing a 2024 law to help families who step in to raise a minor relative, known as kinship care families. 
The Kentucky legislature approved and Gov. Andy Beshear signed SB 151 in 2024 to provide financial relief to grandparents and others who are raising children who otherwise would be in state care by making it easier for the family members to qualify for foster care payments.
Beshear’s administration contended that without specific funding — at one point, an estimated $20 million — it couldn’t implement the law. The General Assembly pushed back, saying he had the responsibility to implement it. 
For the next two years the legislature, auditor’s office and Beshear’s administration debated the issue — including in court — over who is responsible for funding the law and where the money should come from.
In Beshear’s budget request for 2026, he asked the legislature to appropriate $14.6 million in each fiscal year — nearly $30 million over the biennium — to fund the law. 
When the Senate initially added funds for SB 151 implementation, Beshear said “If they provide us $5 million, we’ll provide $5 million to those families.” 
By the end of the 2026 session, lawmakers upped the funding, giving Beshear $6 million each year — $12 million total — to fund SB 151. 
A July 15 letter from the cabinet to regional administrators and supervisors shared the Standard Operating Procedures for kinship care placements — essentially, guidance for cabinet employees on how to follow the law when considering placing a child in a kinship care home. 
Spokeswoman Beth Fisher said the cabinet had “authority” now to implement Senate Bill 151 thanks to language from this year’s House Bill 500, the two-year state budget. 
KY lawmakers increase money for kinship care in final budget 

“House Bill 500 contained language which gives the Dept. for Community Based Services (DCBS) the authority to implement Senate Bill 151 through its existing systems and processes,” Fisher said. “DCBS is using the funding it has access to that was included in the current state budget to support payments to eligible family caregivers.”
Norma Hatfield, a longtime kinship caregiver and advocate, has some concerns about the way the law is being implemented now — and what she sees as a lack of transparency around the new guidance. 
“When the funding came out, you had two years, you had a deficient regulation, and then you put a policy out there, it seems like quietly, without any public input,” she said. “Kinship caregivers deserve better. They — we — deserve a lot more than that. This thing should have been, to me, close to perfect after two and a half years, and that’s not what we got.” 
Hatfield has several main concerns about the policy as written, she said: 

“The placement decision process may be confusing and is tied to services and supports that differ depending on the path a caregiver takes. I feel that information about those options is not always consistent across the policy, forms, handbooks and public-facing materials, which can make it difficult for caregivers to make a fully informed decision.” 
“The qualifying-event application process — including the timeframes, notification methods and wording of the forms — may create unnecessary barriers for caregivers trying to access assistance.”  
“There are questions regarding Kentucky’s approach and about maximizing federal funds ensuring  protecting and supporting kinship caregivers.”   

She’s hoping for a full briefing with lawmakers and the cabinet to learn more about the full procedures to ensure potential kinship care families can both access help and do so without unnecessary confusion. 
In Late July, Fisher said the funds made available in the budget would go to relative and fictive kin foster parents receiving per diem for the children in their care. (Fictive kin are people who aren’t related to a child by blood or marriage but who have a strong connection with the child, such as a longtime family friend). 
Those payments depend on the age and needs of the child, according to Fisher. 

Basic is the primary payment for foster families when they start and ranges from $27 to $47 for medically complicated children. 
Advanced is a rate paid when foster parents have completed 2 years of fostering and 30 specific training hours. Payments for this range from $30 to $81. 


Care plus is a level of foster parenting that requires specialized training to care for youth with complex behavioral health needs. They require both initial and ongoing training hours. 


Medically complex requires specialized training, and the child must be deemed medically complex. 

“Team Kentucky believes every child should have a safe and loving home,” Fisher said, “and values the critical role of family caregivers in supporting children across our commonwealth.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Could Trump’s diminished popularity in Kentucky affect how this year’s midterm races are run?
description: President Donald Trump may no longer be the silver bullet in Kentucky elections that Republicans once had as voters face pains from an ongoing war in Iran and rising gas and grocery prices.  The president’s growing unpopularity in the Bluegrass may play into the central Kentucky 6th Congressional race in the weeks ahead as GOP […]
text:
Ralph Alvarado is the GOP candidate for the 6th District Congressional race in Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Chris Hughes)President Donald Trump may no longer be the silver bullet in Kentucky elections that Republicans once had as voters face pains from an ongoing war in Iran and rising gas and grocery prices. 
The president’s growing unpopularity in the Bluegrass may play into the central Kentucky 6th Congressional race in the weeks ahead as GOP and Democrats hope to use their messaging to sway voters in a general election. 
Ralph Alvarado, the Republican nominee in the election, removed mentions of the president, who had endorsed him in the primary earlier this year, NBC News first reported Aug. 25. The changes included removing a photo of Alvarado and Trump from the homepage and referring to himself as a candidate for “independent leadership” when he once called himself an “America First fighter.”
As of Friday morning, the media page on Alvarado’s campaign site does still include a photo of the candidate and Trump. 
Months ago, Trump’s endorsements did well in Republican primaries. In Kentucky, Trump-backed Ed Gallrein defeated incumbent firebrand U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie in the 4th Congressional District by 10 points. Trump’s late-hour endorsements of Alvarado and U.S. Rep. Andy Barr in the Senate race led to both candidates sailing to comfortable leads in May. 
However, polling shows Trump’s approval underwater in many states, including states he has won in past elections like Kentucky. A YouGov/Economist projection released Aug. 21 showed the president’s job approval rating negative in all but three states. Kentucky was at -13 points in the findings. 
Reacting to the NBC story, the campaign for the Democratic nominee, Zach Dembo, said the move by Alvarado was an attempt “to try and paper over his real record” on the heels of a poll from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee saying Alvarado and Dembo are tied. DCCC has added the 6th District to its “Red to Blue” list, meaning it’s a priority race for funding and support. 
“If this is how Ralph treats his friends, imagine how quickly he will sell us out when it’s convenient,” Dembo said in a statement. “My opponent has proven he is just another two-faced politician who will say anything to try and get elected.”
Zach Dembo is the Democratic candidate for the 6th District Congressional race in Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Chris Hughes)
Andy Westberry, a spokesman for Alvarado said in a statement the campaign has “proudly touted the endorsement” from the president and pointed to the photo of Trump and Alvarado on the site. 
“It’s no surprise this Biden alum is desperately trying to change the conversation,” Westberry said, referring to Dembo’s work as an attorney in the Justice Department during the Biden administration.
Morgan Eaves, the executive director of the Kentucky Democratic Party, said Trump’s lower approval rating is a reaction of voters to “the economic reality that is Trump’s America.” Since Trump began war in Iran, gas prices have gone up, increasing other costs like groceries.
“They’re being faced with the fact that, shockingly, it’s not popular to make those decisions, and so now you’re kind of seeing them play cleanup,” Eaves said of Republicans. “But voters aren’t stupid; they’ve already branded themselves. They’ve already made their views clear, and we’re going to continue to make sure voters don’t forget that.”
Former Democratic U.S. Rep. Mike Ward, of Kentucky’s 3rd Congressional District, said Trump’s approval ratings are a “harbinger of the fall election.” Trump won the 6th Congressional District by 15 points in 2024, and if this “is a place where you have to downplay Trump, imagine the districts where he only won by five to 10 points,” Ward added. 
Kentucky Republicans are not so easily swayed. Adam Hope, the spokesperson for the Republican Party of Kentucky, said the state is still a place Trump has won by 30-plus points and “he still has a pretty significant level of support.” Trump won Kentucky’s electoral votes in 2016, 2020 and 2024. 
“Polling is polling at the end of the day, but you look at the historical presence that the president has had in Kentucky, and that’s not going away anytime soon,” Hope said. RPK is continuing to see engaged GOP voters in Kentucky, as the party maintains a registration edge statewide and counties flip from Democrat to Republican. 
Still, Barr and U.S. Rep. James Comer – who have both tied their campaigns tightly to Trump – feel comfortable enough to address Trump’s new effort to bring down beef prices, something opposed by the Kentucky Cattlemen’s Association. On Thursday, Comer, who is the undeclared but early favorite GOP candidate for governor in 2027, said he has not been happy with Trump’s tariffs and their effects on Kentucky agriculture.
“I’ve expressed my displeasure with the president and the secretary of agriculture, explained why we don’t buy beef from Argentina,” Comer said. “And when you talk about America First, if we’re going to have tariffs — we should stick with it one way or the other.”
Barr’s campaign website has also shifted between the primary and general elections. According to Wayback Machine archives, the Barr website switched a photo on the homepage of Barr and Trump to one of Barr and two of his children in July. The wording also changed from “Kentucky Tough. 100% America First. Trump-Endorsed” to “Kentucky Tough, Kentucky First, Always.” As of Saturday, Barr’s homepage does note that the congressman was the first member of the Kentucky congressional delegation to endorse Trump and that he was the Kentucky chairman for Trump’s 2024 primary campaign.
Alex Bellizzi, a spokesman for Barr’s campaign, said “Kentuckians know that Andy Barr is proud to have President Trump’s endorsement” and the congressman “can’t wait to keep fighting for Kentucky alongside President Trump as our next U.S. Senator.”
Trey Grayson, a former Republican secretary of state, said “all good candidates pay attention to the political environment.” The array of voters candidates must reach in a closed primary election, with just members of their party, is different from a general election. As of July, independent and third-party voters make up about 12% of voters in the 6th District who will also be able to vote for Alvarado or Dembo for the first time. 
Grayson said one thing Republicans do have going for them this election cycle is that Democrats are still unpopular with voters. 
With how it is configured, the 6th District is still “a pretty good Republican district,” Grayson said. Anchored by Lexington, one of the state’s urban areas, it’s surrounded by rural counties. 
“He’s run before. He’s won before. He’s used to navigating some of this,” Grayson said of Alvarado. 
Kentucky’s general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Kentucky House Speaker says we should evaluate data center tax breaks. Let’s expand that idea.
description: Earlier this month, House Speaker David Osborne made an interesting comment to the Lexington Herald-Leader about whether Kentucky’s generous tax incentives to data centers were a good idea. “We should always be asking whether an incentive delivers a return for taxpayers, but we also need to make sure we’re comparing apples to apples before drawing […]
text:
Kentucky gives away about $9 billion in tax breaks every year. (Getty Images)Earlier this month, House Speaker David Osborne made an interesting comment to the Lexington Herald-Leader about whether Kentucky’s generous tax incentives to data centers were a good idea.
“We should always be asking whether an incentive delivers a return for taxpayers, but we also need to make sure we’re comparing apples to apples before drawing false conclusions disguised as economic analysis,” Osborne said. “Instead of looking at this in isolation, Kentucky has to evaluate these programs in the context of the broader economic development landscape.”
Despite the not very subtle dig at the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy, which found that the legislature’s data center incentives could cost the state billions of dollars, Osborne was on to something. 
Kentucky gives away more than $9 billion a year in tax incentives, breaks and rebates, otherwise known as tax expenditures. By 2028, it will be nearly $10 billion. Do they work in the “broader economic development landscape?” 
We don’t know because we don’t “evaluate” them.
But we love to hand them out. We give them to gigantic replicas of Noah’s Ark, we use them to evict mobile home park residents, we give them to millionaire horse owners, fancy shopping malls, ostrich farmers, Hallmark movie directors and much, much more.
You can read all about them in the Tax Expenditure Analysis, a handy report written every year by the Office of State Budget Director. 
Now there are some big ones, like a sales tax break on food and medications, that probably help people. But a lot of these are corporate welfare, plain and simple, and they are often awarded not on merit but on the size of their lobbyists’ delegation. (It helps if the lobbyists are former legislators.)
Once, someone did do something. Or tried. Louisville Republican Rep. Ken Fleming, chaired a task force that concluded Kentucky should keep the top 10 most expensive tax expenditures, like food and medicine, and get rid of the rest. 
Did his colleagues jump at this chance to save money? Not a bit, even though they are now trying to eliminate the state income tax. It would take some brave politicians to stand up to the herdsmen of all those sacred cows.
But maybe Rep. Osborne is ready. Given the statewide outrage over data centers, one of his colleagues hinted the General Assembly might be making some changes to the generous incentives offered to data center developers.
And the aforementioned Kentucky Center for Economic Policy has also pointed out that depending on how data centers are classified – “manufacturing” or “industrial processing” facilities – they could possibly qualify for more breaks in local property taxes or sales taxes on energy costs, which already exist.
Data centers have provoked some deep vein of bipartisan anxiety in Kentucky, ostensibly about pollution and high costs, but more viscerally centered around AI, children and social media, job loss, and fears of being controlled by feckless tech bros. Politicians from both parties, including Gov. Beshear, now say if data centers are so great, they should pay their own  way. 
But while we’re at it, why don’t we see how much good all those other tax giveaways are doing for our economy. It’s exciting that Osborne agrees, and maybe with his political heft, Kentucky could finally see if all these giveaways make any sense.

title: Virginia health leaders, lawmakers share enhanced healthcare resources for rural communities
description: Eastern Shore residents and healthcare providers on Friday told state leaders about the opportunities and challenges they face serving their communities, with Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa outlining how the state government can support them and other rural Virginians.  “We’re here to learn what the challenges are, what the[...]
text:
Eastern Shore Rural Health CEO Jeanette Edwards shows Virginia Health and Human Resources Secretary Marvin Figeuroa a radiology room at the organization's Eastville clinic on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Eastern Shore residents and healthcare providers on Friday told state leaders about the opportunities and challenges they face serving their communities, with Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa outlining how the state government can support them and other rural Virginians. 
“We’re here to learn what the challenges are, what the assets are and ‘how (we can) scale the work,” Figueroa  said at Eastern Shore Community College, one of several stops on the listening tour. 
The same day, the  state announced $122 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund awards were disbursed to healthcare organizations around the state. Former Gov. Glenn Youngkin applied for the new federal grant last year.
The next RHTF funding wave will be allocated by the end of October, and Virginia has $189 million total to spend over time. Figueroa and his team are responsible for distributing the funding and coordinating with Gov. Abigail Spanberger and state lawmakers on its use. 
Del. Rob Bloxom, R-Accomack, joined Figueroa for the multi-stop tour, which highlighted the regional workforce and the unique connection they have with the people they serve. The local community college, the Eastern Shore Area Agency on Aging, Riverside Shore Memorial Hospital, local health centers and various nonprofits participated. 
Juan Gomez, an outreach coordinator with Eastern Shore Rural Health — a set of regional federally qualified health centers — described part of his work helping people  sign up for health insurance at public events. 
One of the clinic’s licensed practical nurses, Nicole Crockett, is an Eastern Shore native and has been with the clinic for 13 years. 
“People know my face and feel comfortable because of that,” she said. 
With her focus on pediatrics, she’s enjoyed watching the children she cares for grow up. To level up her career, she is also taking courses at the Eastern Shore Community College for a Registered Nurse degree. 
Of the clinics’ over 400 employees, CEO Jeanette Edwards said that about half of them have graduated from the local college or are pursuing additional degrees or certifications there. 
The day’s dialogue broached the looming changes stemming from H.R.1, the reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer that’s expected to trigger loss of Medicare and other healthcare benefits for millions nationwide. 
The impact may be felt unequally in the state and hit rural areas hard, Bloxom said.  
“When you go around rural parts of Virginia, not everyone has the network of people like we do. But we have things to worry about and we need to adjust,” Bloxom said. 
Because of the new standards, Figueroa said, “We’re losing more than we’re getting.”
The RHTF money can boost services at clinics, hospitals and nonprofits, and strengthen staffing, telehealth and workforce development, Figueroa added. 
The state is also bracing for eligibility and procedural changes to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
Of Virginia’s two million Medicaid enrollees, about 300,000 are at risk of losing their insurance, while about 5,800 lawful immigrants will lose their eligibility for it. Roughly 749,000 Virginians are also SNAP recipients. 
Additionally, Congress let Affordable Care Act subsidies expire, leading thousands of Virginians to drop that form of insurance due to higher premiums. 
Virginia’s latest budget earmarked $150 million for a state-level version of the ACA subsidy that will be available this fall. The money will also provide a funding boost for federally qualified health centers and free clinics. 
Hospitals are also expected to grapple with a forthcoming change in funding mechanisms it uses to help support Virginia’s Medicaid expansion. The various forthcoming cuts paired with long-established rural healthcare challenges means that 13 rural hospitals are at risk of service cuts or closure, a state report found. 
Last week Spanberger signed an executive order to solidify state and local government directives to streamline H.R. 1 implementation efforts. 
“It’s a new system to build” before the changes kick in Jan. 1, Figueroa said. 
The  state has created plain language toolkits for announcement materials that local agencies and nonprofits can use to make signs and handouts, Figueroa said, to help residents determine if they’re eligible and understand how to navigate the new process.
Even with streamlining efforts by state and local agencies, the event’s attendees said they were concerned that people may lose their benefits due to challenges in their own lives amid the new, twice-yearly verification requirements and eligibility standards. 
Northampton department of social services worker Mozella Francis said that she encounters many Medicaid or SNAP beneficiaries that lack consistent phone or computer access. Others may not have a car or easy access to public transit. 
Francis implored Bloxom and his counterparts in the state legislature to do more to address transportation hurdles in rural areas. 
Throughout the day, Figueroa reiterated the “tough time” patients, providers and public servants will have ahead of them. He noted the “bond” he feels with residents and healthcare workers around the state and said he is “committed” to helping ensure people can navigate the changes as smoothly as possible. 
“We can’t solve all of people’s life problems but it’s our responsibility to not make it worse,” he said.
