text:
At least one dorm at the Holman Correctional Facility in Atmore, located in south Alabama, is uncooled. (Lee Hedgepeth/Inside Climate News)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
ELMORE — Tiffany Montellano can’t sleep.
Instead, she lies awake, worried about her husband Andrew, 31, who is incarcerated at Elmore Correctional Facility just north of Montgomery.
She worries because a few days ago, she received a call during her lunch break from Andrew, who had missed their usual call the night before.
He told her he had become dizzy the previous day because of the overwhelming heat inside the un-air-conditioned, 200-person dorm where he’s housed.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“He said the room wouldn’t stop spinning, and they had to hook him up to an IV,” Montellano said.
Montellano is among many Alabamians whose loved ones inside state prisons are describing intolerable conditions because of the ongoing and more frequently record-breaking heat.
Of the state’s 14 major correctional facilities, none have universal air conditioning, according to Eddie Burkhalter, a researcher for the Alabama Appleseed Center for Law and Justice, a nonpartisan nonprofit that works to reform the state’s justice system.
“Housing humans like this in the extreme heat in Alabama and across the South: It’s torture for people,” Burkhalter said.
The Alabama Department of Corrections did not respond to questions for this story.
In 2022, the U.S. Department of Justice deemed the conditions in Alabama prisons, which operate at around 160 percent of their stated capacity, unconstitutional. Federal courts have so far agreed, repeatedly ordering the state to improve staffing, mental health services and other aspects of its prison operations.
Still, even as the state uses COVID relief funds to help fund construction of a new mega-prison, the 4,000-bed Governor Kay Ivey Correctional Complex, many of the 27,000 currently incarcerated Alabamians continue to suffer in the heat.
The impact of heat in prisons can be pronounced, research shows.
A 2023 study that analyzed data from public and private prisons across the U.S. from 2001 to 2019 showed that extreme heat events led to increases in overall deaths, cardiac-related deaths and suicides.
“These findings suggest that warm temperatures are associated with increased mortality in prisons, yet this vulnerable population’s risk has largely been overlooked,” the study concluded.
Montellano said the state has an obligation to treat those it imprisons fairly. What she hears every day from her husband, she said, doesn’t reflect any commitment to humane treatment.
“They have to go in the shower and dip their towels in water and wrap it around their bodies because it’s so hot,” she said.
Exhaust fans meant to remove hot air from the building are often broken, he told her.
“Everybody takes the sheets off their bed because they’re so drenched in sweat,” she said. “So they either lay on the cold metal bed frame or lay on the floor.”
Christopher Fritz spent two years in St. Clair Correctional Facility, just northeast of Birmingham. He said that every summer, he’s reminded of his time behind bars and worries about the people still suffering in the heat.
“When the heat index was over 100, they would give us a six-ounce cup of Gatorade twice a day,” Fritz said. “That was their idea of dealing with the heat, but it was unbearable.”
While he was incarcerated, Fritz said he witnessed many men faint from the heat. Elderly residents were particularly impacted, he said.
“Some of them couldn’t even get out of the bed because of the heat,” he said.
Matthew Gray Bush has been a pen pal for several incarcerated Alabamians for years. He recently received a message from a friend incarcerated in Limestone Correctional Facility near Huntsville about the consequences of the heat on a 60-year-old dorm-mate.
“I’m a little worried this morning because he has been taken to healthcare three times, and they keep sending him back to the dorm,” the message, reviewed by Inside Climate News, said in part. “He needs to go to the free world hospital.”
Later, the contact said the man had been told by prison medical staff that he’d suffered heat stroke, a severe, life-threatening medical condition.
Burkhalter said he often hears from family members who describe similar incidents and conditions.
“We just don’t treat them like human beings,” he said. “And they are human beings. They have mothers and fathers and children to go home to.”
The overwhelming majority of those currently incarcerated in the state will be released at some point, he said, so it’s critical that society thinks about what that individual is like when they return to the community.
“Do we want them to return shell-shocked? More addicted to drugs? With serious medical conditions? Do we want them to be wracked with PTSD and anxiety and depression?” he asked. “Because that’s what happens when you torture people.”
Despite the impact of the heat, limited data exists about the nature or extent of heat injuries inside Alabama prisons. That’s partly because even among the general population, deaths related to heat in Alabama and across the nation are systematically undercounted, with cause of death often solely attributed to cardiac or other issues, which are often caused or exacerbated by excessive heat.
Burkhalter has worked for years to collect data on deaths in Alabama prisons. As he scrolled through the records of summer months on a hot August day, he scoffed. He began reading causes of death aloud:
“Hypertensive cardiovascular disease. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Pulmonary embolism due to probably deep vein thrombosis. Their deaths are being deemed natural by the state of Alabama,” he said. “But it’s not natural to keep somebody in the heat like that.”
And Burkhalter said he’s not surprised to hear that loved ones like Montellano—those who committed no crime and face no sentence—are filled with anxiety.
“Can you imagine if your loved one—if your spouse or your child was locked away in a place like this,” Burkhalter asked. “Would you be able to sleep at night?”
As the climate continues to warm as a result of greenhouse gas emissions, the impact of heat on Alabamians, both inside and outside prison walls, will likely rise.
As part of its 2022 State Climate Summaries, NOAA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, wrote that while Alabama had so far escaped the near-universal increase in net temperatures, the future includes near-certain record-breaking heat.
“Temperatures in Alabama have not risen since the beginning of the 20th century, one of the few areas globally to experience no net warming. However, recent years have been very warm and the warmest consecutive five-year interval was the most recent, 2016 to 2020,” the report said. “Under a higher emissions pathway, historically unprecedented warming is projected during this century.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State readjusts childcare assistance after complaints about rate change, but concerns remain
description: A Sioux Falls after-school coordinator said she fielded calls from panicked parents this month after the state altered childcare assistance payments — in some cases slashing assistance by more than 80%, she said. Rebecca Wimmer is the coordinator for the Sioux Falls School District’s after-school program. She reported hearing from families who said it would[...]
text:
Students in the Sioux Falls School District play on a playground. (Courtesy of Sioux Falls School District)A Sioux Falls after-school coordinator said she fielded calls from panicked parents this month after the state altered childcare assistance payments — in some cases slashing assistance by more than 80%, she said.
Rebecca Wimmer is the coordinator for the Sioux Falls School District’s after-school program. She reported hearing from families who said it would be more cost-effective for a parent to quit working and stay home with their kids than to pay for the lost assistance. She relayed those stories to state lawmakers, the Governor’s Office and the state Department of Social Services.
Child Care Assistance is a federal-state program that helps low-income working parents, students and job trainees afford childcare. South Dakota’s program costs the state about $6.7 million and the federal government $28.4 million. It covered 3,346 children in June.
At the start of this month, the Department of Social Services made a change to its payment model that Wimmer said would have cut payments to some individual families by hundreds of dollars.
The switch was part of a planned overhaul of the department’s payment model, meant to make payments more predictable for childcare providers. Complaints from affected families and providers resulted in the department readjusting payments a little over a week later for urban after-school programs, where the effects were especially severe. Urban counties include Minnehaha, Lincoln, Meade and Pennington.
Change to tiered, flat rates
State Rep. Brian Mulder, R-Sioux Falls, advocated on behalf of families for the readjustment. Mulder works with Volunteers of America, which provides after-school care. He is grateful for the department’s decision.

Rep. Brian Mulder, R-Sioux Falls, speaks in the House of Representatives at the Capitol in Pierre on March 9, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

“For this school year, we’re in a spot where school can start and families can feel confident they have proper funding for out-of-school care to support their needs and child’s needs,” Mulder said.
Under the old system, program payments were based on a child’s actual hours of attendance, which meant payments could fluctuate and make it hard for providers to predict their income.
The department switched to three tiers of flat weekly rates earlier this month: a full-time rate for more than 28 hours of care per week, part-time for 16-27 hours and limited for 1-15 hours. 
The rates were informed by a 2024 market survey of Child Care Assistance-enrolled providers. For after-school programs in Sioux Falls and Rapid City, the new rates set full-time reimbursement at $185 a week, with part-time dropping to $92.50 and limited to $46.50. 
The change cut some families’ state payments by hundreds of dollars a month, Wimmer said, including one family that would have had state payments cut from $950 a month to $185 — a monthly cost of $765.
After the readjustment, part-time and limited rates were both raised to $101.25 — which “gets us very close” to the cost of after-school care, Wimmer said.
Department spokeswoman Tracy Mercer did not say if such a drastic change for families’ payments was intentional or an oversight by the department. The tiered approach, she said, is a “responsible use of program dollars.” Some providers have called for the state to cover full-time enrollment no matter how many hours children attend.
“Program dollars should not cover significant periods when a child is not receiving care,” Mercer said. “CCA funds are limited, and the department has a responsibility to use those dollars as effectively as possible so they can stretch to serve as many eligible families as possible.”
The state estimated the weekly, tiered payment plan would cost the state $3 million more overall before rolling it out — money that would benefit providers and families across the state. The expected increase was within the department’s budget, Mercer said. The department did not immediately share an updated estimate with the readjusted rates.
Overall ‘revamp’ still needed, provider says
Wimmer said there are staffing and overhead costs outside of a child’s physical attendance. Her program runs at school sites, requiring staff to arrive before the school day ends to transform cafeterias into program spaces. Other off-site providers need staff to drive to a school, wait and then transport children to the off-site care location.
$10 million settlement over online gaming child exploitation will fund safety, after-school efforts

“The market for childcare is just not set up where a part-time rate payment works very well,” Wimmer said.
Wimmer said she expects the department will ultimately have to “revamp the whole model,” because part-time and limited rates for younger children still don’t reflect what it actually costs providers to operate and leave too many costs for providers and families to absorb.
Mulder, the lawmaker, said he heard criticism of the change from after-school providers and families. He did not hear from childcare providers for younger children or their families in the Sioux Falls area. Nor did he hear from suburban or rural after-school programs.
The department will begin its next market rate survey this fall. The department plans to update rates in fiscal year 2028.
Mercer said the department “remains open to receiving additional feedback” on the new payment model from other childcare providers.
Governor candidates react
South Dakota Democratic nominee for governor Dan Ahlers said in a news release that the fallout from the rate change “should never have happened in the first place.” The readjustment is not enough, he said.
Ahlers serves as president of the Dell Rapids before- and after-school program, where he said state funding decisions can “put enormous pressure on providers and families.”
Childcare providers already struggle to balance worker wages, affordability for families and quality care for a service that is “essential to our economy, our workforce and the future of our communities,” he added.
“As governor, I will work with parents, providers, employers and communities to make quality childcare more affordable for families and help providers remain viable,” Ahlers said.
Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden, Ahlers’ opponent in the Nov. 3 election, told South Dakota Searchlight that the Department of Social Services addressed “some of the immediate concerns” of families and providers.
“We’ll continue to peel these issues off as they come and work for solutions for whatever it might be,” Rhoden said, “but I’m pretty happy with the way that our team has responded so far, and we’ll continue to try and respond appropriately on issues as they come forward.”
Billy Mawhiney, with the South Dakota Afterschool Network, said any changes should increase access and affordability, not reduce it.
“If kids are going to an after-school program, their grades will be higher, their self esteem will be higher, their reading scores and math scores — everything we want for a child is going to improve,” Mawhiney said. “The better opportunity, more affordability and more access we can get for after-school care, the more South Dakota kids will have access to a better life.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s population of primary care doctors is declining
description:
A new Vermont Department of Health census gives a snapshot of a dwindling population of primary care docs and a steady increase of specialists statewide.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s population of primary care doctors is declining.
text:
Vermont continues to lose its primary care doctors — but the rate of loss is slowing, a new survey from the state’s department of health shows.
In 2024, Vermont had 529 people working as primary care providers; last time the Department of Health conducted its survey in 2022, 569 physicians practiced primary care in Vermont. Even that figure represented a decline from the 634 practicing primary care when the survey began in 2004.
“I don’t think this is shocking, really, to anyone. It’s not the first time we’ve seen this trend, and unfortunately, we haven’t done enough to make the trend change,” Vermont Health Commissioner Dr. Rick Hildebrant said in an interview.
Primary care doctors are also working fewer hours. The Department of Health calculated that Vermont has the equivalent of 402 full-time primary care clinicians. Only 39% of primary care doctors in Vermont work full time (which the department counts as 40 patient-facing hours for 48 weeks of the year). In 2014, it was 42%.
Hildebrandt is “very concerned” about the trend. “Efforts to address this are not happening fast enough,” he said.
At the same time, Vermont has seen a steady increase in specialists — a broad umbrella that encompasses most other physicians like anesthesiologists, orthopedic surgeons and emergency medicine doctors. 
State leaders want to better recruit and retain Vermont’s stock of primary care physicians. Access to primary care physicians remains a struggle for many Vermonters, who wait long periods of time for an appointment, if they’re able to connect with a clinician accepting new patients. Advocates for expanded primary care access often cite an example from Oregon, where every dollar invested in primary care yielded $13 in savings for services like emergency and specialty care. 
When patients have continuous relationships with their primary care doctor, it can significantly reduce the need for hospitalization and emergency care. They play a role in screening and prevention, explained Jessa Barnard, the executive director of the Vermont Medical Society, and they also play an essential role in coordinating a patient’s care through various specialists.
“It’s that trusted relationship over time with somebody who can help you navigate all of those systems,” she said.
Vermont is not alone in the decline. According to the health policy site KFF, the U.S. has a shortage of more than 15,600 primary care providers — a calculation based on the ratio of population to providers, which federal regulations say should be at least one doctor per 3,500 people. A 2025 study in the Annals of Family Medicine found that, since 2017, rural areas in particular had experienced an 11% year-over-year decrease in the number of practicing family medicine doctors.
In Vermont, however, KFF calculates that the state’s shortage could be solved by simply adding two more primary care docs — a reflection of how small the state’s population really is.
“Vermont actually has a higher per-capita number of primary care providers than almost every other state,” Green Mountain Care Board member Thom Walsh said in an August meeting discussing Vermont’s healthcare workforce initiatives. “The country has a shortage so our numbers overall are lower.”
Still, he noted that “access (to care) has been insufficient for a lot of Vermonters,” but simply increasing the number of more providers does not necessarily improve access for Vermonters to see them.
“A felt shortage can be due to a numerical insufficiency or a structural throughput problem. Both feel on the (patient) end like an access problem, but distinguishing between a numeric shortage and a throughput problem is important,” he said. “Simply adding more numbers on a throughput problem doesn’t fix the throughput problem.”
Getting the number of family physicians to population size right is a tough balance for a small state. Primary care doctors can have anywhere between 1,000 and 3,500 patients under their care.
It’s a conundrum Sen. Ginny Lyons, D-Chittenden Southeast, who chairs the Senate’s healthcare committee and has championed primary care access, hopes this census can help shed light on. 
“That report will help us look at geographic distribution needs, population-based needs, demographic-based needs,” she said. “The question about the (right) ratio of patients to docs is an important one, both for specialists and for primary care.”
Both Orleans and Washington counties saw a declining ratio of full-time primary care doctors, though a number of other counties saw that ratio actually increase, with population shifts.
Doctor demographics
Part of the family medicine decline could be because primary care is often provided not by doctors, but by nurse practitioners, physician assistants or other “advanced practice providers,” which are not included in this census. 
Yet, the same shift away from primary care and into specializations is true in those professions, too, according to Barnard. 
She also underscored that the Department of Health census tracks a sharp uptick in hospitalists, a specialization the department didn’t track until 2014.
“Hospitalists weren’t even really a thing several decades ago,” she said. Instead, family doctors would follow their patients into the hospital, if needed. But it has become harder for doctors to manage outpatient clinic loads and also see patients in the hospital — and thus, the need for hospital-specific general medicine practitioners.
Barnard also noted that emergency medicine has seen some of the largest gains in population, despite being one of the highest burnout specialties. Maybe it’s a reflection of people working shorter shifts in the emergency department, she said, or maybe it’s a reflection of higher volumes of patients coming into the emergency room. 
It’s hard not to map the larger trends in medicine onto the data; that as fewer Vermonters are able to see a primary care physician regularly — or at all — the more likely they are to show up in an emergency room. It’s a trend that’s associated with higher costs of care, too. 
Vermonters and their doctors are both getting older. Statewide, about 30% of primary care doctors are over 60, a trend most pronounced in the most rural parts of the state. 
Another demographic trend is that more and more women are working as primary care doctors, a proportion that outpaces the proportion of women working as specialists.
Barnard suggested the broader decrease in primary care providers’ hours might be linked with the increase of women working in the specialty.
National data shows that women are significantly more likely than men to cut back their hours the further they get from medical training, often because they are bearing the responsibility for childcare or the care of aging parents. 
Barnard hopes that looking at the data will prompt Vermont to make careers in medicine more compatible with the needs and schedules of caretakers.
One way of doing that could be reducing the hours of paperwork and chart notes physicians have to fill out outside of their patient-facing hours. Many doctors see the advent of AI notetakers as a groundbreaking tool to lessen that administrative load and give them more time to devote to patients in the clinic.  
“Through most of my career, I have known and have experienced concerning trends in medicine in general and in primary care, without any real light,” Hildebrant, the commissioner of health, said. “I have seen a light for the first time in my career in the last five years with some of the AI tools that will empower our clinicians to stop spending more than half of their day staring at a computer screen.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s population of primary care doctors is declining.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Ethics panel: WA lawmaker broke no rules trying to thwart challenge from fellow Democrat
description: Washington Democratic state Rep. Tarra Simmons tried hard to keep fellow Democrat Daria Ilgen from running against her this year. It didn’t work. The two will face off in November’s general election after she soundly beat him in the primary. Moreover, Simmons’ aggressive efforts to deter Ilgen did not violate state ethics laws as a […]
text:
The state Legislative Ethics Board found no evidence Rep. Tarra Simmons, D-Bremerton, violated any ethics law in her effort to keep Democrat Daria Ilgen from running against her. (Photo courtesy of Legislative Support Services)Washington Democratic state Rep. Tarra Simmons tried hard to keep fellow Democrat Daria Ilgen from running against her this year.
It didn’t work. The two will face off in November’s general election after she soundly beat him in the primary.
Moreover, Simmons’ aggressive efforts to deter Ilgen did not violate state ethics laws as a local Democratic Party leader had formally alleged.
That’s politics, concluded the state Legislative Ethics Board in dismissing the complaint against the Bremerton lawmaker earlier this month.
“It does not seem to be an ethics violation for a legislator running for re-election to request that a potential opponent not file to run against that legislator,” the board ruled. “There is insufficient evidence to indicate that (Simmons) was using her legislative position to try to convince Mr. Ilgen to drop out of the race.”
Val Torrens, chair of the 23rd Legislative District Democrats in Kitsap County, filed a complaint Jan. 8 accusing Simmons of breaching ethics rules by using her legislative position to pressure a private citizen for “personal political benefit.” 
The ethics board discussed it July 27, and its written opinion is dated Aug. 13.
“It’s frustrating to see people weaponize the process and waste taxpayers’ money, but I simply don’t have time to attend to the frivolous complaints of political opponents,” Simmons said Thursday morning.
Simmons is seeking a fourth term representing the legislative district that includes the communities of Hansville, Kingston, Poulsbo, Bremerton and Bainbridge Island. Ilgen is a member of the state committee of the Washington State Democratic Party.
Ilgen said in an email that Torrens acted “after reviewing messages Rep. Simmons sent me when she learned I was considering challenging her.” Ilgen’s campaign reported a $1,000 contribution from Torrens in February. A month later an amended filing showed the money coming from her husband.
“I respect the Ethics Board’s decision, but I do not regret being transparent about conduct I found alarming or, as a private citizen when the messages were received, holding my elected representatives accountable,” Ilgen said in an email. “No one should be intimidated out of participating in our democracy through threats or pressure from high-powered elected officials whom average citizens don’t have relationships with.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The decision contains excerpts of a Dec. 17, 2025 text exchange in which Simmons told Ilgen that she had “absolutely no clue” he was pondering the race.
“Is this true?” she wrote. “I would personally hope you’d challenge one of the men instead as our district deserves some diversity in gender, race, geographical location, socioeconomic status and lived experience. Anyways, I do hope that is just an awful rumor because it would be disappointing considering all the other work I had planned on doing for our district instead of spending all of my time beating you.”
Ilgen responded that he had not made a decision.
“I hear what you are saying about representation and lived experience and I take that seriously. For me, this isn’t about running against anyone but about thoughtfully considering how I could best serve the whole district,” he wrote.
In subsequent texts, Simmons suggested he consider another elected post, and alerted him that several Democratic elected officials would be reaching out to him.
“If Bob Ferguson calls you will you stop doing this? Because I worked my a** off for our district,” she said.
Simmons reportedly asked several people, including state Sen. Drew Hansen, D-Bainbridge, Rep. Greg Nance, D-Kitsap, Kitsap County Commissioner Christine Rolfes, and Suquamish Tribe chair Leonard Forsman, to talk with Ilgen about his potential candidacy.
Ilgen told ethics board staff that he was aware “because many of them, in turn, contacted him to let him know they had been contacted,” according to the decision.
Simmons made no secret of her desire not to be primaried by Ilgen. And her actions came up at the legislative district Democrats’ meeting on Feb. 26.
“I don’t see anything remotely resembling an ethics act violation in any of this,” Hansen said, according to an excerpt included in the ruling.
He said that while he wouldn’t have expressed himself the same way as Simmons, he interpreted her response to the intraparty challenge as “this is somebody who I thought was a friend, I have heard you are going to primary me, I am very hurt by that, (and) would you change your mind if I have the following people who I know who have positions of influence in the Democratic Party explain to you why that’s a bad idea.” 
“That’s not harassment, intimidation, bullying,” he added. “That’s campaigning.”
Meanwhile, in an unrelated case, the Legislative Ethics Board, in a decision dated Aug. 14, fined Simmons $15,000 for improperly using her position to steer public funds to a nonprofit where she worked, and trying to retaliate against the person who filed the original complaint against her in February 2025.
The nine-member board issued its finding after conducting a trial-like proceeding into the allegations in June. The board will soon issue a final order that could require Simmons pay some or all of the state’s $37,000 in legal costs. 
Simmons adamantly denies wrongdoing and has said she plans to appeal.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Scott Colom has a ‘puncher’s chance’ against Cindy Hyde-Smith in Senate election
description: Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom speaks with attendees at an event held at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026.
text:
Mathematically speaking, Democrat Scott Colom’s chances of defeating Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy-Hyde-Smith this November might be underestimated.
Many prediction markets give Democrats a near even money chance of capturing the Senate in the November midterm election, based on surprising polling numbers in usual red states including Texas, Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. 
But neither those prediction markets nor the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee are counting on Mississippi being a state that helps put the Democrats over the top.
Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, left, listens as U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins speaks during Hyde-Smith’s reelection campaign launch at the Mississippi Agriculture Museum in Jackson on Thursday, Aug. 28, 2025.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Granted, the odds are far from favorable for Colom, a district attorney from Lowndes County, to upset Hyde-Smith, who was appointed in 2018 to the Senate by then-Gov. Phil Bryant after Thad Cochran stepped down. This is her third election campaign since the appointment.
The reasons Colom is considered a long-shot are many. Mississippi last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1982, and the last Democratic governor was elected in 1999. A Democrat has not won a statewide election in Mississippi since 2015, when Jim Hood was reelected as attorney general.
In addition, a U.S. senator from Mississippi has not been defeated since 1942. From an historical standpoint, things don’t look good for Colom
And on top of everything else, it is not clear how many votes independent Senate candidate Ty Pinkins, a former Democrat, will siphon from Colom. Pinkins could erase the slight chance Colom has.
But let’s consider a path forward for Colom with the assumption that Pinkins’ impact will be minimal.
Based on recent election results, there is a mathematical path forward – at least the proverbial puncher’s chance – for a Colom victory.
The outcomes of the two most recent statewide elections – the 2024 U.S. presidential election and the 2023 gubernatorial election – provide a roadmap for Colom and his supporters.
In the 2024 general election, 1,228,008 Mississippians voted and gave Republican Donald Trump a sizable 60% to 38% victory over Democrat Kamala Harris. The turnout will be less in this November’s midterm. History tells us it will be much less.
But perhaps turnout in a midterm election could equal that of the 2023 Mississippi gubernatorial election, when some 821,000 people voted. In that election, Republican incumbent Tate Reeves held on to defeat Northern District Public Service Commissioner Brandon Presley 51% to 48% or by a mere 26,619 votes.
Every election is different, but some patterns do emerge.
Granted, these are big ifs, but it is reasonable to assume that the turnout this November will be similar to that in the 2023 gubernatorial election – higher than most federal midterm elections but less than a presidential election.
And if that is the case, it is not far-fetched for Colom to find 27,000 more votes, or enough to put him over the top.
Consider the possibility that national polls are correct and the enthusiasm among Democratic and Democratic-leaning voters is much higher than that of Republican voters. A recent national poll indicates that Trump is underwater – more unpopular than popular– in every state except Idaho, Wyoming and West Virginia. His approval rating in Mississippi is minus 15, according to the YouGov polling tracked by The Economist.
Still, where does Colom find 27,000 additional votes if, indeed, the 2023 gubernatorial election is the benchmark?
In just five larger counties, – Hinds, Rankin, Harrison, Madison and DeSoto – if the Democratic turnout is similar to the 2024 presidential election in Mississippi, Colom could easily garner 30,000 votes. That is not even taking into account whether he could make similar inroads in other larger counties, such as Lee, Lowndes, Forrest and others.
Heck, just in DeSoto County in northwest Mississippi, 14,000 more people voted for Harris in 2024 than voted for Presley in the 2023 gubernatorial contest.
Can Colom convince the people who came out to vote for Kamala Harris in 2023 to go to the polls in November and vote for him?
If Colom can gain a margin closer to the 2024 Democratic turnout and Republicans vote at their traditional midterm election numbers, Colom can win. He does not need to equal the turnout Harris received in 2024. He just has to be considerably closer to it than to the Presley turnout in 2023.
Sure, it is a big if, but mathematically speaking, it is possible.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Who Trump’s immigration crackdown is really hurting
description: This story was originally published in Down from DC, a Substack newsletter by Phoebe Zerwick and Natalie Jennings. It’s reprinted here with permission. One of the biggest stories of President Trump’s second term is his often violent crackdown on immigration. According to CBS News, enforcement surged this summer, with an average of 1,500 people taken […]
text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer's badge and weapon are seen during a vehicle checkpoint on Georgia Ave. in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 30, 2025. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)This story was originally published in Down from DC, a Substack newsletter by Phoebe Zerwick and Natalie Jennings. It’s reprinted here with permission.
One of the biggest stories of President Trump’s second term is his often violent crackdown on immigration. According to CBS News, enforcement surged this summer, with an average of 1,500 people taken into custody daily in July, including at routine check-ins at immigration offices, airports and traffic stops. And more than half of those detained last month had no criminal history, which means no pending charges or past convictions, Austin Kocher, a researcher at Syracuse University, reported this week.
We’ve been tracking how the crackdown has played out in our state since we first started publishing a year ago. As regular readers know, I am not a neutral observer. While we haven’t seen large-scale public raids here since Operation Charlotte’s Web last fall, the enforcement efforts haven’t stopped. But they are being carried out more quietly. According to an analysis by NC Local, data through March shows that enforcement picked back up earlier this year, with more than 6,300 immigrants detained during Trump’s second term.
Helen Parsonage, via EMPLawfirm.com
Down from DC recently spoke with Helen Parsonage, an immigration attorney based in Winston-Salem, to better understand the nitty gritty of immigration law and its impact on immigrant communities and workplaces in NC.
Helen moved to the United States more than 30 years ago from England with her husband, a biochemist, and landed in Winston-Salem in 1991. When her boys started school, she began working as a paralegal with a local immigration firm and soon went to law school at night, motivated by her own experience navigating our complicated immigration system. She now represents many of the North Carolinians caught up in the crackdown.
She had intended to wind down her practice this year, but when Trump was re-elected, she knew that an escalation in immigration enforcement was coming.
“And those who know me, particularly those who live with me, will confirm that I’m stubborn and hard-headed and I was not going to quit,” Parsonage said. “So now I’m working full-time, probably more hours than I was before, because I’m pigheaded and I’m not going to walk away.”
The conversation below, edited here for length and clarity.
Phoebe Zerwick: At the end of last month, immigration agents arrested 13 people at a swimming hole in the Pisgah forest that’s popular with families. According to news reports, it was the first ever coordinated raid involving the Forest Service and local sheriffs, at least in North Carolina. Are you representing anyone detained there and what do you make of the raid?
Helen Parsonage: I’ve spoken to a couple of folks about the Pisgah Forest incident. I’ve always been a great fan of the National Park Service and the National Forests. So it was particularly disappointing to see folks from the National Forest Service participating in this when I never really thought of their role as anything even tangentially related.
I spoke to one young man who had no criminal history. I think several people there were picked up because they had an old deportation order that may have been on appeal or they may have been going for check-ins. I have not heard anything to indicate that anybody in those 13 people were “the worst of the worst.” No rapists, murderers or anything like that.
I really don’t know why this raid was conducted except as a scare tactic, because this is one place where you might think you were safe. ICE likes to find easy targets. This was an easy target.
Wilson Creek in Pisgah National Forest, the site of the July 26 immigration raid. Credit: Sasha Schroeder/NC Local
Phoebe Zerwick: There’s a closed down private prison in the northeast corner of the state called Rivers Correctional. We first reported on negotiations between the owners and ICE to reopen for immigration detention. The New York Times just confirmed that the prison will reopen this year for around 1,400 detainees.
I’m curious about several things. First of all, whether having a local detention center will increase arrests in North Carolina and, also, whether or not in some ways a nearby facility might make it easier for the families of those detained who now have to travel all the way to Georgia or further to see loved ones.
Helen Parsonage: Well, it’s clearly not meant to substitute for taking people to Georgia. This is all part of the increased capacity. And if it’s got space for 1,400 immigrants, I guarantee you it’ll be over capacity fairly quickly. It’s also very convenient for parts of Virginia, so I imagine it will serve that area as well. I’m concerned about these older facilities being reopened almost certainly without proper upgrades and improvement. Profit margin is the driving force — these are for profit prisons so every corner they can cut increases their profit margin. Rivers has been closed, I think, for a significant period of time and I think there were some concerns about its state of repair when it closed down. So I’m not optimistic that the upfit will have been anything other than the minimum.
Phoebe Zerwick: What do you hear from your clients who are in some of these privately run detention centers about the conditions?
Helen Parsonage: There are things like lack of privacy. Most of these places are dorm-type.
But the two things I hear most about are food and medical. The food is substandard even by jail or prison standards. The bologna sandwich is ubiquitous. There is insufficient food, particularly given that most of the folks they detain are adult men who have the highest calorie need and they’re not getting those. I hear a lot of concerns about lack of respect for dietary restrictions, whether religious or cultural. I have a client in detention right now who does not eat beef for religious reasons. So if there is beef in the meal, they just take it out. There’s no substitute. You may just get the bread bun.
And then access to medical care. Everybody’s hearing the extremes, but the clients I’m thinking of, one needs a special diet because he has a medical condition that makes it hard for him to absorb nutrients. This lady who does not eat beef is insulin-dependent. They’re just not taking care. Every time I see the clients, they look a little thinner.
Phoebe Zerwick: And remind us, have these two individuals committed crimes?
Helen Parsonage: No.
Phoebe Zerwick: What are they detained for?
Helen Parsonage: One was living in New Bern, North Carolina, and had a pending affirmative asylum claim. He had a work permit, a driver’s license. He was working as an imam in the local mosque and was getting medical treatment from a clinic there. He was the victim many years ago in his home country of numerous gunshot wounds. He was picked up on false allegations following an argument and rather than allowing him to face his accuser and potentially get the charges dismissed, he was whisked away to Georgia where he has been ever since. His special diet has been discontinued. He’s in pretty poor health. It’s hard to keep his spirits up. That’s half my job these days – trying to help keep people’s spirits up while they’re in detention and encouraging them that there may be light at the end of the tunnel.
The other lady was a green card holder for years. She traveled outside the United States to visit her father who was dying. It was the end of his life and those things don’t run on schedule. So she ended up outside the United States for seven months, which is over the six month presumptive. When she got back, they accused her of abandoning her green card. Now in past decades it would be like getting a traffic ticket, saying “Okay show up to the court on such and such a day.” But this time they have her in detention.
Phoebe Zerwick: People fleeing persecution and violence can come to this county and apply for asylum. Can you explain what the new asylum rules mean and how that’s playing out in North Carolina?
Helen Parsonage: Let me tell you how it used to work. If you came to the United States seeking asylum, you would file your asylum application with the asylum office, which is part of U.S. Customs and Immigration Service and has nothing to do with the court system or the deportation system.
You would be interviewed by an asylum officer, a non-adversarial interview, potentially with an interpreter and your attorney, if you have one. The asylum officer’s role has traditionally been to ask the right questions so that somebody who’s got a valid asylum claim could provide the information that the officer needed to approve and grant asylum. If the asylum officer felt there was insufficient information or there were inconsistencies, or if the person had filed their asylum claim late, the officer could refer the case to an immigration judge, which is an adversarial hearing: there’s a prosecutor there, cross-examining, trying to find inconsistencies.
What this administration has just done is said that the asylum office can send people to the deportation court without conducting an interview. So the asylum officers are more than happy to shift their backlog of cases over to the immigration court. I am not sure how the immigration court system feels about that. They’re already backlogged. This is just taking one silo of cases and moving them somewhere else. Under this administration, we’re seeing court asylum grant rates of about 6 or 7 percent. Which is a staggering drop. [Before] it varied from court to court and judge to judge, but the national average was closer to 40.
The asylum seekers I represent cover the full range of humanity because they’re from different backgrounds, different cultures, different education levels, everything from somebody who only has a second grade education all the way through to professionals in the medical and legal profession in their home countries. I can tell you that asylum seekers have a pretty low criminal rate. Immigrants have a lower rate of committing crime than the native-born American population anyway. But it’s even lower among asylum seekers.
Phoebe Zerwick: Until last month’s raid in the Pisgah Forest, we hadn’t seen large-scale public raids since the wave of arrests last fall in Charlotte and Raleigh. Still, the numbers of detentions are up and they seem to be happening way more quietly, out of public view. What are you seeing in North Carolina in terms of where people are getting arrested and what they’re being arrested for?
Helen Parsonage: I think the change in leadership at the Department of Homeland Security had something to do with that, the departure of Greg Bovino and his theatrics. People were not happy with what they were seeing, so I think that it is quieter.
There’s a number of different ways they’re trying to meet their numbers. One is that they are trying to pick up individuals at their check-ins. These typically are people who have a pending case or something on appeal who are doing check-ins with ICE. In North Carolina, everybody goes to Charlotte for their check-ins. What I’m seeing is most of them are people who’ve got maybe a final order that is on appeal, mostly men. They are also picking up people at traffic stops. Getting yourself into one of our county jails is a really good way to have ICE come across you and detain you. Regardless of what happens in the criminal case, even if the charges are dropped or they’re found not guilty, they’re still taking folks, which didn’t used to happen. A misdemeanor larceny is something that gets charged a lot of times based on either a misunderstanding or a falling out. It can be whatever, people call the police. They’re often dismissed or not guilty. But once somebody is in jail, it’s almost impossible to get released because ICE is taking people directly to Georgia. ICE likes easy targets. County jails are easy for them because people are being held there.
I have not heard of any incidents at Charlotte airport, though I’m advising clients to be very cautious about going to airports because TSA is clearly sharing passenger lists with ICE and some airlines are cooperating and others are not. So, you want to figure out which airline you’re going to fly with if you absolutely have to fly.
Phoebe Zerwick: The legislature here in North Carolina passed new laws earlier this year requiring local law enforcement and some state law enforcement to cooperate with ICE. How is that playing out in North Carolina?
Helen Parsonage: All of this is anecdotal, but from my experience the one way in which we’ve seen it is magistrates at the jails giving bond and ICE being alerted that people are there. The bond form that the magistrates fill out now has a question about immigration status. That is not a legal assessment that most of our magistrates are equipped to make. They’re getting it wrong both ways.
Phoebe Zerwick: With all those public raids in North Carolina and of course in Minneapolis, a lot of people were appalled by what they were seeing, and a lot of people in North Carolina trained to be ICE observers, myself included. I’m curious about what the legal ramifications are for American citizens who document what ICE agents are doing.
Helen Parsonage I think there’s two separate questions there. What are the legal ramifications, what are the practical ramifications?
From a legal standpoint, it’s fairly clear. Do not physically interfere with ICE officers or police officers, but it’s well established that you can video and film them.
That said, some of the officers do not take kindly to being videoed and we’ve all seen occasions where they will do everything from snatching the phone to slamming observers to the ground, pepper spraying.
Are there personal risks? Yes. So that’s something everybody has to figure out for themselves and we’ve seen the extremes that they will go to with people observing.
Phoebe Zerwick: And are there legal risks for employers who prevent immigration agents from entering workplaces?
Helen Parsonage: So, they can’t come into private spaces without a warrant. So I’ve been advising employers to put “employees only” signs up, to have a clear divide. I tell them, if it’s an area I can’t go into then ICE can’t. So I can go into a restaurant and sit but I can’t just willy-nilly wander back into the office or into the kitchen. Restaurants and public places like that do have the right to refuse service to anybody they choose. And I’ve seen some rather gratifying videos of ICE officers being politely but firmly required to leave restaurants and cafes and had service refused them. And that’s something that can be done and it’s growing as people are seeing that that can work.
Phoebe Zerwick: And what about churches? Can churches still offer sanctuary?
Helen Parsonage: Sanctuary is an interesting word because sanctuary as a legal concept has not existed since 1515. It’s a moral concept and it is one that even in those cases that we had here in North Carolina of individuals in sanctuary as we called it, it relied on kind of a gentleman’s agreement between DHS or between immigration services and the community that they would not force their way into a church to snatch somebody out. The optics are not good. I think that’s why they’re still not doing it. That would be a bridge too far for most people. It doesn’t stop them waiting outside, of course, but I’ve not seen them do that.
Phoebe Zerwick: An issue that’s gotten a lot of attention recently is the decision by the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold the president’s decision to rescind temporary protected status for Haitians and Syrians, which has consequences for immigrants from more than a dozen counties. How is that playing out in North Carolina?
Helen Parsonage: Well, what it’s really hurting are businesses. Obviously, it’s hurting the individuals. All of a sudden, after many years, their work permits have just been cut off. You’ve gone from being in lawful status to having no lawful status. It shows you the hypocrisy of this administration because it’s always about people should do it the right way and people should get their legal status and what they’re doing is actually turning tens of thousands of lawful residents of the United States into undocumented immigrants. A lot of them have been established professionals. I know individuals who are working in our finance system and banking, individuals who are working in optometrist’s offices, people who are working in schools, people who’ve been working in hospitals and not just as nurses but as physicians and physicians assistants and social workers.
Everybody thinks when they talk about mass deportations and picking people up that we’re going to lose construction workers and agricultural workers and we certainly are in some places. But we’re also losing school teachers, doctors, lawyers, professionals, finance folks, all kinds. I’m having clinics call me up saying that they’re losing qualified staff and so it’s impacting patient care.
Phoebe Zerwick: This is a time of enormous confusion and fear. Back last fall, immigrant families were afraid to send their kids to school. What’s your sense of what they’re going through with all of this uncertainty?
Helen Parsonage: Folks are very afraid of being detained or having a loved one detained. They’re particularly afraid for somebody if they’ve got any kind of medical condition because everybody’s reading about folks who are not getting medical treatment and, in several horrific cases, have passed away in immigration detention through neglect.
I think a lot of folks are looking for reassurance. They’re hunkering down. Everybody’s a little more cautious about where they go. But it’s a very resilient community, so I don’t want to give the impression that they’re cowering in fear somewhere. These are folks, many of whom have been through much worse in their home countries or to get here. Many of them have lived with being undocumented for many years or decades even. They don’t need me to tell them how to cope with this. I can try and help them if the worst happens. I can do small things to protect people just in terms of legal strategy to try and minimize the risks. But most of these folks have lived with uncertainty for most of their lives.
This story was originally published in Down from DC, a Substack newsletter by Phoebe Zerwick and Natalie Jennings. It’s reprinted here with permission.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Democrats finalize nominations, continue calls for unity heading into November
description: Michigan Democrats on Saturday gathered to finalize their nominations for several key offices as the party shifts its members into gear for the Nov. 3 general election. The Michigan Democratic Party held its 2026 nominating convention at the Lansing Center, where it formally nominated its candidates for lieutenant governor, secretary of state, attorney gener[...]
text:
Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, at the Michigan Democratic Party's nominating convention on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Michigan Democrats on Saturday gathered to finalize their nominations for several key offices as the party shifts its members into gear for the Nov. 3 general election.
The Michigan Democratic Party held its 2026 nominating convention at the Lansing Center, where it formally nominated its candidates for lieutenant governor, secretary of state, attorney general, the State Board of Education, University of Michigan Board of Regents, Michigan State University Board of Trustees, Wayne State University Board of Governors and State Supreme Court. 
While the party’s spring endorsement convention showcased the divisions between the party’s more moderate and progressive wings — and its divide over Israel’s war against Gaza — party leadership and nominees at Saturday’s event preached a message of unity against rising costs and President Donald Trump’s administration. 
As Democrats look to defend their control of the governor’s seat, the attorney general’s office and the Department of State, in addition to flipping Republican seats in Congress and the Michigan Legislature, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel stressed to attendees, “If you’re waiting for the cavalry to come, we are the cavalry. 
While some Democrats, like Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, said they planned to forgo the convention out of concerns of harassment and antisemitism, Hertel circulated a message to party members in the days leading up to the gathering emphasizing that “disruptive behavior or harassment of any kind will not be tolerated.”
Ultimately, the nomination process proceeded without disruption, though the convention held more than a few empty seats which grew in number as nominations continued.
Party delegates nominated Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) to run alongside Michigan Secretary of State and Democratic nominee for governor Jocelyn Benson, formalizing Benson’s selection for a running mate.
The Michigan Democratic Party’s 2026 nominating convention at 4:15 p.m. on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
While accepting the nomination Brinks pointed to her 13 years of experience serving in the Michigan Legislature, including the last three, where she’d served as the state’s first female Senate Majority Leader. 
“Together, we delivered historic change, cutting taxes for working families and seniors, guaranteeing free breakfast and lunch for every Michigan school student,” Brinks said. “Protecting reproductive freedom and LGBTQ rights, strengthening gun safety laws, restoring workers’ rights, and investing in clean energy. But Michigan Democrats, I am here to tell you I am not done yet.”
Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) accepts the Michigan Democratic Party’s nomination for lieutenant governor at the party’s nominating convention in Lansing on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
The party also nominated Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist for secretary of state and Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit for attorney general. Both Gilchrist and Savit pledged to stand against the Trump administration if elected.
“I want to be really clear about this moment, about the stakes and what we face. Donald Trump is coming for our votes and our election system in the State of Michigan,” Gilchrist said, noting that just this week the U.S. Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, had allowed an executive order restricting mail-in voting to move forward. 
The executive order remains blocked under a separate court ruling.
While the U.S. Department of Justice has sought access to Michigan’s voter rolls which contain information such as voters’ birthdates, driver’s license info and Social Security numbers, Gilchrist told delegates that when he is elected “your data will belong to you and not the federal government.”
“That data doesn’t belong to Donald Trump,” Gilchrist continued. “It doesn’t belong to his political appointees, and it is not theirs to use as a weapon against the people of the state of Michigan. As your next secretary of state, I will stand tall in between this administration and Michigan voters every single time they try to interfere with your rights and our elections.”
Michigan Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist accepts the Michigan Democratic Party’s nomination for secretary of state at the party’s nominating convention in Lansing on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Savit said Democratic attorneys general across the nation have stood up to the Trump administration, recovering federal funding that otherwise would have been eliminated by the federal government. 
“What I can tell you is this: as Attorney General, I will stand up for the people of the state of Michigan, each and every time any president violates the law and hurts us, and that includes attacks on our right to vote,” Savit said. 
The party also nominated its candidates for the Michigan Supreme Court, State Board of Education and the governing boards of the University of Michigan, Michigan State University and Wayne State University. 
Delegates re-nominated Judith Pritchett and Tiffany Tilley for State Board of Education. 
For the university boards Amir Makled was nominated to serve on the University of Michigan Board of Regents, while Regent Paul Brown was renominated. The party also nominated MSU trustees Kelly Tebay Zemke and Brianna Scott for another term. For Wayne State, the party nominated Shereef Akeel and Richard Mack. 
The Michigan Democratic Party also nominated Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh and Justice Noah Hood for reelection to the supreme court.
Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh accepts the Michigan Democratic Party’s nomination for re-election to the state supreme court at the party’s 2026 nominating convention on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
El-Sayed aims to mend fences with Jewish Dems, apologizes for Temple Israel comments
In the weeks since the primary election, Michigan Democrats have stood divided over the party’s Senate nominee, former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed, who secured a narrow primary victory against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) with just under 1% of the vote.
El-Sayed’s criticism of Stevens over her connection to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, his opposition to the U.S.’s support Israel – which he, along with multiple international organizations, says is committing genocide in Gaza – and his previous decision to campaign with the controversial streamer Hasan Piker, have alienated some Jewish Democrats. 
While speaking with reporters on Saturday, El-Sayed noted that while meeting with the Michigan Democratic Party’s Jewish Caucus Saturday, he was asked about comments he’d made in the wake of the attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield Township, in which a gunman drove a Ford F-150 into the synagogue before dying of a self-inflicted gunshot wound during an exchange of gunfire with security.
El-Sayed condemned the attack, but stated that “Hurt people, hurt people,” noting that the gunman’s family had lost family members in an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon.
“My comments might have been misconstrued to be justifying something I did not intend to justify,” El-Sayed said. “To anybody who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I’m really sorry that was not my intention. We condemned that terrorist attack. We condemned it outright. What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn’t the time for context. And you don’t ever want to trample somebody’s pain.
Abdul El-Sayed takes questions from reporters at the Michigan Democratic Party’s nominating convention on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
However, when asked about Jewish Democrats’ concerns over his ties to Piker, El-Sayed shut down the question.
“We’re in the state of Michigan,” El-Sayed said. “If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you’re missing the boat. This is about affordability in Michigan. This is about being able to see a doctor in Michigan. This is about Donald Trump’s disastrous policies in Michigan. That’s what I’m focused on right now. I am not interested in a conversation about a social media person in California.”
While El-Sayed met with the party’s Jewish Caucus on Saturday and he told reporters he would continue having conversations with Jewish Democrats. 
They may not agree on everything, El-Sayed said. While he believes deeply in equal rights, peace, dignity and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike, El-Sayed said he would not stop fighting for Palestinian self-determination, arguing that the money the U.S. has spent supporting Israel’s military should have been spent in the United States.
“People get real mad about that, I understand,” El-Sayed said. “But that does not mean that I will not stand up forthrightly for safety for all communities, and I believe in the safety and the dignity of Jewish kids like I believe in the safety and dignity of my own kids.”
Are Michigan Dems United?
Closing out the convention, El-Sayed and Benson each offered remarks to rally attendees, though they did not appear on stage together.
When speaking with reporters after her speech Benson was met with a crucial question that Democrats face heading into the general election: “Are Democrats united right now?”
“We are united around our vision of lowering costs to the people of Michigan, of fighting corruption, of ensuring that we have people-driven leaders at every slot in this ticket. And I think that’s what you heard a lot from today,” Benson said. “We’re all singing the same song, all talking about the same thing, particularly when it comes to health care, ensuring everyone has access to affordable, accessible care.”
When another reporter pressed her on that answer, Benson re-stated that Democrats are singing the same song. 
“I do believe we’re all talking about raising wages, driving down costs, and I think you know what I love about democracy and what I believe in is a true multiracial, multiethnic, multifaceted democracy is that we all have space to be our own individuals while also fighting for the same things for the people and for what the people of Michigan need,” Benson said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma prison inmates operated political, insurance calls centers behind bars
authors: Keaton Ross, Oklahoma Watch, J.C. Hallman, Oklahoma Watch
description: When Oklahoma inmate Steve Wilbanks spoke to a reporter by phone in late July, it had been six weeks since he worked in a prison call center, placing calls on behalf of insurance companies attempting to poach business from competitors and making political calls as primary elections were underway across the country. “I had good […]
text:
The exterior of Joseph Harp Correctional Center in Lexington is pictured on Friday, Oct. 13. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)When Oklahoma inmate Steve Wilbanks spoke to a reporter by phone in late July, it had been six weeks since he worked in a prison call center, placing calls on behalf of insurance companies attempting to poach business from competitors and making political calls as primary elections were underway across the country.
“I had good numbers,” Wilbanks, who is incarcerated at the James Crabtree Correctional Center in Helena, said. “I was a producer.”
Wilbanks was one of four inmates who spoke with reporters about the call center work. Contracts obtained via an open records request confirm that a company called HBW Leads and the Oklahoma Department of Corrections have established several call centers since January. As of Aug. 21, call centers are active at four state prisons: James Crabtree in Helena, Mabel Bassett in McLoud, Lexington Correctional in Lexington and Joseph Harp in Lexington.

The contracts specify that the call centers may engage in “telemarketing and political polling activity.” HBW Leads agreed to pay the Department of Corrections $10 per inmate hour worked. Prisoners employed at the call centers earn $2 per hour, plus possible bonuses for generating leads or completing surveys.
The remaining $8 per hour is allocated as overhead for Oklahoma Correctional Industries, a self-supporting sub-entity of the Department of Corrections that provides work programs and job training to inmates.

Three of the four Crabtree inmates, whose identities were independently confirmed, requested anonymity for fear of retribution.

“They definitely know what they’re doing is a no-no,” one of the inmates said.
The inmate described calls that resemble push-polling, in which the caller masquerades as a pollster but intends to influence voters. Several polling and marketing organizations denounced such tactics.
Wilbanks said there were statements specifying that calls were paid for by Make Liberty Win, a Virginia-based super PAC that aims to help elect conservative lawmakers.
“They weren’t surveys at all, they were campaigning,” he said. “They just had one question at the end of the call: ‘Do we have your vote for such and such?’”
Multiple inmates said they felt uneasy making partisan phone calls. Two indicated that they had been in prison so long that they were not familiar with the names of political candidates. One was unsure what MAGA or a Trump Republican was.
“We were talking about the swamp and everything like that,” Wilbanks said. “I don’t even know what a swamp is. I’ve been in prison too long to catch up on some of these terms.”
The Department of Corrections refused multiple interview requests for this story. In an emailed statement, an agency representative wrote that the calls that inmates described in interviews, including advocating for candidates, fall within the contract description of political polling. The representative added that the agency regularly reviews call center material to ensure compliance with state and federal law.
 RINOs and Democratic Socialists
Founded in Oregon, HBW Leads was acquired by Toledo, Ohio-based Double A Solutions in 2020. In January 2025, HBW Leads launched a separate entity called Visible Trends, which specializes in live calling for political campaigns. Both share a physical address at an office in Ohio.
Federal Election Commission records show that Make Liberty Win has paid Visible Trends almost $600,000 since March for political calling services. Most of the money went toward state legislative races, though the PAC also paid the company to make phone calls supporting Thomas Massie, the Republican congressman from Kentucky who lost a primary election in May.
The super PAC touts its ability to engage in direct voter contact for state legislative candidates.
“We go directly to the voters’ doorsteps, cellphones, and mailboxes to mobilize them to oust RINOs and socialist Democrats alike,” reads Make Liberty Win’s mission statement.
Barrett Young, executive director of Make Liberty Win, said the organization was unaware that Visible Trends used prison labor. He said the super PAC recently terminated its contract with the vendor due to poor performance. Make Liberty Win’s most recent payment to Visible Trends was dated June 29.
As descriptions of calls made across the country — Connecticut, Kentucky, Ohio, Florida — turned to Oklahoma, the inmates provided, without prompt, prominent names on the recent Oklahoma election landscape: Gentner Drummond, Mike Mazzei, Jon Echols, Chip Keating, Justin “J.J.” Humphrey.
“I only did a few Drummond, and a few J.J. Humphrey,” one inmate said. “Mostly it was Mazzei, because he was Trump-endorsed, I guess.”
No Oklahoma candidate has reported paying Visible Trends for campaign work during the 2026 election cycle, according to reports filed with the Oklahoma Ethics Commission. Similarly, no outside group has reported payments to the company, though KFOR-TV reported that some organizations have not compliedwith state reporting requirements.
 800 Calls Per Day
It’s not the first time that prison call centers have been established in Oklahoma, for political calling or otherwise.
In 2019, The Intercept published a report detailing direct payments from the presidential campaign of former New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg to a third-party vendor operating a call center at Eddie Warrior Correctional Center in Taft. The campaign said it was unaware that its vendor used prison labor and severed ties with the company after the reporter’s inquiry.
In 2021, a James Crabtree inmate serving eight life sentences for child sexual abuse succeeded in obtaining full internet access through a call center job and downloaded child sexual abuse material from his work computer. He received two additional life sentences for the offense in August 2022.
Oklahoma prison call centers were temporarily shut down after the scandal but were never abolished. In 2023, prison officials said they had instituted new safeguards to restrict inmate internet access and were considering relaunching the program.
The new call centers, which are not listed as Oklahoma prison businesses on Oklahoma Correctional Industries’ website, appear to be an expansion of Oklahoma prison call center operations.
The inmates described the scope and conditions of the call centers.
The center at James Crabtree was average for call centers, Wilbanks said, describing a relatively clean space with 120 cubicles equipped with computers and dialing systems. At first, they worked from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., then hours were expanded to 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., Wilbanks said.
The inmates said they made as many as 800 calls per day, of which 500 might connect. Of those 500, perhaps 20 calls would be passed off to a waiting insurance agent after key information was obtained. Information visible to inmates on their computer screen included names, addresses, phone numbers, and current insurers.
“If you get everything right on the paper, get all the information from the customer, you get the birthday, and the email address, it’s like a $2 bonus,” one inmate said.
On political calls, the inmates said only names and phone numbers were visible.
Wilbanks said inmates could also be subject to penalties if they missed quotas or failed to meet managers’ expectations.
Reached by phone to respond to the inmates’ claims, a representative from Visible Trends said “no comment” and hung up. Executives for HBW Leads did not return messages seeking comment.
 ‘Threw Me For a Loop’
Prison telemarketing is a few decades old. Prison political calls date to at least the 1990s, when a Washington–based organization employed inmates to place calls on behalf of a congressional candidate.
“Leading up to the November 1994 election, WMG prisoner telemarketers called voters in Republican congressman Jack Metcalf’s congressional district to conduct a phony ‘opinion poll’ designed to inform voters that Metcalf supported the death penalty while his opponent did not,” said a 1998 Prison Legal Newsreport.
Prison telemarketing has its champions. Call center organizations cite reduced recidivism rates, durable and transferable skills, and opportunities for inmates who are anxious to learn.
“Operating these programs makes it possible to help as many adults in custody as possible gain work skills and be prepared for a successful release,” reads a statement on the website of Oregon Correctional Enterprises.
By way of contrast, an ACLU report on prison labor highlighted legislation nationwide that enabled various industries to exploit workers behind bars.
“The United States has put in place a system of domestic laws and policies designed to exploit the labor of those incarcerated rather than to strengthen their capacity to productively participate in society,” the report said.
Wilbanks said he decided to leave the job because it became monotonous, but the nature of the calls left a mark.
“It was stuff like you don’t want to have your kids around creepy such and such, or they believe in transgender ideas not protecting your children,” Wilbanks said. “It’s like, whoa. That threw me for a loop there.”
Despite the concerns of exploitation, one inmate said they did not feel coerced to work at the call center.
“It’s just better money,” the inmate said. “It’s the best money on the yard.”
Oklahoma Watch, at oklahomawatch.org, is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization that covers public-policy issues facing the state.
